theme: Basket-13 catalyst funnel — event-driven special situations (diagnostic)
regime: NEUTRAL / GOLDILOCKS quadrant (macro_regime.json 2026-08-03, score 0.5975, VIX 16.03) over a DISCIPLINE debt-cycle phase (4 weeks in, high confidence; positive real long rates imposed and holding, duration punished, cash flow rewarded, expected horizon 18mo). Catalyst-Watch v4 (2026-07-20) carries the first tripwire BREACH in the doc's life - oil/Hormuz, Brent ~$89, with VIX and HY 271bp conspicuously refusing to reprice - ranks spins + forced-sellers the FATTEST lane and holds hard-binary / biotech PDUFA the THINNEST, most efficiently-priced lane for a THIRD consecutive run.
risk_stance: SELECTIVE-DEFENSIVE, floor-first. The funnel is aimed at the wrong lane: 12 of 21 names are FDA/biotech binaries - the doc's own thinnest, two-sided, efficiently-priced lane - while the fattest lane (spins/forced-sellers) arrived here as undated parent-discretion stories (BLCO, KDP, MP, PRX.AS) rather than dated events. So I demand a third-party statutory date AND a countable floor, treat the 12 biotech binaries as ONE sized bet per the doc's #4 independence rule, and refuse exposure that is really a proxy for AkzoNobel, Tencent, gold or the AI-capex tape wearing an event label. Under DISCIPLINE every name here is a story-duration bet - advisory, not a cap, but it is the honest frame.
correlation_memo:
The funnel is badly concentrated. 12 of 21 names (CAPR, EYPT, MLYS, SRRK, DBVT, AQST, WVE, AMLX, ZYME, VIR, OLMA, AVIR) are ONE shared factor - FDA/clinical risk-on-off plus biotech beta. Seating several is not diversification, it is one bet in twelve wrappers, and this run supplies the proof: CAPR (adcomm 9-3 against, floor broken by 45%) and AVIR (positive Phase 3, stock DOWN) resolved within eight days of each other, opposite on the science and the same direction on the equity. Note also the couplings the cluster label hides. EYPT and AMLX are literally the same trade shape - a fully-enrolled pivotal readout landing in the same weeks over a modelled, not countable, floor. EYPT's own re-rating case is priced off OCUL, a competitor, so a Q1-2027 SOL-R print moves it independent of its own trial; and EYPT carries an unhedged SECOND binary (LUCIA, ~2 months later) that the $35 target already assumes. VIR, OLMA and AMLX all share the same failure mode: a floor set as a multiple of net cash that each stock's own tape has already traded through.

The supposedly independent names are mostly proxies for something else. AXTA is an unhedged long of AkzoNobel plus EUR/USD - its 'floor' broke by 32% in March on nothing but the acquirer's tape, with the deal intact. PRX.AS is 75% Tencent: it moved +3.22% against Tencent's +3.20% with the discount unchanged. AAUC is gold plus African state take. BLCO is really the PARENT'S leverage and Xifaxan's 2027-28 cliff. MP looks idiosyncratic but its only in-window date is a Chinese geopolitical decision, correlating it straight into the tariff/Hormuz axis the regime doc flags as BREACHED. FIG is contractually independent but its 5 Aug print reloads exposure to the AI-displacement factor the doc names as swamping factor (i) - the same factor that took 16.5% out of it in a week on somebody else's product launch.

PUREST STANDALONE ASYMMETRIES - resolution drivers genuinely orthogonal to FDA, biotech beta, oil and AI-capex: (1) DDL, decided by China's SAMR and then by a Cayman board's distribution vote - nothing else in the funnel or the book touches either; the cleanest independent driver here even after the governance correction. (2) FIP, decided by a FERC docket and PJM market-monitor politics - a genuinely independent driver, but the common equity is the wrong instrument to express it through, sitting behind ~$3.8bn of debt and PIK-compounding preferred. (3) FIG, decided by a lock-up clock no macro variable can move - mechanically independent, though the sign is inverted and the earnings print two days earlier re-correlates it. KDP would be the fourth (staples, board-discretion spin) except it has no event at all. Everything else resolves on a factor something already in the book resolves on.
director_memo:
THE HEADLINE, ANSWERED PLAINLY: ZERO. Not one of the 21 names cleared verdict A + CRO conviction 5 + a Director score of 80 or better. Five earned verdict A from the CRO (EYPT, MLYS, ZYME, DDL, VIR); two of those carried conviction 5 (EYPT, ZYME); none reached 80, and the highest score in the funnel is MLYS at 64. The conviction-ceiling record stands - now 0 for 428.

And the reason is not that I reflexively suppressed them. The reason is that the independent skeptic REFUTED both conviction-5 names, and refuted them on the same leg: THE FLOOR. EYPT's $4.75 floor writes off the Durasert/Verisome platform in one sentence and capitalises it at ~$290m in the next; on the file's own stated method the floor is ~$2.00, turning a 3:1 into a 1:1. ZYME's $18 floor counts the same assets twice, twice over - the cash pile IS the Royalty Pharma borrowing secured on 30% of the very royalties the floor books as untouched, and the OMERS note is serviced out of the very YUPELRI profit share booked as free cash flow to equity; stripped, book equity is $2.24 a share against a claimed $1.32bn. That is the whole finding. The catalysts in both cases are genuinely live, dated and unfired - the funnel found real events. What it could not find was a real floor underneath one.

That pattern is the run's actual result, and it repeats. Fifteen of the 21 floors were broken, refuted or materially downgraded on inspection: CAPR's $7.00 broke by 45% and the residual net-cash floor turns out to have a live ~$75m ATM tap on it; FIP's $3.90 broke into the catalyst; PRX.AS's 37.365 broke; AXTA's is an uncollared claim on a Dutch share that already fell 32% below it with the deal intact; KDP's is the 200-day moving average to within twelve cents; FIG's is a level the market recently PAID; AMLX's $6 is falsified by the same management team's own 2024 tape, where an identical shell with MORE cash per share cleared at $1.62; WVE's machine-readable field overstates verified cash by 43%; and MP, BLCO, OLMA, DBVT, SRRK and VIR each had the claim ahead of equity understated or the share count under-counted. The recurring failure is not analytical pessimism - it is that a modelled clearing price is being written into a field the sizing engine reads as if it were a contract.

WHAT THE BANDS ACTUALLY DEMAND: a 90-100 needs catalyst IMMINENT plus a huge live-to-target spread plus a HARD floor. This funnel produced imminence (ZYME 22 days, EYPT and AMLX weeks, FIG four days) and it produced spreads (EYPT +186%, DBVT +152%, FIP +135%, AQST +130%). It produced hard floors essentially nowhere - because in a book made of pre-revenue biotech and undated corporate-action stories the only countable backstop is net cash, and net cash here is dilutable, burning, or behind a secured lender in almost every case. A 5 requires a dated event with a contractual payout and a break price; the one name that HAS a contractual payout, DDL, has an undated Chinese regulator in front of it and a board with 'absolute discretion' over the distribution behind it. That is the structural reason the top bands stay empty, and it matches the standing conviction-ceiling note: this shape of opportunity does not arrive from a priced tape, it arrives from a dislocation.

WHAT I WOULD ACTUALLY SEAT: one name. MLYS at 64, scaled in rather than taken at size - the only file where the skeptic's verdict was that nothing refutes the event, the timing or the floor as drawn: a statutory 22 Dec 2026 PDUFA that has not moved, no advisory committee called, into a mechanism the agency validated by approving baxdrostat on 18 May. It is a defined-ODDS bet, not a defined-RISK one, and must be underwritten as though half the capital is at risk on a single day in December. Two names earn a dated watch with a specific trigger rather than a price: DDL on whether the US$280m reaches the parent by 31 Aug 2026 (which repairs the floor and restores 2:1 at the same price), and SRRK on either a print near $40-42 or confirmation that the second fill-finish site cleared a product-specific pre-approval inspection. Nothing else earns capital today.

REGIME FIT: the Catalyst-Watch doc has held hard-binary/PDUFA the THINNEST lane three runs running, and this funnel is 12/21 hard-binary. The doc's fattest lane - spins and forced-sellers - arrived here as BLCO (six years, three abandoned routes, gate receding), KDP (no Form 10 anywhere in the SEC universe, no CEO), MP (first output 2028) and PRX.AS (the forced sale was in someone else's shares). The funnel is fishing the thin lane and mislabelling the fat one. Two dated hazards land inside 72 hours and belong on the board: AAUC's Q2 print on 5 Aug - missing from its file entirely, with the net loss WIDENING as gold rose on a US$290m tax charge - and FIG's double binary of 5 Aug earnings into the 7 Aug lock-up release.

ONE PROCESS FIX, worth more than any single seat: stop writing modelled clearing prices into downside_floor. CAPR, FIP, PRX.AS and FIG all broke a published floor this cycle, and in three of the four the field was a chart level - a 52-week low, a 200-day average, a recent print - dressed as a backstop. Either that field carries only contractually or balance-sheet countable value, or it carries a verified/modelled flag the sizing engine can read. A floor that breaks by 45% is a valuation error, not bad luck.

AAUC.bull_thesis:
State the conclusion first: the takeover this position was built on is gone, so the bull case is no longer a spread to a contracted price. It is now a bet that Allied Gold is a genuinely cheap gold producer whose biggest asset has not yet started.

The facts that support it are real and recent. On 29 July 2026 Zijin Gold walked away from buying the whole company at C$44.00 a share in cash, but on the same day it agreed to put US$295 million of new money in, subscribing for about 12.8 million shares at C$32.55 each for roughly 9.2% of the company, with rights to top up its stake later. That subscription price is about 28% above where the shares trade today at US$18.23. A buyer who has spent months in the data room chose to invest rather than leave, and Allied's Chairman and Chief Executive and its Vice Chairman voluntarily locked up their own shares alongside it. That closing is expected on or about 10 August 2026 and needs only routine Toronto and New York exchange consents.

Operationally the company is delivering. It produced 97,429 ounces of gold in the second quarter, up about 7% on the same quarter of 2025, and 193,445 ounces in the first half, tracking full-year guidance of 385,000 to 425,000 ounces from the existing mines. All-in sustaining cost, the industry's fully loaded cash cost per ounce sold, is expected to be below US$2,200 against a realized gold price of roughly US$4,380 an ounce, leaving a cash margin over US$2,100 per ounce. Reserves at Agbaou rose more than 60% over the 2025 year-end estimate, lifting that mine's life to 2030, and the Cote d'Ivoire complex now underwrites at least 200,000 ounces a year for more than ten years, raised from 180,000.

The step-change is Kurmuk in Ethiopia. Management says operations start in August 2026 with first gold a few weeks later, on budget and on schedule, and guides Kurmuk to 240,000 to 270,000 ounces in 2027 and roughly 300,000 ounces in 2028 at what it calls industry-leading costs. Adding that to the existing mines takes the company toward roughly 650,000 to 690,000 ounces a year in 2027, from a first-half rate near 390,000 annualized. Pro-forma for the Zijin money, cash is about US$485 million against roughly US$248 million of debt, so the balance sheet carries net cash of about US$237 million and no long-term borrowings.

For this to work, three conditions must hold: Kurmuk must start on time and ramp without a metallurgical surprise; the gold price must stay near current levels long enough for two or three quarters of visible cash generation; and Mali must leave Sadiola alone. If all three hold, a re-rating toward the mid-twenties needs no takeover at all. If Beijing's posture on large outbound acquisitions later softens, Zijin's 9.2% stake and top-up rights make it the obvious renewed bidder, and C$44 is the anchor it has already accepted.
AAUC.bear_thesis:
The bear case starts from what already happened rather than what might. The event failed. On 29 July 2026 the two companies terminated the arrangement agreement, stating there was no reasonable likelihood the closing conditions would be satisfied by the 29 July outside date or within any reasonable time after it, and they agreed not to extend again. The cause was described as broader external factors applicable to cross-border transactions of this scale, meaning the Chinese approval never arrived. The shares fell 18.3% in one session, from US$20.84 to US$17.03. There is no break fee payable to Allied, so the structural floor that normally bounds a broken deal does not exist here.

Strip out the takeover and what is left has been losing money at record gold prices. Over the trailing twelve months to 31 March 2026 the company earned about US$1.37 billion of revenue and roughly US$301 million of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and US$210 million of pre-tax income, yet a US$290 million income-tax charge produced a net loss of about US$124 million, or US$1.05 a share. That is the eighth consecutive quarterly loss. Cash margins per ounce look outstanding; almost none of it reaches the bottom line, because African tax regimes, state free-carried interests and minority partners take the difference. Any valuation built on cash cost margin rather than on money that actually reaches a shareholder is overstating this business.

Jurisdiction is the deeper problem. Sadiola in Mali produced 92,184 ounces in the first half, roughly 48% of group output, in a country whose 2023 mining code has already been used against a peer major, with gold stock seized and staff detained. Management devoted a section of the 29 July release to rebutting media commentary about security matters in host nations, insisting they are effectively managed and that operations continue without interruption. Companies do not write those paragraphs when nothing is being said. A Mali action would remove nearly half of current production and most of the perceived floor.

Cash is also tighter than the headline suggests. The balance fell from US$425.6 million at 31 March to about US$190 million at 30 June, consumed by Kurmuk capital, tax payments and working capital, a US$236 million drain in a single quarter. The Zijin money refills it, but that is a 9.2% dilution and it is being spent on commissioning a new mine in Ethiopia. Kurmuk has not yet poured an ounce; the 2026 contribution guidance of 100,000 to 150,000 ounces is already being withdrawn for restatement once operations begin.

Finally, ownership has turned over violently. Merger arbitrage funds, who bought a contracted payout, are sellers of an operating gold miner; the 3.9 million shares traded on 31 July against a 696,000-share average is that handover in progress. What confirms the bear case: a Kurmuk commissioning slip past September, a gold price below roughly US$3,600, or any Malian administrative action at Sadiola. Any one of those takes the shares to the low teens, and there is nothing contractual to stop it.
AAUC.sop_bull:
Event-win value of about US$31.50 a share, which is the terminated Zijin price of C$44.00 converted at the current exchange rate of roughly 1.395 Canadian dollars to the US dollar. This is no longer reachable through the original agreement, which was terminated on 29 July 2026; it is reachable only two ways. Either Zijin, which now owns 9.2% with top-up rights and has already accepted C$44 as fair, returns with a renewed offer once Chinese outbound-transaction policy allows, or the company delivers Kurmuk and re-rates to a normal multiple on its own.

Built from the parts, on 2027 as the first full year with Kurmuk: existing mines roughly 400,000 to 420,000 ounces at an all-in sustaining cost near US$2,100 an ounce, plus Kurmuk at 240,000 to 270,000 ounces at a materially lower cost, call it US$1,250. That is about 660,000 ounces at a blended cost near US$1,780. At a US$4,380 gold price the cash margin is roughly US$2,600 an ounce, or about US$1.7 billion, less around US$80 million of corporate overhead and exploration outside the cost measure and roughly US$45 million of interest, leaving about US$1.6 billion of pre-tax operating earnings. Capitalising that at 2.5 times, a deeply discounted multiple that reflects West African political risk, gives an enterprise value of about US$4.0 billion. Adding pro-forma net cash of about US$237 million and dividing by the 139.3 million shares outstanding after the Zijin placement gives roughly US$30.50 a share. The C$44 anchor and this build agree at about US$31. Contributions: existing Cote d'Ivoire and Mali mines about US$17, Kurmuk about US$12, net cash about US$1.70.
AAUC.sop_bear:
Verified downside floor of about US$13.00 a share. Our board carried US$17, but that figure is simply where the shares closed on the day the deal broke, not a floor with anything behind it. There is no break fee and no cash election, so the only genuine backstop is the asset base at a stressed gold price with the Mali risk realised.

The build: assume Sadiola, 92,184 ounces in the first half and about 48% of production, is heavily impaired under a Malian administrative action of the kind a peer major has already suffered. What remains is the Cote d'Ivoire complex at roughly 200,000 ounces a year and Kurmuk at roughly 250,000 ounces, about 450,000 ounces at a blended all-in sustaining cost near US$1,700. At a stressed gold price of US$3,800 an ounce that is a cash margin of about US$945 million, which after the local tax take, state free-carried interests and minority partners leaves roughly US$450 million attributable. Capitalising at 3.5 times gives about US$1.58 billion of enterprise value, plus pro-forma net cash of about US$237 million, or US$1.82 billion of equity across 139.3 million shares, which is about US$13.05 a share.

Contributions in this case: Cote d'Ivoire complex about US$7.50, Kurmuk about US$3.80, net cash about US$1.70, Mali written to zero. Note that this floor is an estimate of value, not a contractual minimum, and it would break further if gold fell below roughly US$3,400 or Kurmuk's ramp disappointed.
AAUC.sop_breakdown:
Base case is a probability weighting of three outcomes, not a single model. A renewed control transaction at roughly US$31.50 carries about a 20% chance: Zijin holds 9.2% with top-up rights and has already accepted C$44, but the blocking factor is geopolitical, outside either party's control, and both companies stated on record that conditions would not be met within any reasonable time. A standalone re-rating to about US$26 carries about 55%, and requires only that Kurmuk starts as guided in August 2026 and that two or three quarters of visible cash generation arrive at a gold price near US$4,380. A stress case at about US$13.00 carries about 25%, driven by Malian action at Sadiola or a gold price retreat. That weighting gives 0.20 x 31.50 plus 0.55 x 26.00 plus 0.25 x 13.00, or about US$23.85, which we round to US$23.50.

The cross-check is reassuring: Zijin is subscribing at C$32.55, about US$23.33 at 1.395, which sits almost exactly on this base case. A strategic buyer with full diligence access is writing a cheque at our reconciled fair value.

Parts contributing to the base case, per share on the 139.3 million shares outstanding after the placement: Cote d'Ivoire complex (Bonikro and Agbaou, 101,261 ounces in the first half, reserves extended to 2030) about US$9.00; Sadiola in Mali (92,184 ounces in the first half, carried at a heavy political discount) about US$5.50; Kurmuk in Ethiopia (starting August 2026, guided to 240,000 to 270,000 ounces in 2027) about US$7.30; pro-forma net cash of roughly US$237 million about US$1.70. Total about US$23.50.
AAUC.risk_reward:
Roughly one to one on the base case, and about two and a half to one measuring the best case against the floor. From US$18.23 the upside to the reconciled fair value of US$23.50 is about 29%; the downside to the verified floor of US$13.00 is about 29%. Measuring instead to the renewed-bid case of US$31.50 gives 73% up against 29% down, or about 2.5 to 1, but that outcome carries only about a 20% probability and no date.

This is materially worse than the 1.27 our board carried, and for a specific reason: that figure was computed against a US$31.50 target that was a contracted cash price and a US$17.00 floor. As of 29 July 2026 the contract is void, so the target is now a hope rather than a claim, and US$17 was never a floor at all, merely the closing price on the day the deal broke. Adjusting both inputs to what can actually be verified takes the asymmetry from attractive to ordinary.
AAUC.catalyst_summary: The takeover fired and failed: Allied Gold and Zijin Gold terminated their C$44.00-a-share cash arrangement on 29 July 2026 when Chinese cross-border approval never came, and the shares fell 18.3% in a day; what replaces it is a US$295 million Zijin minority investment at C$32.55 closing about 10 August 2026 and first gold at Kurmuk in Ethiopia within weeks, leaving roughly 29% upside to a US$23.50 fair value against 29% downside to a US$13.00 floor that nothing contractual protects.
AAUC.dated_milestone: 29 July 2026: arrangement agreement terminated, outside date not extended (verified in Allied Gold's Form 6-K filed 29 July 2026, Exhibit 99.1). On or about 10 August 2026: Zijin Gold's US$295 million subscription for about 12.8 million shares at C$32.55, roughly 9.2% of the company, is expected to close, subject only to Toronto Stock Exchange and New York Stock Exchange approval. August 2026: Kurmuk mine start of operations, with first gold a few weeks thereafter, on budget and on schedule per the same filing. Second-half 2026 production guidance to be restated once Kurmuk operations commence.
AAUC.forcing_function:
The transactional catalyst is spent, so the only thing left that can force a re-rating is operational: first gold at Kurmuk, guided for August 2026 with pour a few weeks after start-up, followed by the restated second-half guidance the company has promised once operations commence. Kurmuk is guided to 240,000 to 270,000 ounces in 2027 and roughly 300,000 ounces in 2028 at industry-leading costs, against 193,445 ounces for the entire company in the first half of 2026. If it starts on time and the first two quarters of consolidated cash flow show the blended cost falling as promised, the market has to price a company producing well over 600,000 ounces rather than under 400,000.

A secondary and much smaller trigger is the 10 August 2026 closing of Zijin's US$295 million subscription. It puts a fresh, publicly disclosed strategic price of C$32.55 on the shares, roughly 28% above the market, and removes any financing question over the Kurmuk ramp. It pays existing holders nothing directly.

There is no date behind the outcome that would matter most, a renewed Zijin offer. Both companies stated on 29 July that the conditions would not be satisfied within any reasonable time, and the obstacle is Chinese policy toward large cross-border acquisitions, which neither company controls. Assigning that a date would be invention.
AAUC.consensus_delta:
The market and this position were both wrong, in opposite directions, and only one of them has corrected. Through July the shares traded around US$20.85 while the contracted price was about US$31.50, implying the market gave the deal roughly a five-in-a-hundred chance of closing. Our board still carried the full US$31.50 as the target and US$17.00 as the floor. The market was right and it has now been proved right: the agreement was terminated on 29 July 2026.

Where a genuine disagreement remains is on what the company is worth without the deal. The market is marking the shares at US$18.23. Zijin, which spent months inside the data room, is subscribing at C$32.55, about US$23.33, for a 9.2% stake it cannot sell for four months and a day. Those two prices cannot both be right. Our read is that the selling is mechanical rather than informed: merger arbitrage funds bought a contracted payout and are now holding an operating African gold miner they were never mandated to own, and the 3.9 million shares that traded on 31 July against a 696,000-share average is that handover.

The second disagreement is on earnings quality, and here we side with the sceptics rather than the bulls. Management leads with a cash cost below US$2,200 an ounce against a realized gold price near US$4,380, which sounds like an enormous margin. But over the trailing twelve months the company turned US$210 million of pre-tax income into a US$124 million net loss because of a US$290 million tax charge, the eighth consecutive quarterly loss. Anyone valuing this on cost margin per ounce rather than on cash that actually reaches a shareholder is making the same error twice over. The correct disagreement to hold is narrow: the shares are probably too cheap against a strategic's own fresh cheque, but nowhere near as cheap as the operating margins make them look.
AAUC.valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months carry three specific hazards, and the position has no contractual protection against any of them.

First, the cash trough is real and only just being refilled. Cash fell from US$425.6 million at 31 March 2026 to about US$190 million at 30 June, a US$236 million drain in one quarter, consumed by Kurmuk construction capital, normal-course tax payments and working capital. The company is commissioning a new mine on a thinner balance sheet than at any point this year. The US$295 million from Zijin, expected on or about 10 August, restores it to roughly US$485 million against about US$248 million of debt, but until that closes there is no buffer, and the money is earmarked for the Kurmuk ramp, the Sadiola expansion and Cote d'Ivoire production increases rather than for shareholders.

Second, commissioning risk. Kurmuk is guided to start in August with first gold a few weeks later. New mines slip; metallurgy disappoints; ramp curves stretch. Management has already said it will restate the 2026 contribution, previously 100,000 to 150,000 ounces, once operations commence, which is an honest signal that the number is uncertain. A slip past September would leave the company with a spent balance sheet, no new production and no deal.

Third, and most severe, Mali. Sadiola is roughly 48% of current output and sits under a 2023 mining code that has already been used against a peer major, with gold stock seized and executives detained. Allied felt it necessary on 29 July to publish a rebuttal of media commentary on security matters in its host nations, asserting that they are effectively managed and that operations continue without interruption. That may be entirely true, and the operating record supports it, but the need to say it at all is the risk. A Malian administrative action would remove half the production base in a single announcement.

Behind all three sits the gold price. At roughly US$4,380 an ounce the cash margins are extraordinary. The entire floor in this analysis assumes gold no lower than about US$3,800. Below roughly US$3,400 the floor does not hold.
AAUC.positioning_washout:
The forced selling is happening now and is the clearest short-term feature of the tape. A merger arbitrage shareholder base bought one thing, a contracted C$44.00 cash payout with a defined date, and on 29 July was handed something else entirely, an equity position in a mid-tier African gold producer. Most such funds have mandates that do not permit holding it, so the selling is mechanical rather than a judgement about value.

The evidence is in the volumes. Against an average of about 696,000 shares a day, 3.19 million traded on 29 July as the shares fell 18.3% to US$17.03, then 927,900 on 30 July, then 3.90 million on 31 July as the price recovered to US$18.23. Heavy volume with a rising price on the third day is the signature of a handover: arbitrage sellers meeting value buyers, rather than a one-way liquidation.

Two things cushion it. Zijin's 12.8 million subscription shares are locked for four months and a day under Canadian rules, and the Chairman and Chief Executive and the Vice Chairman voluntarily matched that lock-up. So roughly 9.2% of the enlarged register plus the largest insider holdings are immobilised into December 2026. That removes supply rather than adding it.

The offsetting risk is index and rating flow. The shares were added to a strong-sell screen on 21 July, and a busted transaction typically triggers a round of estimate withdrawals and coverage resets. Expect the arbitrage exit to be substantially complete within a few weeks, but do not expect a natural long-only buyer base to form until Kurmuk has actually poured gold.
AAUC.moderator_conclusion:
The honest verdict is that this seat no longer holds the investment it was underwritten for. Allied Gold came into the book as a merger arbitrage: a contracted C$44.00-a-share cash price, roughly US$31.50, with a hard outside date and what looked like a bounded loss. On 29 July 2026 both companies terminated the agreement, stating there was no reasonable likelihood the conditions would be met by the deadline or within any reasonable time after it, and agreed not to extend. The cause was Chinese approval for a cross-border deal of that size, which never came. The shares fell 18.3% in a session. There is no break fee payable to Allied. The spread did not narrow; it ceased to exist, and no amount of residual quality changes that this particular event has resolved and resolved badly.

What is left is a genuinely interesting company that belongs in a different lane. Zijin walked from the takeover but immediately committed US$295 million for 9.2% at C$32.55 a share, roughly US$23.33 and about 28% above today's price, closing on or about 10 August with only routine exchange consents outstanding, and it took top-up rights to stay pro-rata. Allied's own Chairman and Chief Executive and its Vice Chairman locked up their shares beside it. Operationally the company is executing: 97,429 ounces in the second quarter, up 7% year on year; 193,445 ounces in the first half against 385,000 to 425,000 ounces of full-year guidance; cash costs below US$2,200 against a realized gold price near US$4,380; Agbaou reserves up more than 60%. And Kurmuk, the Ethiopian mine that roughly doubles the growth profile, starts within weeks, on budget and on schedule.

Against that sit two facts that keep us honest. The company has now posted eight consecutive quarterly losses at record gold prices, because a US$290 million tax charge on US$210 million of pre-tax income is what African operation costs; the cash margin per ounce is not the shareholder's margin. And nearly half of current production sits in Mali, under a mining code already used against a peer major, in a country where the company found it necessary to publicly rebut commentary about security. That is why our floor is US$13.00 rather than the US$17.00 the board carried, which was only the closing price on the day the deal broke, with nothing behind it.

Reconciling the parts gives a base-case value of about US$23.50 a share, which lands almost exactly on Zijin's own subscription price of US$23.33, a satisfying cross-check from a buyer with full diligence access. From US$18.23 that is 29% up against 29% down to the floor, roughly one to one. For a dated-event sleeve that is not enough. Pass for now, and retire the seat. If the residual value case is wanted, and there is a real one, it should be re-underwritten as an operating gold producer with a first-gold catalyst in August, not carried forward as a spread that no longer exists.
AAUC.interrogator_dossier:
# Allied Gold Corporation (AAUC) — Forensic Dossier on the Event

*Prepared 3 August 2026. All facts below are sourced to filings with the U.S. Securities and
Exchange Commission (SEC) or company press releases, with dates given.*

## The headline finding, stated plainly

**The takeover is dead.** On 29 July 2026 Allied Gold and Zijin Gold International jointly
terminated the arrangement agreement under which Zijin was to buy all of Allied for C$44.00 a
share in cash — roughly US$31.50, which is exactly the target price our board was carrying. The
two companies concluded there was "no reasonable likelihood that the conditions relating to
completion of the Transaction will be fulfilled by the outside date of July 29, 2026 or within
any reasonable time thereafter," and mutually agreed **not** to extend the deadline again. The
stated cause was "broader external factors applicable to cross-border transactions of this
scale" — the polite formulation for the Chinese outbound-investment approval that never came.

The merger-arbitrage spread this position was built on no longer exists. It did not narrow; it
vanished. Any analysis that still treats US$31.50 as a reachable, contractual payout is working
from a stale board.

**Source:** Allied Gold Corp, Form 6-K filed 29 July 2026, Exhibit 99.1 (accession
0001171843-26-004981 / -004980), and the company's release of the same date.

## 1. What actually happened, in sequence

| Date | Event | What it told us at the time |
|---|---|---|
| 29 May 2026 | Zijin receives approval under the Investment Canada Act; Allied announces the Canadian approval process is "complete" and **extends the outside date to 29 July 2026** | Progress on the approval that was never the binding constraint; silence on the one that was |
| 10 June 2026 | Allied states both parties "remain fully committed to fulfilling the conditions for completion... by the extended outside date of July 29, 2026" | A confidence statement seven weeks before the deal died |
| 27 July 2026 | Stock trades at US$20.85; third-party commentary notes the market was pricing roughly a 5% chance of completion | The market had already voted; the company had not updated its language |
| 29 July 2026 | **Arrangement agreement terminated.** Concurrently, Zijin signs a subscription agreement for a US$295 million minority stake | The event resolved — against holders |
| 29 July 2026 | Shares close at US$17.03, down 18.3% from US$20.84 the prior session | The break was repriced in a single day |
| 31 July 2026 | Shares close at US$18.23 on 3.9 million shares (roughly 5.6x the 696,000-share average) | Partial recovery on heavy volume — arbitrage funds exiting, value buyers arriving |

### The consolation prize, and what it is worth

Zijin did not simply walk away. On the same day it agreed to subscribe, through a non-brokered
private placement, for approximately **12.8 million Allied common shares at C$32.55 each**, for
gross proceeds of roughly **US$295 million (about C$417 million)**, leaving it with about
**9.2%** of the company. Three details matter:

- **The price is a real, third-party mark, but a backward-looking one.** C$32.55 is stated in
  the filing to be the 30-day volume-weighted average price on the Toronto exchange as of 27
  July 2026 — a mechanical formula struck before the break, not an independent valuation. It
  now sits roughly **28% above** where the shares trade (C$32.55 ≈ US$23.33 versus US$18.23).
- **It is a dated, near-term event.** Closing is "expected to occur on or about **10 August
  2026**," subject only to Toronto Stock Exchange and New York Stock Exchange approval. Those
  are administrative consents, not discretionary ones.
- **It pays common holders nothing.** This is a capital raise, not an exit. It dilutes existing
  holders by about 9.2% at a price above market — which raises net asset value per share
  modestly — and hands the company US$295 million of cash. Zijin gets participation and top-up
  rights to hold its pro-rata stake, and the shares carry a four-month-and-a-day Canadian hold
  period. Allied's Chairman and Chief Executive and its Vice Chairman voluntarily locked up
  their own shares for the same window.

**No termination fee is disclosed as payable to Allied.** The termination was mutual and by its
terms, so the usual break-fee backstop that bounds a busted-deal position is absent here.

## 2. Is there still a real, dated, binding catalyst?

Only in a much smaller sense, and it is operational rather than transactional.

- **Binding and dated (low value):** the 10 August 2026 closing of the US$295 million placement.
  Near-certain, but it is a financing, not a re-rating event.
- **Dated but not binding (high value):** **Kurmuk**. Allied's new Ethiopian mine is guided to
  "start of operations expected in August and first gold following a few weeks thereafter,"
  on budget and on schedule, per the 29 July release. This is the genuine forcing function.
  Kurmuk is guided to produce 240,000–270,000 ounces in 2027 and roughly 300,000 ounces in 2028
  at what management calls industry-leading costs — a step-change against 193,445 ounces
  produced across the whole company in the first half of 2026.
- **Undated and speculative:** a renewed Zijin bid. Zijin now holds a 9.2% foothold with top-up
  rights and has demonstrated it wants the asset at C$44. But the obstacle that killed the deal
  is geopolitical and outside either company's control, and both sides went out of their way to
  say the conditions would not be met "within any reasonable time." Assigning this a date would
  be fabrication.

## 3. Management credibility — split verdict

**Operationally, they have delivered.** Second-quarter production of 97,429 ounces was up 7%
against the same quarter of 2025 and in line with plan; first-half production of 193,445 ounces
tracks the 385,000–425,000-ounce full-year guidance for the producing mines. All-in sustaining
cost — the industry's fully loaded cash cost per ounce sold — is expected to come in below
US$2,200 for the quarter against a realized gold price of roughly US$4,380 an ounce, a margin of
more than US$2,100 per ounce. Reserves at Agbaou rose more than 60% over the 2025 year-end
estimate, extending that mine's life to 2030, and Bonikro's life was previously extended. That
is a credible operating record.

**On the transaction, the communication was one-sided.** Allied publicised the approval it had
obtained (Canada, 29 May) and reiterated commitment to the 29 July deadline as late as 10 June,
while the approval it actually needed remained unresolved. That is not misrepresentation — the
Chinese decision was not Allied's to make or to disclose — but investors reading only the
company's releases would have been materially more optimistic than the market was. Anyone sizing
this position off management's tone rather than the tape was hurt.

**A related governance tell:** on 30 July, one day after the break, Allied filed an update
conceding that during the deal "it was initially determined that a shareholder meeting would not
be required given the expectation of a closing of the transaction beforehand," and that board
refreshment discussions were not possible. The company has now committed to nominating at least
20% women to the board at the 2027 annual meeting and 30% at the 2028 meeting. In plain terms:
the pending sale was used as a reason to defer normal shareholder governance for a half-year,
and that deferral is only now being unwound.

## 4. The verified downside floor — and why it is softer than the board assumed

Our board carried a floor of US$17. That number is the post-break trading print (the 29 July
close was US$17.03), not a floor in any structural sense. There is no cash-election, no break
fee, and no collateral behind it. What genuinely backstops the price is the operating asset base
and the balance sheet:

- **Balance sheet (hard).** Cash was approximately US$190 million at 30 June 2026, down from
  US$425.6 million at 31 March, drained by Kurmuk construction capital, tax payments and working
  capital. Adding the US$295 million placement takes pro-forma cash to roughly US$485 million
  against about US$248 million of total debt — net cash of roughly US$237 million, or about
  US$1.70 a share on the 139.3 million shares outstanding after the placement. That is real, but
  it is 9% of the share price, not a floor.
- **Producing asset base (soft).** Three producing mines plus Kurmuk. The floor is whatever the
  market will pay for those cash flows at a stressed gold price — and, critically, at whatever
  jurisdictional discount it chooses to apply.

**The floor's real weakness is Mali.** Sadiola produced 92,184 ounces in the first half, about
48% of group output, and sits in a jurisdiction where a peer major saw its gold stock seized and
staff detained under the 2023 mining code. A stress case in which Sadiola's value is heavily
impaired, leaving the Côte d'Ivoire complex and Kurmuk, supports something closer to **US$13**
per share than US$17. That is the honest floor. Note also that management felt compelled to
devote a section of the 29 July release to "Addressing Certain Commentary Related to Security
Matters in Host Nations," stating that such matters "have been, and continue to be, effectively
managed" and that operations continue "without interruption to supply chains or otherwise." A
company that must publicly rebut security commentary is a company whose floor carries a
political discount, whether or not the rebuttal is accurate.

## 5. Red flags

- 🔴 **The load-bearing event failed.** Not delayed — terminated by mutual agreement, with both
  parties on record that it will not be revived "within any reasonable time."
- 🔴 **No break fee to Allied.** The defined-risk structure that normally bounds a broken
  arbitrage position is simply absent.
- 🔴 **Eight straight quarters of bottom-line losses at record gold prices.** Trailing
  twelve-month revenue of about US$1.37 billion produced roughly US$301 million of earnings
  before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation and US$210 million of pre-tax income — but
  a US$290 million income-tax charge turned that into a US$124 million net loss, or US$1.05 per
  share. Cash margins are excellent; reported earnings are not. The gap between "all-in
  sustaining cost margin" and money that reaches a shareholder is the single most important
  number in this story, and African tax and state-participation regimes are eating most of it.
- 🔴 **Jurisdiction concentration.** Mali, Côte d'Ivoire and Ethiopia. No developed-market asset
  to anchor the valuation.
- 🔴 **A one-day 18% drawdown on a scheduled deadline.** The market knew; the company's own
  disclosure tone did not reflect it.

## 6. Green flags

- 🟢 **A sophisticated strategic is buying, not leaving.** Zijin is putting US$295 million of new
  money in at C$32.55 — roughly 28% above today's price — for 9.2% and top-up rights, days after
  walking from a full takeover. That is the most informative single data point in the file.
- 🟢 **Kurmuk arrives within weeks,** on budget and on schedule, and roughly doubles the growth
  profile from 2027.
- 🟢 **Genuine reserve growth:** Agbaou up more than 60%, mine life to 2030; the Côte d'Ivoire
  complex now underwrites at least 200,000 ounces a year for over ten years, raised from 180,000.
- 🟢 **Insider alignment:** the Chairman/Chief Executive and Vice Chairman voluntarily locked up
  their shares alongside Zijin's hold period. They were not required to.
- 🟢 **Pro-forma net cash** of roughly US$237 million, with no long-term debt on the balance sheet.

## 7. What the director must weigh

This name entered the book as a merger arbitrage with a contractual payout and a bounded loss.
It is now neither. What remains is a mid-tier African gold producer, trading at roughly US$18.23
against a strategic investor's fresh US$23.33-equivalent subscription price, with a new mine
starting in weeks and a very large, very real political discount attached to nearly half its
current production.

That may well be a good investment. **It is not the investment this seat was underwritten for,
and it carries no floor worth the name.** The correct action for a dated-event sleeve is to
retire the position and, if the residual value case is wanted, re-underwrite it in a lane built
for operating companies rather than for spreads.

This supersedes the prior AAUC shard, which reached REFUTED on the same core fact but cited two secondary sources (Bloomberg, Globe and Mail) and one broker note. Every load-bearing fact below has now been read directly out of the filings on EDGAR.

The event did not slip, it terminated, and the replacement floor does not hold. Primary source, verbatim: the Arrangement Agreement 'has been terminated effective as of today's date', both parties concluded there is 'no reasonable likelihood that the conditions ... will be fulfilled by the outside date of July 29, 2026 or within any reasonable time thereafter', and they 'mutually agreed not to extend the Outside Date further' (6-K filed 29 Jul 2026, Ex. 99.1). The stated cause 'relates to broader external factors applicable to cross-border transactions of this scale'. NO termination fee payable to Allied is disclosed anywhere in the release; the termination was mutual and by its terms. The spread did not narrow, it ceased to exist. An event sleeve is left holding an ordinary Mali / Cote d'Ivoire / Ethiopia gold miner with no contractual downside support.

The board already concedes that much (catalyst_status FIRED, moderator recommends retiring the seat). The independent kill is that the REPLACEMENT numbers fail too, in ways the file did not check:

(1) THE US$13.00 'VERIFIED DOWNSIDE FLOOR' IS NOT A FLOOR. Its own build is CDI ~US$7.50 + Kurmuk ~US$3.80 + net cash ~US$1.70. So 29% of the floor is a mine that has never poured an ounce. The stress case writes Mali to zero but simultaneously assumes Kurmuk survives intact, while the file's own valley_of_death lists a Kurmuk commissioning slip and a Malian action as CONCURRENT hazards over the same three-to-nine-month window. Joint realisation of the two triggers the file itself nominates leaves roughly US$9.20 per share, not US$13.00. A floor that assumes away one of its two stated stressors is a point estimate, not a floor.

(2) THE BASE-CASE CROSS-CHECK IS CIRCULAR. sop_breakdown validates US$23.50 by asserting 'a strategic buyer with full diligence access is writing a cheque at our reconciled fair value' at C$32.55. The filing states the opposite: 'The Subscription Price equals the 30-day volume-weighted average trading price of the Company's common shares on the TSX as of July 27, 2026.' It is a mechanical, backward-looking formula struck while the shares still carried deal hope, not a valuation opinion. The interrogator_dossier concedes this in section 1 ('a mechanical formula struck before the break, not an independent valuation'), then sop_breakdown reverses it and rests the entire base case on it. The load-bearing anchor is the pre-break VWAP validating a post-break fair value.

(3) A HARD-DATED EVENT IS MISSING FROM THE FILE ENTIRELY. The same 29 Jul 6-K states full Q2 2026 operational and FINANCIAL results release after market close on Wednesday, 5 August 2026, call 6 August, AGM 7 August. That is two days from the 3 August write date and appears in neither dated_milestone nor forcing_function. The skew is negative: verified TTM figures to 31 Mar 2026 show the net loss WIDENING as gold rose (TTM net income -US$38.5M at Q3-25, -US$51.8M at Q4-25, -US$124.5M at Q1-26) while TTM income-tax expense climbed US$146.8M to US$234.0M to US$290.1M. The African tax and state take is scaling faster than the gold price. The positioning_washout narrative ('expect the arbitrage exit to be substantially complete within a few weeks') is blind to the next hard print landing inside 48 hours.

(4) THE ONLY REMAINING RE-RATING CATALYST IS GATED ON A THIRD-PARTY STATE UTILITY. The file's commissioning risk is generic ('new mines slip; metallurgy disappoints'). The filing names the actual critical-path item: 'The Company is working closely with the Ethiopian Electric Power ("EEP") and its EPC contractor to complete and energize the power line ahead of full commissioning.' First gold depends on grid energization by an Ethiopian state utility, an unpriced dependency in a third African jurisdiction the analysis never surfaces.

Catalyst fired, spread gone, no break fee, floor breaks under the file's own concurrent stressors, base-case anchor circular, and the nearest dated event unexamined and negatively skewed. Nothing survives that a dated-event sleeve can underwrite.

ALTI.bull_thesis: The bull case is that a genuinely sale-able franchise finally transacts, and it transacts high enough to leave real money for common shareholders. The ingredients are there. AlTi Global is an independent global wealth manager with $90.1 billion of assets under advisement and $48.7 billion under management, serving more than 830 ultra-wealthy families at an average relationship of about $60 million, with 96% client retention since 2021. That is an authentic, sticky franchise. The operating trajectory is improving, not decaying: first-quarter 2026 revenue was $73 million, up 28%, with adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) of $14.9 million, up 21%, and a margin of 20% against 13% the prior quarter. Management targets $20 million of recurring annual gross savings by the end of 2026. Since December 9, 2025 the board has run a formal review with J.P. Morgan as banker and Wachtell, Lipton as counsel, and the catalyst density is unusual: three separate insiders have filed activist Schedule 13D notices. Allianz holds about 26% of the Class A stock, having bought common at $5.69 with warrants struck at $7.40; Constellation Wealth Capital holds $150 million of Series C preferred plus common with warrants at the same $7.40; and co-founder Michael Tiedemann, ousted as chief executive on March 30, 2026, holds 9.8% and has disclosed he is exploring a take-private. Those insider marks sit well above today's $3.58. For the bull case to work, three things must hold: a bidder must bridge a valuation gap that press reporting puts at more than $600 million; the price must clear the $352 million preferred stack with enough left over for the common; and it must happen before the 9.75% compounding dividend grows that stack much further. If a strategic buyer pays a full multiple for scarce ultra-wealthy distribution rather than a sponsor's cash-flow multiple, the common can reach the mid-$4s.
ALTI.bear_thesis: The bear case is not that the sale fails. It is that the arithmetic says the sale cannot succeed at a price that helps common shareholders, and that waiting costs money. Start with the capital structure, because it is the whole story. At the March 31, 2026 balance sheet, the common is worth about $529 million at $3.58, but sitting ahead of it is $352.2 million of preferred stock, plus $37.5 million of net debt. That implies an enterprise value near $919 million. Annualize the best quarter the company has printed and adjusted EBITDA is about $60 million; be generous and credit the full $20 million cost programme. The enterprise is therefore trading at roughly 15 times EBITDA. Private-equity buyers underwrite wealth managers at 9 to 13 times. At 12 to 13 times on $58 to $60 million, the whole enterprise is worth $700 to $780 million; subtract net debt and the preferred, and the common is left with roughly $2.10 to $2.65 a share. That is the reported $600 million gap, and it is not a haggle to be split. ALTI.consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is not about the business — it is about the capital structure, and we think almost nobody is doing the arithmetic. The prevailing frame treats AlTi as a cheap option on a sale: the stock is down about 64% from its $10 January 2023 listing, three activists are circling, and J.P. Morgan is running a process. The street's first error is anchoring on insider cost bases — Allianz's $5.69 common basis and the $7.40 warrant strike — as if they were valuations. They are the marks of investors who bought before the preferred compounded and before the stock halved. Sunk cost is not fair value. The second and most important error is reading the stalled process as a negotiation that patience will resolve. It is not. The $600 million gap exists because a rational buyer's multiple leaves the common at roughly $2.10 to $2.65 after the preferred is served — below today's $3.58. Neither is large on its own — the shelf is about 2.8% of the Class A count — but this is a thinly traded, poorly covered micro-cap with a float near 59.7 million shares, where modest supply moves price. Third, the operating base keeps burning at the reported line: the company has posted net losses every year since listing, most recently $119.7 million in 2025, and cash is $39.7 million against $77.2 million of total debt. The adjusted EBITDA that carries the story does not survive to the bottom line. Fourth, the franchise itself leaked assets — net client outflows of $0.2 billion in the first quarter of 2026 — and management churn compounds the risk: the co-founder chief executive was ousted March 30, 2026, the international president departed, an interim chief executive is in the seat, and a new chief financial officer took over July 1, 2026. In a relationship business, departing principals and departing assets tend to travel together. The specific event that would decimate the stock in this window is the quietest one: the special committee simply going dark, or disclosing that the review concluded without a transaction. Given the disclosed absence of any timeline, there is no date by which that risk resolves.
ALTI.positioning_washout: The shareholder base is concentrated and structurally awkward, but the mechanical selling here runs the wrong direction for the thesis. Allianz holds about 26% of the Class A stock (subject to a 24.9% ownership cap that pushes excess into non-voting Class C shares), Constellation holds preferred and common, and ousted co-founder Michael Tiedemann holds 9.8% — leaving a small, thinly traded public float of roughly 59.7 million shares with poor sell-side coverage. Our watch board tagged this a forced-seller flow on the theory that overhang clears and the price recovers. That mechanic does not survive verification. The verified supply is the Form S-3 that went effective around July 10, 2026, registering 3,053,263 Class A shares — about 2.8% of the 110.7 million Class A outstanding — for holders who took stock as consideration in the April 2023 Alvarium Wealth Management acquisition. The July 31, 2026 lapse of the Series A preferred transfer restriction, and the concurrent 30% step-down in Allianz's staged common lock-up, are likewise permissions to sell, not clearing events. The genuine mechanical pressure is the opposite one: the preferred pays part of itself in new common each period, a steady, price-insensitive issuance into a thin float. A capitulation flush toward the low-$2s on that dilution and the mid-2026 supply is plausible, but it would be the start of price discovery toward the residual's true worth, not a bottom to be bought.
ALTI.moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now. AlTi Global is a legitimate special situation -- a real, sticky franchise with $90.1 billion under advisement, 96% client retention, an improving margin, three activist filers and a J.P. Morgan mandate -- and it still fails both tests that would earn capital in this funnel.

The catalyst is soft and undated, and it is now decaying. The December 9, 2025 announcement said in terms that there is no definitive timeline; eleven months after J.P. Morgan was retained there is no buyer, no price, no drop-dead date and no vote. But the decisive evidence is what the company said itself. Asked on the May 11, 2026 call when review expenses would normalize, interim chief executive Nancy Curtin answered that AlTi is “evaluating opportunities that come as opposed to a strategic review process in place at the moment.” The formal sale process is not running. Her chief financial officer corroborated it on cost grounds -- the advisory fees “should start to diminish back half of the year” -- and advisory fees are the truest instrument for measuring whether a banker is still working. Two further markers point the same way: the June 17, 2026 annual meeting, the natural forcing window, passed with a routine slate and no contest; and the June 25, 2026 chief financial officer succession was framed as “a long-planned internal leadership transition designed to support AlTi’s next phase of growth” -- standalone language, not deal language. The arc runs from “we are for sale” to “nothing to report” to normal-course succession.

The deeper finding is why it stalled, and it is not a haggle that patience resolves. The preferred stack is the thesis. Roughly $352 million of Allianz Series A and Constellation Series C preferred -- $290 million of face accreted, each compounding at 9.75% -- sits ahead of a $531 million common, so the enterprise is capitalized near $921 million against about $58 to $60 million of normalized adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization), roughly 15 times, for an asset class that transacts at 9 to 13. Run a buyer’s real multiple and the common is left at about $2.10 to $2.65 -- below today’s $3.58. The bidders are not lowballing. Press reporting quotes a mathematical disparity between what a sponsor would pay on a reasonable multiple of AlTi’s cash flow and its market cap and enterprise value: read plainly, the buyers think the stock is already above their pay-line. The special committee is holding out for a number the arithmetic does not produce. The one structure that clears is Allianz rolling its own preferred and buying the rest -- but that makes the buyer a conflicted insider who holds the instrument capping everyone else’s value, with no disclosed majority-of-the-minority protection. The best-positioned bidder is the one most motivated to pay least.

That reframes our own board’s entry. The forced-seller flow that put this name on the list does not exist as described. What I could verify is a 3,053,263-share resale shelf effective around July 10, 2026 -- 2.8% of the Class A count, from 2023 Alvarium acquisition holders -- and a July 31, 2026 lapse of the preferred transfer restriction alongside a 30% step-down in Allianz’s common lock-up. Both are supply. The largest holder is a would-be acquirer under a standstill, not a seller, and it is accumulating through payment-in-kind dividends -- it took 1,272,328 shares on July 2, 2026. There is no overhang clearing and no washout to buy; the one hard date in the file has the opposite sign to the thesis it was filed under.

Nor is there a floor. Tangible common equity is roughly negative $550 million once $815.9 million of goodwill and intangibles comes out -- about 72% of the balance sheet is acquisition accounting. The company has never posted a reported profit: losses of $165.6 million, $103.0 million and $119.7 million in 2023, 2024 and 2025. Cash is $39.7 million against $77.2 million of debt. Nothing tangible, contractual or earnings-based stops the price. The $2.75 low is a chart reference, not a backstop.

So the asymmetry inverts: about +23% to a generous 16-times take-out at $4.40, against about -35% to $2.30 if the process lapses, with the likelier path being the bad one. And time is the adversary rather than the ally -- the rarest failure mode in this funnel. The preferred compounds at 9.75%, roughly $34 million a year or $0.23 a share, and settles part of itself in newly issued stock at multi-year-low prices, so every quarter of delay grows both the claim ahead of the common and the share count beneath it. A special situation is supposed to pay you for waiting as a dated catalyst approaches. This one charges you.

This is not a case for waiting on a flush either, which is why it is a pass rather than a watchlist item: a cheaper price would not fix a structure in which the equity sits behind a growing preferred with no floor. The honest trigger to revisit is narrow and knowable -- a signed agreement with disclosed terms that clears the $352 million preferred with room to spare. Underwrite that on the terms if it ever prints. Do not own the hope.

# AlTi Global, Inc. (ALTI) — Interrogator Dossier
**Event-driven special situation | Web-verified 17 July 2026 | Live price $3.58 | Market value of the common ~$531M**

*This pass reconciles with, and updates, the 16 July 2026 pass on this name. The verdict is unchanged and independently re-derived. Three new pieces of evidence are added in section 2, and they all point the same way: the event is decaying. One figure from the prior pass is corrected in section 3.*

## Summary judgment up front

Judge the event, not the franchise. AlTi Global is an independent global wealth manager with roughly $90 billion of assets under advisement that hired a bank to sell itself and, eleven months on, has produced no buyer, no price and no date.

Two findings carry the file:

1. **The catalyst on our watch board is mis-specified.** The board entry reads "forced-seller / forced divestiture flow," undated. There is no forced seller. The only supply event I can verify is a Form S-3 registering 3,053,263 Class A shares — about 2.8% of the 110.7 million Class A outstanding — for holders who took stock in the April 2023 Alvarium Wealth Management acquisition. That is earn-out housekeeping, not a thesis. The largest holder, Allianz, is a would-be *acquirer* under a standstill, and it is accumulating, not distributing.
2. **The preferred stack is the whole story.** Roughly $352 million of preferred, compounding at 9.75%, sits ahead of a $531 million common. Run any multiple a real buyer pays and the preferred consumes the equity. This is why eleven months with J.P. Morgan produced nothing — and it is why the spread runs the wrong way.

## 1. The event — real, well-advised, and going stale

## 2. New evidence — the company has stepped back from the process

This is what the prior pass did not have, and it matters.

**First, and most important.** On the 11 May 2026 call, a Raymond James analyst asked when strategic-review expenses would normalize. Interim CEO Nancy Curtin's answer is the most load-bearing sentence in this file:

> "Obviously, if any proposal comes to the company, to the Board, the Board will need to evaluate it consistent with its fiduciary responsibilities. CFO Mike Harrington corroborated the wind-down on cost grounds — review expenses "should start to diminish back half of the year... contingent on the process being complete."

Note the divergence between the prepared remarks ("the committee continues its work") and the unscripted Q&A twenty minutes later ("as opposed to a strategic review process in place at the moment"). The script preserves the board's optionality; the Q&A describes the actual state. When a company's scripted and unscripted accounts of the same process diverge, the unscripted one is the evidence. And advisory fees are the truest instrument for measuring whether a banker is still working — they are being guided down.

**Second.** The 17 June 2026 annual meeting came and went with a routine seven-director slate and auditor ratification. No contest, no consent solicitation, no resolution of the review. The natural forcing window on the calendar passed without incident.

**Third.** On 25 June 2026 the company announced CFO succession framed as "a long-planned internal leadership transition designed to support AlTi's **next phase of growth**." That is standalone language. Companies do not describe long-planned internal succession supporting future growth two weeks before selling themselves.

All three markers point one direction. The arc runs from "we are for sale" to "nothing to report" to normal-course succession. That is a process losing energy.

## 3. The capital structure — the load-bearing arithmetic

As of the 31 March 2026 balance sheet:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Market value of common (~148.5M economic shares at $3.58) | ~$531M |
| Preferred stock, carrying value | **$352.2M** |

- **Series A** — 140,000 shares at a $1,000 liquidation preference (**$140M face**), held by Allianz. 9.75% cumulative, compounding, generally paid half in additional preferred and half in newly issued Class A shares. Non-voting, capped at 24.9%.
- **Series C** — 150,000 shares at $1,000 (**$150M face**), held by Constellation. 9.75% cumulative, compounding, payable at the company's option in kind or in cash.

> **Correction to my own first read:** I initially took Allianz's Series A face as $250M. That is wrong. The $250M was Allianz's *total package* — common purchased at $5.69, $140M of Series A preferred, and warrants struck at $7.40. Total preferred **face** is $290M ($140M + $150M), which has accreted to the **$352.2M carrying value** on the balance sheet. The carrying value is the figure the math turns on, and it is not in dispute.

The accretion is directly observable: $339.7M (Q3 2025) → $345.8M (Q4 2025) → **$352.2M (Q1 2026)**. That is about **$6.25M a quarter, roughly $25M a year**, of balance accretion. The full economic cost is larger — 9.75% on $352M is about **$34M a year, roughly $0.23 per share** — because the remainder is settled in newly issued common rather than added to the preferred balance. **Now run the buyer's math.** Q1 2026 adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization — a rough cash-profit proxy) was $14.9M at a 20% margin, up from 13% the prior quarter, annualizing near $60M. Management targets $20M of gross annual savings by year-end. Be generous: call normalized EBITDA $58–60M.

- Sponsors underwrite wealth managers at **9–13x** → enterprise value of **$700–780M** at the top of that band
- Subtract $37.5M net debt and the $352M preferred → common gets roughly **$310–390M**
- Across ~148.5M economic shares → **about $2.10 to $2.65 per share**

The stock is $3.58. **The common trades above what a rational buyer can pay.** That is the $600M gap, explained. It is not a haggle to be split.

The bidders have said so almost in terms. Press reporting quotes "a mathematical disparity between what a private equity sponsor would pay for a reasonable multiple on AlTi's cash flow and its market cap and enterprise value." Translated: **the buyers think the stock is already too expensive.** When the bidders' complaint is that the tape is above their pay-line, the sale is not a source of upside — it is a source of downward price discovery.

The one structure that clears is Allianz rolling its Series A rather than cashing it, and buying the common it does not own. That is real. But note who it makes the buyer: a conflicted insider holding the instrument that caps everyone else's value, with no disclosed majority-of-the-minority protection. The best-positioned bidder is the one most motivated to pay least.

## 4. Claims versus financials

| Management claim (Q1 2026) | The evidence |
|---|---|
| "$73 million in total revenue, representing 28% growth" | True, but **$21M was lumpy investment distributions, up 75%** — of which ~$18M came from a single manager, Zebedee, on its 15.3% 2025 return. Recurring fees grew 16%. The headline overstates the run-rate. |
| "Adjusted EBITDA... $15 million, up 21%" | True, up 32% sequentially — but driven by the same incentive income plus the absence of a prior-quarter bonus. Not durable. |
| "costs remain too high and addressing that is a near-term priority" | Credible and corroborated: reported operating expenses **rose** $18M year-over-year to $84M; normalized expenses $58M versus $45M. Management is candid the numbers are bad. |
| "anchored in high recurring revenues and long-duration client relationships" | Fair. $52M of recurring fees is the majority of revenue; 830+ ultra-wealthy families at ~$60M average; **96% retention since 2021**. The franchise is authentic. |
| FY2025: revenue $255M (+25%), adjusted EBITDA $35M (+45%) | Alongside an **operating loss of $74M and a net loss near $120M**. Adjusted EBITDA and reality are far apart here. |

Balance sheet: **goodwill of $384.6M plus intangibles of $431.3M is $815.9M against $1,138M of total assets** — about 72% is acquisition accounting, the residue of an expensive 2023 blank-cheque roll-up. Retained earnings are negative $410.3M.

Credit where due: management's account of the *business* is broadly honest, and Curtin did not oversell the review. Candor is not the problem. The arithmetic is.

## 5. The floor — this is the weakest link

This funnel exists to buy defined-risk asymmetry: a hard-dated catalyst above a verified floor. Test the floor honestly. What backstops $3.58?

- **A deal-break price?** There is no deal. Nothing to break.
- **Cash?** $39.7M against $77.2M of debt. Net debt, not net cash.
- **Liquidation or recovery value?** The common sits behind $352M of accreting preferred. In a liquidation it is a stub, plausibly zero.
- **Tangible book?** Roughly **negative $550M** once $815.9M of goodwill and intangibles comes out.
- **Earnings?** Never profitable on a reported basis: net losses of $165.6M (2023), $103.0M (2024), $119.7M (2025).
- **The tape?** The 52-week low is $2.75; the 200-day average is $3.92. Grinding down, not basing.

The honest no-deal value is **$2.10–$2.65** on sponsor math, with a genuine clearing print lower still. The practical adverse case is a break of the $2.75 low toward **~$2.30**. None of that is a floor in the sense this funnel requires. It is a forecast of where a subordinated stub settles — no contract, no cash, no acquirer underwriting it. **The "floor" is an estimate, not a backstop.**

## 6. The dated events cut the wrong way

The verifiable hard dates all add supply rather than forcing value out:

- **31 July 2026** (two weeks out): the transfer restriction on the Series A preferred lapses, and a further 30% of Allianz's common becomes transferable under its staged lock-up (full release 31 July 2027).
- **~10 July 2026**: the S-3 resale shelf went effective — 3,053,263 Class A shares, ~2.8% of the Class A count.

Both are permissions to sell. Neither is a clearing event. **The single hard date in the file has the opposite sign to the thesis it was filed under.**

Meanwhile the payment-in-kind dividend is a *reverse* forcing function: it compounds the claim ahead of the common at 9.75% and settles part of itself in new stock at multi-year-low prices, into a thin ~59.7 million share float with poor coverage.

## 7. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- Management stated on 11 May 2026 there is no review process in place "at the moment" — only reactive evaluation of inbound proposals. **The company has verbally downgraded its own catalyst.**
- Eleven months with J.P. Morgan and no bid; Corient walked; a reported impasse on a $600M+ gap that the arithmetic says cannot close.
- Buyers say the stock is *already* above their pay-line.
- $352M of preferred compounding at 9.75% ahead of a $531M common, settling part of itself in new shares. Time is a cost to the common, not an option premium.
- The most credible bidder (Allianz) is a conflicted insider with no disclosed minority protection.
- Tangible common equity ~negative $550M; never profitable on a reported basis; cash $39.7M.
- Governance rupture: founder-CEO ousted 30 March 2026 and now filing 13Ds against the company he built; international president departed; new CFO from 1 July 2026. Companies rarely change all three while closing a sale.
- **Net client outflows of $0.2 billion in Q1 2026** — the franchise leaked assets in the quarter the story was strongest. In a relationship business, departing principals and departing assets travel together.
- The 17 June annual meeting passed uncontested; the CFO succession was framed around "the next phase of growth."

**Green flags**

- The operating business is genuinely improving: revenue +28%, adjusted EBITDA +21% to $14.9M, margin 20% versus 13%, $20M of savings targeted by year-end, normalized expenses down $19M sequentially on zero-based budgeting.
- The franchise is real and sticky: $90.1B under advisement, $48.7B under management (+9%), 830+ relationships, 96% retention — a narrow but authentic switching-cost moat.
- Q1 2026 GAAP net income from continuing operations was positive at $8M.
- Three motivated 13D filers and a J.P. Morgan mandate: the option is live, even if poorly priced.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING.** Not the operating business, which is slowly improving — the *event*. Every dated marker since March 2026 has moved against the catalyst: the process wound down to reactive posture, the annual meeting passed uncontested, the advisory fees are being guided off, the CFO succession was framed for a standalone future, and the preferred accreted another $6.25M. (The prior pass read this as PIVOTING on the leadership change; the new evidence in section 2 makes DETERIORATING the more accurate read of the event we are actually underwriting.)

**The one thing the director must weigh: the spread runs the wrong way.** This funnel buys a live price *below* an event-resolved value. Here the $3.58 price sits **above** what any disclosed bidder can rationally pay — sponsors clear at $2.10–$2.65 after the preferred, and even a generous strategic take-out at a full 16x lands near $4.40, about +23%. Against roughly −35% to a low retest on the likelier no-deal path, the asymmetry inverts. There is no defined risk here because there is no floor — only a subordinated stub behind $352M of paper that accretes whether or not anyone ever bids.

And time is the adversary rather than the ally — the rarest failure mode in this funnel. A special situation is supposed to pay you for waiting as a dated catalyst approaches. This one charges you about $0.23 a share a year.

On moat and secular risk, which are secondary in an event name: ultra-wealthy wealth management carries a narrow but real moat built on relationship intangibles and switching costs, evidenced by 96% retention — but the continuing net outflows and the governance rupture mark it as eroding at the margin. There is no terminal secular threat to independent wealth management itself; fee compression bites hardest at the mass-affluent end, and artificial intelligence reads as a tool for these advisers rather than a replacement (AlTi is deploying it as such). The terminal value is not melting. That is not the problem. The problem is that the common's claim on it is deeply subordinated and shrinking every quarter.

AMLX.bull_thesis: The whole case is one scheduled event: topline results from the Phase 3 LUCIDITY trial of avexitide in post-bariatric hypoglycemia, guided to the third quarter of 2026 and confirmed as not yet released as of 2026-08-03. Post-bariatric hypoglycemia is a complication of weight-loss surgery in which the gut over-releases the hormone GLP-1 after meals and blood sugar crashes to dangerous levels. Avexitide is a first-in-class GLP-1 receptor antagonist, meaning it blocks that hormone rather than mimicking it as the familiar weight-loss drugs do. No drug is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for this condition today, so every current option is used off-label. The bull case is that LUCIDITY hits its FDA-agreed primary endpoint, a reduction in composite Level 2 and Level 3 low-blood-sugar events through Week 16 versus placebo. Four things support that. The prior mid-stage study showed a large effect, roughly a 64% reduction in composite events versus placebo, which is big enough to power a 78-patient confirmatory trial well. The endpoint is objective machine-measured glucose data rather than a subjective symptom scale. The drug carries FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designation, which commits the agency to closer engagement on the review path. And roughly 160,000 U.S. patients have no approved alternative. A win supports an approval filing by the end of 2026, a first-ever launch in this indication in 2027 at orphan-style pricing of roughly $5,000 to $15,000 a year, and a re-rating toward the $28 to $40 analyst target range. Importantly, the company is not negotiating from weakness: cash and short-term investments were $279.8 million at 31 March 2026 against $5.6 million of debt, burn is a steady $37 million a quarter, and the runway reaches well into 2028, so no financing is forced before the print. Beyond the lead asset there is ballast: avexitide in congenital hyperinsulinism, AMX0035 in Wolfram syndrome with positive Phase 2 data published in a peer-reviewed journal in May 2026 and a Phase 3 planned for the second half of 2026, and an early antisense candidate in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Management has also executed on schedule: enrollment of all 78 participants closed in March 2026 and a U.S. expanded access program for up to 250 patients launched in May 2026, a costly commitment a sponsor makes only when it expects to commercialise.

At $20.31 the stock sits a whisker below its 52-week high of $20.94, has nearly tripled off its $7.48 low, and trades well above its 50-day average of $16.42 and its 200-day of $14.83. Work the implied odds backwards and the point is stark: at $20.31, against a $28 win value and a $6 failure value, the market is already pricing roughly a 65% chance of success. The street is not looking the wrong way here; it has front-run the event. If LUCIDITY misses or reads ambiguously, the story reverts to cash plus an early-stage pipeline and the equity gives back 70% or more in a session. And the specific reason not to underwrite a high success probability is on this management team's own record: their prior drug AMX0035, marketed as Relyvrio, won FDA approval for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in 2022 on a small trial, then failed its larger confirmatory Phase 3 and was withdrawn from the market in 2024.
