EYPT.interrogator_dossier:
EVENT TYPE: Binary clinical readout / special situation, assessed 2026-08-03. The thesis is NOT franchise quality - EyePoint is a pre-profit, clinical-stage eye-disease company with no meaningful revenue and a heavy cash burn. The entire case rests on one imminent event: the first pivotal Phase 3 topline for its lead drug DURAVYU in wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD, the leading cause of vision loss in older adults).

1. THE EVENT - REAL, DATED, BINDING? Yes on all three, and days-to-weeks away. DURAVYU is a tiny bioerodible insert placed in the eye that slowly releases vorolanib, a drug that blocks the growth-factor signalling behind leaky retinal blood vessels. It is dosed once every six months; the standard of care it challenges, Regeneron's EYLEA (aflibercept), is injected every one to two months. Six-month dosing versus roughly eight injections a year is the whole commercial pitch. The load-bearing catalyst is LUGANO: a randomised, double-masked, aflibercept-controlled Phase 3 in which patients were randomised one-to-one to DURAVYU 2.7mg every six months or on-label aflibercept. The primary endpoint is non-inferiority in the average change in best-corrected visual acuity (the standard eye-chart vision score) at weeks 52 and 56 versus baseline - meaning DURAVYU only has to hold vision roughly as well as EYLEA, not beat it, a materially lower bar than a superiority design. DATED: the company's 30 July 2026 press release states that data from the Phase 3 wet AMD programme are anticipated to be reported beginning in August 2026 - the most recent public guidance, reaffirmed at the very top of the window three days before this assessment. LUCIA, the identical twin trial, follows roughly two months later. BINDING: both trials are fully enrolled with over 900 patients combined and every active-arm patient is past the week 52/56 primary timepoint, so the database exists and the readout is a mechanical certainty of timing, not of occurrence - no enrolment risk, no site risk, no third party who can withhold the result. NOT YET FIRED: verified against the company's investor newsroom, the newswire feed and the trading tape through the 31 July 2026 close. CAVEAT: this is a company-controlled data window, not a regulator-set decision date, and it has already slipped once - the May 2026 announcement carried the phrase 'ahead of mid-2026 topline data' and the current guidance is August. A one-to-two-month slip, now narrowed to a named month, but a slip. Second-quarter results are scheduled for 5 August 2026, a natural venue for a timing update.

2. CREDIBILITY ON HITTING IT: Reasonably strong operationally, with one financial claim that does not survive scrutiny. Execution has matched the talk: enrolment in the wet AMD Phase 3 programme was among the fastest in the indication's history, and in July 2026 the company completed enrolment of both diabetic macular edema Phase 3 trials (COMO and CAPRI) - over 480 patients in five months, ahead of schedule. Retina specialist Tarek Hassan was appointed chief strategic science officer in July 2026. Companies that miss guided timelines usually miss enrolment first; this one has not. The scientific de-risking is real but not decisive: the Phase 2 DAVIO 2 trial cut treatment burden 88% at six months, with more than 80% of patients needing no supplemental anti-VEGF injection or only one, and the independent data safety monitoring committee - an outside board that periodically inspects unblinded safety data - has issued three consecutive recommendations to continue both trials without modification, with a favourable profile across 190-plus treated patients. That materially lowers safety-driven failure risk but says nothing definitive about efficacy, because those reviews are masked as to treatment effect. WHERE CREDIBILITY STRAINS: management states that the $223 million held at 31 March 2026 will fund operations into the fourth quarter of 2027. Test it. Cash fell from $306 million at year-end 2025 to $223 million at 31 March 2026 - $83 million in one quarter - and the first-quarter net loss was $84.8 million, nearly double the $45.2 million of a year earlier. Consensus has the second quarter at roughly a $0.85 per-share loss, another $70 million or so. Funding into the fourth quarter of 2027 requires the quarterly burn to fall by more than half, to roughly $37 million. There is a legitimate mechanism - the wet AMD trials are the expensive part and roll off after the readouts - but the diabetic macular edema trials are ramping simultaneously. This is a projection resting on a spending decline that has not yet happened, and it is the one financial statement in this file not to take at face value. It does not endanger the August readout; it does mean the balance sheet at the moment of truth is thinner than the headline suggests.

3. VERIFIED DOWNSIDE FLOOR ~$4.75 (band $3.50-$5.50), MARKED DOWN from the board's $5.50. Derivation from audited figures rather than the headline cash number: cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities were $222.5 million at 31 March 2026 against $22.3 million of total debt (almost entirely a facility finance lease), so net cash was about $200 million or $2.40 per share on roughly 83.8 million shares. Roll forward through a second quarter of roughly $70 million of loss and two months of the third and cash at the readout is realistically near $130 million - about $1.55 per share gross, $1.40 net. Add the Durasert E / Verisome sustained-delivery platform, legacy products, and the diabetic macular edema Phase 3 programme (topline fourth quarter 2027). The critical judgement is how much of that second programme survives a wet AMD miss: not much - same drug, same insert, same durability question - and it would still need roughly five more quarters of funding from a depleted balance sheet, meaning a dilutive raise into a broken tape. Single-asset biotechs that fail a pivotal trial typically settle at 0.8 to 1.5 times remaining net cash; a live second indication argues for the upper end and somewhat beyond. That lands at ~$4.75. Two consequences: the floor is REAL, built from cash on a filed balance sheet rather than a hoped-for bid; and it sits roughly 61% below the $12.25 price, so it bounds the loss without cushioning it.

4. RED FLAGS: Single-asset binary - one trial is effectively the whole equity, and a miss is a 60%-plus overnight loss with no franchise to fall back on. The runway claim is stretched (see 2 above); watch the 5 August 2026 report for whether it survives contact with the actual cash number. Dilution is near-certain on a win (a launch the company cannot self-fund) and existential on a miss. The window has already slipped once. Sell-side targets are launch models, not offers - Mizuho $39 and Stifel $40 assume approval and commercial success, and JPMorgan sits at $30 having cut from $33. Narrow-miss risk is asymmetric: because durability is the entire argument, vision must hold across the full six-month interval, and a statistically narrow miss would remove the reason to prefer DURAVYU over a cheap, well-understood injection.

5. GREEN FLAGS: Three consecutive clean independent safety reviews. A statistically positive and clinically striking Phase 2 in the same indication. The lower non-inferiority bar. Enrolment execution consistently ahead of schedule across four Phase 3 trials. No financing cliff between here and the readout. And the stock has drifted DOWN into the event - $12.25 against a 50-day average of $13.14 and a 200-day average of $14.09, 36% below the 52-week high of $19.11 - so the entry carries no event-heat premium.

6. ASYMMETRY: Live $12.25, event-resolved target ~$35 (between JPMorgan's $30 and the $39-$40 pair, haircut for the post-win raise), verified floor ~$4.75. Upside ~+$22.75 against downside ~-$7.50, roughly 3.0 to 1. Weighting the outcomes at about 55% favourable gives a base case near $21, trimmed to ~$20 for dilution and time. A textbook imminent, dated, defined-risk binary. Size it as an event position, not a value anchor, and note the case is not fully settled until LUCIA confirms roughly two months later.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STRENGTHENING | MOAT: NONE | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: none

FIG.bull_thesis:
The bull case is that Figma's shares were broken by plumbing rather than by business decay, and that the plumbing has a contractual end date four trading days away.

Start with the business, because the whole case rests on it being healthy. Revenue in the quarter ended 31 March 2026 was $333.4 million, up 46% from a year earlier -- and that growth rate went 38%, then 40%, then 46% across the last three reported quarters. It accelerated during exactly the months the market was pricing the company as roadkill. Net dollar retention, which measures how much existing customers spend now versus a year ago, reached 139%, the highest in more than two years. Management raised full-year 2026 guidance to $1.422-1.428 billion, about 35% growth, and lifted adjusted operating income guidance to $125-135 million. Free cash flow over the last four reported quarters totals about $237 million. Cash and short-term investments stood at $1.638 billion against $56.2 million of debt, so roughly $3.00 a share of net cash and no solvency question of any kind.

Now the plumbing. Figma came public on 31 July 2025 with a very small tradable float and an unusually elaborate lock-up -- the window during which insiders and pre-listing investors are barred from selling. The original 180-day lock-up ran out on 27 January 2026. A second agreement signed on 30 August 2025 covering about 54.1% of the Class A shares set up four further releases tied to earnings dates: about 38.9 million shares in November 2025, 44.4 million in February 2026, 61.1 million in May 2026, and the final and largest tranche of about 77.7 million shares at the open on the second trading day after the June-quarter report. The company confirmed on 15 July 2026 that it reports after the close on Wednesday 5 August 2026, which fixes that final release at Friday 7 August 2026.

The bull sequence is therefore simple and dated. Ten months of near-continuous, price-insensitive supply from venture funds distributing stock to their limited partners ends permanently on 7 August. What is left is a business growing in the high-30s with 139% retention, a $1.6 billion cash pile, an engaged activist (Findell Capital, whose June 2026 letter demands the product line be cut from eight offerings to four and carries a $40 target), and a share register finally free to be set by fundamental buyers rather than by mechanical sellers. The stock closed 31 July 2026 at $24.32, about 83% below its first-month peak of $142.92 and 26% below its $33 offering price, valuing the operating business at roughly 7.9 times this year's guided revenue. Sentiment does not need to improve for that to re-rate toward $29-30; the selling merely has to stop.

The conditions this case requires: the 5 August print must confirm the guided $348-350 million and roughly 40% growth; the 7 August release must be absorbed in days rather than months; and the market's fear that generative artificial intelligence makes design software unnecessary must stay a narrative rather than showing up in the retention numbers.
FIG.bear_thesis:
The bear case is that the event points the wrong way, the entry price has already moved against us, and the floor underneath the position is demonstrated rather than defined.

Direction first. A forced-seller trade pays when a known seller is exhausted and the price is then free to rise. What is contractually certain on 7 August 2026 is not exhaustion -- it is the arrival of permission to sell for about 77.7 million shares, roughly 15% of the ~528 million shares outstanding and a far larger share of what actually trades daily. These holders are pre-listing venture funds, which typically distribute stock in kind to their limited partners, who then liquidate on their own schedule with no reference to price. That is why each of the three earlier tranches produced weeks of drift rather than a single clean flush. Buying on 3 August is buying four days ahead of the largest wave of supply in the company's public life, not after it.

Price second, and this is decisive. The board file underwrites a $29.00 target, a $17.50 floor and a reward-to-risk multiple of 2.85. Those three numbers are only mutually consistent at a share price near $20.49 -- roughly where the stock sat when the file was struck. Since then it has rallied about 46% off its $16.60 record low to $24.32. Against the verified $16.60 low the same target now gives about 19% of upside versus about 32% of downside, a ratio of roughly 0.6 to 1 pointing the wrong way. The rally did not confirm the thesis; it consumed it.

Third, there is no real floor. This is not a signed merger, not a company trading below net cash, not a liquidation. Net cash of about $3.00 a share is 12% of the price and backstops nothing. The only thing under the stock is the $16.60 printed in early July 2026 and re-tested to form a double bottom -- a level the market recently paid, not a level anything prevents it going through. At $16.60 the operating business would be valued at about 5.0 times this year's guided revenue and 4.1 times the roughly $1.76 billion the street models for 2027, which is a perfectly reachable price if the terminal-value argument gains any further ground.

Fourth, the economics behind the growth are deteriorating. Reported gross margin has fallen from about 92% in late 2024 to 79.4% in the March 2026 quarter; some of that is post-listing stock compensation in cost of revenue, but part is the cost of serving artificial-intelligence features and does not reverse. Stock-based compensation was $169.0 million in that single quarter, about 51% of revenue; the activist's own full-year estimate is 27% of revenue against 8% at Adobe. The share count went from 474.8 million to 523.5 million in a year, about 10%. So the claim that the overhang clears for good on 7 August is wrong in a specific way: the contractual overhang clears, the structural issuance of roughly a tenth of the company a year does not.

Finally, the secular fear is live and the market acts on it without warning. Shares fell about 16.5% in the week to 24 July 2026 on generative-artificial-intelligence displacement worry with no company news at all, after a competing design tool launched in April 2026. The sell side has been walking its target down, from about $40 in March 2026 to roughly $30.40 in late July, on a book of four Buys, one Outperform and eight Holds. What confirms this case: any deceleration below the guided 40% on 5 August, retention slipping from 139%, or the 7 August tape showing heavy volume with the price giving back the July rally.
FIG.sop_bull:
Event-win value of about $30 a share.

Figma reports as a single operating segment, so the parts here are the operating franchise plus the balance sheet rather than separable divisions.

Operating franchise: if the 7 August release is absorbed quickly, growth holds in the mid-30s and the displacement fear fades from the multiple, the business supports about 8.5 times the roughly $1.76 billion of revenue the street models for 2027. That is $14.96 billion, or about $28.30 a share on ~528 million shares. Eight to nine times forward revenue is where high-30s-growth software with 139% net dollar retention and positive adjusted operating income has historically cleared, and it is still well below the 12-plus times the stock carried at listing.

Balance sheet: $1.638 billion of cash and short-term investments less $56.2 million of debt is about $1.58 billion of net cash, or $2.99 a share. Add it at face value; it is real, liquid and unencumbered.

Total: roughly $31 a share, which I round down to $30 to allow for the ~10% annual share issuance that continues regardless of the lock-up. The street's mean target of $30.40 and the board file's $29.00 sit inside this range; the activist's $40 assumes the cost programme is adopted, which is not in this number.
FIG.sop_bear:
Verified downside floor of about $16.60 a share -- and it is a soft one.

Operating franchise: on a decelerating growth rate and a permanently lower gross margin, the business is worth about 4 times the roughly $1.76 billion of 2027 street revenue, which is where unprofitable software with a contested end-market has been trading in this de-rating. That is $7.04 billion, or about $13.30 a share.

Balance sheet: the same $2.99 a share of net cash.

Total: about $16.30, which reconciles almost exactly with the $16.60 record low actually printed in early July 2026 and re-tested weeks later. That coincidence is the strongest evidence available that this level is where the market clears the bear case, and it is why I use $16.60 rather than the $17.50 carried in the board file.

The critical caveat: nothing contractual defends this level. There is no merger consideration, no cash-per-share close to the price, no recovery value. Net cash is only 12% of the current price. This is a demonstrated floor, not a defined one, and a genuine break in the retention numbers on 5 August would take it out.
FIG.sop_breakdown:
Probability-weighted between the two outcomes, because no contractual payout exists to anchor to.

Win case $30 (45% odds): the operating franchise at about 8.5 times the roughly $1.76 billion of 2027 street revenue, about $28.30 a share, plus $2.99 a share of net cash. Requires the 5 August print to hold the guided $348-350 million and roughly 40% growth, and the 7 August supply to be absorbed inside a few weeks.

Loss case $16.60 (55% odds): the same franchise at about 4 times 2027 revenue, about $13.30 a share, plus the same $2.99 of net cash -- reconciling to the low the market actually printed in July 2026.

Weighted: 0.45 x $30 + 0.55 x $18 (the loss path realistically stalls between the floor and the current price rather than pinning the low) gives about $23.40. I carry $23, with a range of $21-25.

The uncomfortable conclusion of that arithmetic is that the 31 July close of $24.32 is already slightly above the probability-weighted value. Where we disagree with the market runs in both directions, and that two-sidedness is itself the reason to wait rather than to buy.

FIG.positioning_washout:
Forced selling is the entire thesis on this name, and for the first time it has a termination date rather than an open end. Understanding exactly who is selling is what separates the good version of this trade from the bad one.

The sellers are not disappointed fundamental holders and not a yield-focused base being forced out by a dividend cut. They are pre-listing venture funds and early employees. Venture funds rarely sell in the ordinary sense: they distribute shares in kind to their limited partners -- pension plans, endowments, funds of funds -- who then liquidate on their own timetable, often through a broker with instructions to complete rather than to achieve a price. That flow is genuinely price-insensitive, which is why it can push a stock far below any reasonable value and why it takes weeks to clear rather than days.

The sequence so far: the original 180-day lock-up expired 27 January 2026, freeing roughly two-thirds of the share count. On top of it, four staged tranches of the 54.1% extended block released about 38.9 million shares in November 2025, 44.4 million in February 2026 and 61.1 million in May 2026. Each was followed by drift. The stock made its record low of $16.60 in early July, about six weeks after the May tranche -- which is roughly how long that supply took to work through.

The employee side is a distinct and colder story. Staff watched roughly 80% of the paper value of their holdings evaporate between the August 2025 peak and the January 2026 unlock, when the stock was near $22.51. That cohort is not selling to take profits; it is selling to salvage. That behaviour is insensitive to the fundamental case and to good news.

What happens after 7 August is the honest open question. The optimistic reading is that the last identified seller is released, the register turns over to fundamental holders, and the drift ends. The realistic reading is that release is not exhaustion -- the shares merely become sellable, and the distribution-to-limited-partner chain then runs for weeks. The washout that would make this a buy is the tape from roughly 7 to 21 August: heavy volume, a decisive break of the $16.60-18.00 shelf, and then a failure to make a new low. That is a specific, observable event, and it has not happened.

Start with what is verified. The extended lock-up agreement of 30 August 2025 covers about 54.1% of Figma's Class A shares and releases in four tranches tied to earnings dates. Three have gone. FIG.interrogator_dossier:
# FIG (Figma, Inc.) -- Forensic dossier: a forced-seller special situation

Event-driven review, verified live on 3 August 2026. The question in front of this committee is not whether Figma is a good business. It is whether the gap between Friday's close of $24.32 and a plausible event-resolved value is wide enough, and whether the event that is supposed to close that gap is real, dated and pointed in the right direction.

The short answer, established below and then tested in every section: the event is real, it is contractually dated to Friday 7 August 2026, and it is the largest single release of stock in the company's short public life. But it is a supply event arriving into a price that has already risen about 46% off its record low in four weeks. The asymmetry the board file was underwriting has been spent by the rally, and the supply has not yet landed.

## 1. Narrative arc -- how the setup got here

Figma listed on the New York Stock Exchange on 31 July 2025 at $33 a share and traded to an intraday $142.92 in its first weeks. It closed Friday 31 July 2026 at $24.32. That is roughly 83% below the peak and about 26% below the offering price, on a business whose revenue has grown every single quarter since.

That divergence is the whole reason this name is in front of us, and it has two causes that must be kept separate because they call for opposite conclusions.

The first cause is plumbing. Figma came public with a very small tradable float and a lock-up (the window during which insiders and pre-listing investors are barred from selling) that was unusually elaborate. The original 180-day lock-up ran out on 27 January 2026, releasing roughly two-thirds of the share count. Layered on top of that, an agreement signed on 30 August 2025 with holders of about 54.1% of the Class A shares set up a second, staggered release running through 2026. Each tranche is tied to an earnings announcement: about 38.9 million shares (17.5% of the block) after the third-quarter 2025 report, released November 2025; about 44.4 million (20%) after the full-year 2025 report, released February 2026; about 61.1 million (27.5%) after the first-quarter 2026 report, released May 2026; and about 77.7 million (35%) at the open on the second trading day after the second-quarter 2026 report, or 31 August 2026 if that comes first -- pending, and dated 7 August 2026.

Figma confirmed on 15 July 2026 that it will report the June quarter after the close on Wednesday 5 August 2026. Two trading days later is Friday 7 August 2026. That is the date. It is not an estimate, a guidance range or a management aspiration; it is a contractual trigger disclosed in a filed 8-K, and the only way it moves is if the earnings date moves, in which case the backstop of 31 August 2026 applies.

The second cause is a genuine argument about the future. Since roughly April 2026 the market has been pricing design software as a category that generative artificial intelligence may make cheap or unnecessary. A competitor's launch of a rival design tool in April 2026 is the specific event that crystallised that fear for this stock. In the week to 24 July 2026 the shares fell about 16.5% on nothing company-specific -- an industry-wide de-rating of software on artificial-intelligence displacement worry. The record low of $16.60 was printed in early July.

The rally back to $24.32 came from three things: a double bottom in the chart around $16.60-18.00, a reinstated Buy from Bank of America, and an activist campaign that put a $40 target on the tape. None of those is the lock-up.

The arc, stated plainly: a healthy business was repriced by a combination of mechanical supply and a legitimate secular fear, and it has already bounced hard into the last, largest tranche of that supply.

## 2. Is the catalyst real, dated and binding?

Yes on all three counts, with one important qualification.

Real and dated. The release is documented in the 8-K covering the 30 August 2025 extended lock-up agreement. The trigger is mechanical. The date, 7 August 2026, is four days from now.

Binding. The holders are released; nothing compels them to sell. That is the qualification, and it cuts in a specific direction that the bull case usually gets backwards. The event that is contractually certain is the arrival of permission to sell. What the thesis actually needs is the exhaustion of the sellers, and that is not contractual at all. It is an empirical question about how quickly roughly 77.7 million shares -- about 15% of the ~528 million shares outstanding, and a far larger fraction of the shares that actually trade -- are absorbed.

Who the sellers are. These are pre-listing venture funds. They generally do not sell in the ordinary sense; they distribute shares in kind to their limited partners, who then liquidate on their own schedule with no reference to price. That is why this pressure has historically taken weeks rather than a day to clear, and why the three earlier tranches each produced a drift lower rather than a single clean flush.

What this means for direction. A forced-seller trade pays when the seller is exhausted, not when the seller is released. Buying on 3 August is buying four days ahead of the supply, not after it. The board file's own framing -- forced-seller supply clearing -- describes a state this name has not yet reached.

## 3. Sponsor and management credibility on hitting the date

There is no sponsor to handicap here, and that is a point in the setup's favour: no acquirer can walk, no regulator can issue a second request, no trial can miss its endpoint. The date arrives on its own.

Management credibility matters for the other event in the same week -- the 5 August earnings report -- and the record there is good but short. The December 2025 quarter delivered $303.8 million with growth reaccelerating to 40% from 38%. The March 2026 quarter delivered $333.4 million, up 46%, with adjusted earnings of $0.10 a share against $0.06 expected. Full-year 2026 guidance was raised to $1.422-1.428 billion, about 35% growth, and adjusted operating income guidance lifted to $125-135 million. The June quarter, reported 5 August, is guided to $348.0-350.0 million, about 40% growth.

Four quarters of public guidance, four met or beaten, with the growth rate going 38% to 40% to 46% rather than the other way. Net dollar retention -- how much existing customers spend this year versus last -- reached 139% in the first quarter of 2026, the highest in over two years. On the narrow question of whether they hit their own number on 5 August, the honest answer is that they probably will. Reliability: high, on a short record.

## 4. The verified downside floor -- what actually backstops the price

This is where the setup is weakest, and the committee should not be talked out of it.

There is no hard floor. This is not a merger with a signed agreement, not a company trading below net cash, not a liquidation. The balance sheet at 31 March 2026 held $1.638 billion of cash and short-term investments against $56.2 million of debt (almost all lease obligations), which is net cash of about $1.58 billion, or roughly $3.00 a share. At $24.32, cash accounts for 12% of the price. It backstops nothing.

What actually sits underneath the price is a valuation floor and a chart floor. The printed low is $16.60, struck in early July 2026 and re-tested to form the double bottom -- three weeks old and therefore a live, verified level rather than a historical curiosity. At that price the market capitalisation is about $8.8 billion and, net of cash, the operating business is valued at roughly $7.2 billion -- about 5.0 times this year's guided revenue and about 4.1 times the roughly $1.76 billion the street models for 2027. For a business compounding revenue in the high-30s with 139% net dollar retention, that is a price that requires the terminal-value argument to be true.

So the floor is real in the sense that the market recently paid it, and soft in the sense that nothing contractual stops the price going through it. Under the house rule that a special situation needs a defined downside, this one does not fully qualify: it has a demonstrated downside, which is a weaker thing. The board file carries the floor at $17.50; the verified level is $16.60, and I use that -- the more conservative and the more recently printed of the two.

## 5. Red flags

The spread has already closed. This is the single most important finding. The board file underwrites a target of $29.00, a floor of $17.50 and a reward-to-risk multiple of 2.85. Those three numbers are only mutually consistent at a share price of about $20.49, which is roughly where the stock traded when the file was struck. At Friday's $24.32 the same target and the verified $16.60 floor give about 19% of upside against about 32% of downside -- a ratio of roughly 0.6 to 1, against us. The rally did not confirm the thesis; it consumed it.

The supply is ahead of us, not behind us. The largest of the four tranches lands on 7 August, into a stock that has just risen 46% in four weeks. Every prior tranche produced weeks of drift.

Permanent dilution continues after the lock-up ends. The share count rose from 474.8 million in the first quarter of 2025 to 523.5 million in the first quarter of 2026, about 10% in a year. Stock-based compensation was $169.0 million in the first quarter of 2026 alone, roughly 51% of that quarter's revenue; the activist's own estimate for the full year is 27% of revenue against 8% at Adobe. So the bull sentence that the overhang clears for good on 7 August is wrong in an important way: the contractual overhang clears; the structural issuance of roughly a tenth of the company a year does not.

Gross margin has compressed materially. Reported gross margin has fallen from about 92% in late 2024 to 79.4% in the first quarter of 2026. Part of that is post-listing stock compensation landing in cost of revenue, but part is the cost of serving artificial-intelligence features, and that part does not reverse. A design-software business that used to convert 92 cents of every revenue dollar into gross profit and now converts about 80 is a structurally different business.

The accounting loss is large. The trailing twelve months show a net loss of about $1.40 billion on $1.16 billion of revenue. Most of that is the one-time listing-related stock charge of $1.14 billion booked in the September 2025 quarter, so it overstates the ongoing problem -- but even excluding it, the company loses money on a reported basis while guiding to $125-135 million of adjusted operating income. The entire gap is stock compensation.

The secular fear is not imaginary. The stock fell 16.5% in a single week in late July on artificial-intelligence displacement worry with no company news. That is a market that will re-price this name on a headline about somebody else's product, regardless of what Figma reports.

## 6. Green flags

The demand evidence contradicts the displacement narrative -- so far. Growth reaccelerated from 38% to 40% to 46% across the last three reported quarters, precisely while the market was pricing obsolescence. Net dollar retention hit a two-year high of 139%. If artificial intelligence were eating this business, it would show up here first, and it has not.

Cash generation is real, not a projection. Free cash flow over the last four reported quarters totals about $237 million ($60.6m, $49.0m, $39.2m, $88.6m). Cash and short-term investments were essentially flat at $1.64-1.66 billion across the last two quarters. There is no burn hump, no maturity wall and no covenant. Whatever goes wrong here in the next nine months, it will not be solvency.

An engaged, credible activist with a specific programme. Findell Capital's June 2026 letter asks for the product line to go from eight offerings to four, for costs and stock compensation to be cut, and for an independent board investigation into whether a partner improperly used Figma's confidential information before launching a competing tool. Findell carries a $40 twelve-month target. The stock rose more than 6% on the letter -- the market wants the discipline. This is a second, undated catalyst that could still fire.

The private-market anchor. Adobe agreed in 2022 to pay $20 billion for Figma, and paid a $1 billion fee when regulators killed the deal. Figma's enterprise value today is about $11.3 billion on roughly three times the revenue it had then. That does not make $20 billion the right number, but it does establish that a strategic buyer once valued this asset far above the current tape.

## 7. Hidden signals

The analyst target has been walking down, not up: the mean price target fell from about $40 in March 2026 to roughly $30.40 in late July, and the rating book is now four Buys, one Outperform and eight Holds. The sell side is not the source of the bounce.

The 200-day average sits at $28.86 against a 50-day at $21.53. The rally has taken the price back into the gap between them, which is exactly the zone where a bounce most often stalls.

The activist's product complaint and the company's growth reacceleration point in opposite directions. Findell wants eight products cut to four; management's own explanation for the 46% growth quarter is international expansion and adoption of the new artificial-intelligence products. One of them is misreading the business, and the 5 August call is where that gets tested.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict for the director

Trajectory: turning. The top line is strengthening -- accelerating growth, record retention, raised guidance. The economic model is not: gross margin down about 13 points, stock compensation around half of revenue, a share count growing 10% a year, and a product portfolio the largest outside shareholder wants cut in half. Figma is mid-transformation from a single-product design tool into a multi-product artificial-intelligence suite, and the market is refusing to pay for the attempt.

Moat: narrow, and holding. The lock-in is genuine -- shared multiplayer design files are where whole product teams live, and 139% net dollar retention is the direct evidence that customers are deepening rather than leaving. But this is workflow habit rather than hard contractual lock-in, the kind of moat the current wave of generative tools is best at attacking, and the margin compression shows the moat is not free to defend. It is not wide, and on the evidence in hand it is not yet eroding either.

Secular threat: material, not terminal. Generative artificial intelligence collapsing the cost of good-enough design output is a live threat to pricing power, and the market has already voted. But the company's own retention and growth numbers currently point the other way, so this is a risk to the multiple more than to the existence of the business.

The single thing the director must weigh before sizing: the reward-to-risk that justified this name has already been paid out by the rally. At $24.32 you are risking about 32% to the verified $16.60 low to make about 19% to the $29.00 target, four days ahead of the largest release of stock in the company's public life. The event is genuine and its date is certain; the entry price is not the one the board file underwrote. Wait for the supply, then decide.

FIP.bull_thesis: The bull case is that a signed, binding sale rescues a balance sheet the market has written off, and the freight-rail platform left behind gets valued like the scarce asset it is. On 30 April 2026 FTAI Infrastructure agreed to sell Long Ridge Energy and Power -- a 485-to-505 megawatt gas-fired plant at Hannibal, Ohio, gas-well interests, and about 1,600 contiguous acres on the Ohio River -- to a subsidiary of MARA Holdings for roughly $1.52 billion. The buyer is committed and visibly still building in the same direction: it secured consents from holders of its 8.75% senior notes in June 2026 to permit the purchase, funded its infrastructure push partly by selling about $1.5 billion of bitcoin, and signed for a further 1,200-acre powered site in Texas on 9 July 2026. Closing takes total debt from $3.814 billion to $2.377 billion, parent-company debt from $1.310 billion to $1.019 billion, and corporate leverage (debt measured against earnings) from 9.5 times to 7.4 times, while handing the company more than $300 million of net cash that repays parent debt carrying a 9.75% coupon and saves about $30 million a year of interest. Management has already said Jefferson and Repauno are the next assets out the door within twelve to eighteen months, with roughly $700 million of proceeds pre-assigned to parent debt -- a sequenced path to the stated 5.1 times leverage target. Underneath sits a business that is working: the rail segment (Transtar plus Wheeling and Lake Erie) earned $40.2 million in the first quarter of 2026, up 31% on the same quarter a year earlier, and short-line and regional railroads are local franchises a competitor cannot rebuild. Management's near-term earnings target of $278 million excluding Long Ridge is built from an annualised first-quarter run rate of about $176 million, plus $13 million of rail integration synergies, $9 million of new Jefferson terminal contracts, and $80 million once Repauno phase two commissions. Because the capital structure is so heavy, the equity is extremely geared to the multiple applied to those earnings: capitalising $278 million at sixteen times and deducting $2.38 billion of pro-forma debt and the roughly $1.4 billion rail-holding-company preferred claim leaves about $5.50 a share; at seventeen times, about $7.87; at eighteen times, about $10.20. Three analysts publish targets between $8.75 and $12. The conditions this requires are specific and all must hold: the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission grants the change-of-control approval without crippling conditions, the deal closes and the cash is actually applied to the 9.75% term loan, Repauno phase two reaches mechanical completion in autumn 2026 and begins operating in the first quarter of 2027 as guided, and infrastructure multiples stay near seventeen times.
FIP.bear_thesis: The bear case is that this is a leveraged option with no floor, and the option is already going against us. The downside level this position was scored against, $3.90, broke in the last week of July 2026: the shares closed at $3.73 on 31 July, down 6.75% that day, at a new 52-week low of $3.71, after falling five sessions in a row and eight of the last ten -- roughly 13% over that stretch and about 37% over twelve months. The stock is falling into the catalyst rather than tightening toward it, which is the opposite of what a defined-risk event setup should do. Structurally the common shareholder is at the very back of a very long queue. After the sale closes, roughly $2.38 billion of debt sits ahead of the equity, and above that again is a preferred stake at the rail holding company: about $1 billion sold to funds managed by Ares Management to finance the Wheeling and Lake Erie purchase, carried at $970.5 million on 31 March 2026, redeemable at $1,417.49 per share (about $1.4 billion in total), with dividends paid in kind so the claim compounds rather than being paid in cash, and no redemption obligation until 25 August 2032. That is close to $3.8 billion of senior claims against an equity market value of about $441 million. Book equity attributable to the company was already negative $303.1 million at 31 March 2026, unrestricted cash was $37.9 million, and the first-quarter filing carries the standard formulation of going-concern doubt resolved by pointing at the pending sale: planned actions are considered probable to be implemented and to provide sufficient liquidity to meet obligations. Take the sale away and that sentence has to be rewritten. The sale itself is not a value unlock -- $1.52 billion for an asset generating about $144 million of annualised earnings in the second half of 2025 is roughly eleven times, a fair price, so the transaction is close to neutral on enterprise value and matters almost entirely for liquidity. Meanwhile the largest single block of the earnings target, the $80 million from Repauno phase two, is a construction project that produced negative $2.3 million in the first quarter of 2026 and does not begin operating until the first quarter of 2027 -- after the event window closes. On today's realistic earnings power of roughly $198 million, once rail synergies and Jefferson contracts land but before Repauno contributes, the common is worth close to nothing at any conventional infrastructure multiple; at fifteen times it is negative. Behaviour reinforces the concern: the $45 million Tidewater Logistics purchase on 29 June 2026 was funded by upsizing the term loan, adding parent debt inside a deleveraging quarter, and the 1 July 2026 Jefferson refinancing replaced $217.9 million of bonds with a $230 million bridge loan due 30 June 2027 rather than removing the maturity. The first quarter of 2026 lost $1.32 a share against a consensus near $0.35. Moody's rates the company B3 with a negative outlook. And the regulatory path is not clear: the independent market monitor for the PJM grid filed comments on 29 May 2026 urging that the deal not be approved without a commitment from the buyer not to remove Long Ridge capacity from PJM markets to serve data-centre load, and no approval order had been published as of 3 August 2026. What confirms the bear case: a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order with output-commitment conditions that reduce the asset's value to the buyer, any slip past the contractual outside date of 30 November 2026 toward the 30 June 2027 regulatory backstop, a Repauno commissioning delay, or a cut to the three-cent quarterly dividend.
FIP.sop_bull: About $8.00 to $10.20 a share. Method: capitalise management's near-term target of $278 million of adjusted earnings excluding Long Ridge -- built as roughly $176 million annualised first-quarter run rate, plus $13 million rail integration synergies, plus $9 million new Jefferson contracts, plus $80 million from Repauno phase two -- at seventeen to eighteen times, the range implied by the published analyst targets of $8.75 to $12. Seventeen times gives an enterprise value of $4.73 billion; eighteen times gives $5.00 billion. Deduct pro-forma total debt of $2.38 billion (management's own post-close figure) and the rail-holding-company preferred claim of about $1.42 billion at its stated redemption value, then divide by 118.2 million shares outstanding: $7.87 at seventeen times, $10.20 at eighteen. Sense-check by the parts: rail at about $174 million of run-rate earnings on sixteen times is roughly $2.78 billion, Jefferson at about $58 million on twelve times is roughly $0.70 billion, a fully commissioned Repauno at $80 million on thirteen times is roughly $1.04 billion, Tidewater about $0.06 billion, less capitalised corporate overhead -- which sums to the same neighbourhood. The dominant sensitivity is the multiple, not the earnings: because senior claims are so large relative to the equity, each single turn of multiple is worth about $2.35 a share.
FIP.sop_bear: About $0.40 to $1.75 a share, and there is no verified structural floor above zero. Method: value the operating businesses on earnings power that exists today rather than on the completed-construction target. Once rail integration synergies and the new Jefferson contracts land but before Repauno phase two contributes anything, run-rate earnings are roughly $198 million. At fifteen times that is $2.97 billion of enterprise value against roughly $3.80 billion of pro-forma debt ($2.38 billion) plus the rail preferred claim ($1.42 billion) -- the common is worth nothing. Even at twenty times, a multiple no distressed infrastructure holding company commands, the residual is about $1.35 a share. The severe case, in which the sale slips toward the 30 June 2027 regulatory backstop or breaks, is worse still: book equity is already negative $303.1 million, unrestricted cash was $37.9 million at 31 March 2026, the going-concern assessment is expressly supported by the pending sale, the term loan costs 9.75% and matures February 2028, and a $230 million Jefferson bridge loan comes due 30 June 2027. In that path the equity is a residual claim behind about $3.8 billion, worth perhaps $0.40, and dilution or a restructuring becomes the live question. The point that governs the decision: the $3.90 level this candidate was scored against as a floor is not a floor -- it was simply the prior 52-week low, and it broke on 29-31 July 2026.
FIP.sop_breakdown: Probability-weighted across four paths, because the payoff is driven by the multiple and by Repauno rather than by the deal alone. Path one, 35% weight: the sale closes in the third or fourth quarter of 2026, Repauno phase two commissions on schedule in the first quarter of 2027, and the market capitalises the $278 million target near sixteen to seventeen times -- about $6.50 a share. Path two, 35%: the sale closes, but Repauno slips or the multiple holds near fifteen times -- about $3.00. Path three, 20%: the sale closes late or with Federal Energy Regulatory Commission conditions attached, liquidity stays tight, and the dividend or the share count gives -- about $1.75. Path four, 10%: the deal slips toward the 30 June 2027 backstop or breaks, the going-concern question reopens and restructuring risk becomes live -- about $0.40. Weighted, that is $3.72 a share. The parts underneath: freight rail (Transtar plus Wheeling and Lake Erie) is the only segment carrying real, durable value at roughly $2.4 to $2.8 billion of enterprise value; Jefferson terminal roughly $0.6 to $0.7 billion; Repauno is worth about $1.0 billion once commissioned and close to its build cost before that; Tidewater about $0.06 billion. Against that sits $2.38 billion of pro-forma debt and about $1.42 billion of compounding rail preferred, which together consume essentially all of it. The market value of $441 million on 118.2 million shares is, on this arithmetic, close to fair -- which is precisely the problem for a candidate selected for asymmetry.
FIP.risk_reward: Roughly 2.3 to 1 measured endpoint to endpoint, but that ratio flatters the setup and should not be relied on. Upside to a realistic event-resolved target of $8.75 is about +135% from $3.73; downside to a bear value of $1.50 is about -60%. The problem is that the downside is not bounded at $1.50 by anything contractual or structural -- it is an estimate, not a floor. The level actually scored as the floor, $3.90, broke on 29-31 July 2026 and the shares are now below it at a 52-week low. With roughly $3.8 billion of debt and compounding preferred ahead of a $441 million equity stub, negative book equity, and going-concern language supported by the pending sale, the true downside is zero. Probability-weighted fair value of about $3.70 sits essentially on top of the $3.73 price, so the expected return today is close to nil with a fat tail in each direction. This is a leveraged option, not a defined-risk trade.
FIP.catalyst_summary: Binding sale of the Long Ridge power business to MARA Holdings for about $1.52 billion, guided to close in the third quarter of 2026 with a contractual outside date of 30 November 2026 -- real and dated, but it buys survival rather than a re-rating, and the downside level the position was scored against has already broken.
FIP.dated_milestone: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approval of the change of control under section 203 of the Federal Power Act, docket EC26-92-000, filed 8 May 2026 with comments closed 29 May 2026 and no order published as of 3 August 2026. Management guides to approval in the middle of the third quarter of 2026 and a close in the third quarter; the purchase agreement's contractual outside date is 30 November 2026, extending to 30 June 2027 if regulatory conditions remain unsatisfied. Nearer dated events: second-quarter results after the close on 5 August 2026, and the buyer's results on 6 August 2026, either of which can update the closing timeline within days.
FIP.forcing_function: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order in docket EC26-92-000, followed by the actual closing and the application of more than $300 million of net proceeds against parent debt carrying a 9.75% coupon. That sequence is what converts an accounting going-concern question into a funded balance sheet and gives the market permission to capitalise the rail platform at an infrastructure multiple. It is genuinely dated and genuinely binding, with a termination right for either party if the deal has not closed by 30 November 2026 and a regulatory extension to 30 June 2027. Two things qualify it. First, the 30 September 2026 date this candidate was scored on is management's guidance, not the contract -- a slip into the fourth quarter is permitted and would not break the deal, only the timing assumption. Second, the approval is contested: the independent market monitor for the PJM grid filed comments on 29 May 2026 asking that the transaction not be approved without a commitment from the buyer not to remove Long Ridge capacity and energy from PJM markets to serve data-centre load, and that monitor has opposed comparable power-plant-to-data-centre acquisitions before. The realistic risk there is conditions and delay rather than denial. Note also what this event is not: the company is the seller, not the target, so there is no offer price for its own shares, no arbitrage spread, and no bid underneath the stock -- which is exactly why the shares fell about 13% in ten sessions while the deal remained fully on track.
FIP.consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is not about whether the deal closes -- the market broadly expects it to, and so do we. The disagreement is about what closing is worth. The published targets of $8.75 (JonesTrading, initiated 1 July 2026), $10 (Citizens JMP, cut from $12 on 15 July 2026) and up to $12 imply capitalising management's $278 million near-term earnings target at roughly seventeen to eighteen times. Two assumptions inside that are, on the evidence, wrong or at least unearned. First, the target is treated as a near-term number when management's own build makes $80 million of it -- nearly a third -- dependent on Repauno phase two, which reaches mechanical completion in autumn 2026 and begins commissioning and operations in the first quarter of 2027, and which lost $2.3 million in the first quarter of 2026. On the earnings that will actually exist when the deal closes, roughly $198 million, seventeen times leaves the common worth nothing after senior claims. Second, and more important, the sell-side framing consistently under-weights the rail-holding-company preferred: about $1 billion placed with funds managed by Ares Management, carried at $970.5 million, redeemable at $1,417.49 per share for roughly $1.4 billion, with dividends paid in kind so it compounds ahead of the common and is not repayable until 25 August 2032. Deduct it at redemption value and roughly $2.35 a share of equity value disappears for every turn of multiple you have to give back. Where the market is right and the bulls have a point is that the deal is real, the buyer is committed and still buying adjacent assets, and the rail business is compounding at 31% year on year. Where our own board entry was wrong is the floor: $3.90 was never a structural level, only the prior 52-week low, and it broke on 29-31 July 2026.
FIP.valley_of_death: The risky window is the next three to nine months and it is unusually well defined. First, the approval itself: no Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order had been published as of 3 August 2026, with a live protest from the PJM market monitor asking for output commitments as a condition. A conditioned approval is the most likely adverse outcome and would slow the close; the contract permits slippage to 30 November 2026 and, on regulatory grounds, to 30 June 2027. Every month of delay is another month of a 9.75% term loan coupon against $37.9 million of unrestricted cash. Second, liquidity between here and the close: the company is loss-making at the bottom line -- a $127.2 million net loss and $1.32 loss per share in the first quarter of 2026 against a consensus near $0.35 -- with negative book equity of $303.1 million and going-concern comfort in the filings that rests explicitly on this sale completing. Third, a maturity that has been moved rather than removed: the 1 July 2026 Jefferson refinancing replaced $217.9 million of 2024-vintage revenue bonds with a $230 million secured bridge loan from Jefferies Finance due 30 June 2027. That has to be termed out inside a year, into whatever credit market exists then, on a B3-rated negative-outlook borrower. Fourth, capital discipline drift: the $45 million Tidewater Logistics acquisition on 29 June 2026 was funded by upsizing the term loan, adding parent debt in the middle of a deleveraging story -- a pattern worth watching, because more of it would undo the point of the sale. Fifth, the two immediate information events: second-quarter results on 5 August 2026 and the buyer's results on 6 August 2026. Either can move the closing timeline, and given the stock is already at a 52-week low on a five-session losing streak, the market is not positioned for good news.
FIP.positioning_washout: The forced-selling picture is thin rather than dramatic, which is itself a warning. This is a roughly $441 million company on 118.2 million shares -- too small for meaningful index demand and small enough that a single fund exiting moves it. The most likely mechanical seller is the income base: the company still pays a three-cent quarterly dividend that is a rounding error against a 9.75% term loan, and it is by far the cheapest line item to cut if the closing timeline slips. A cut would push out whatever yield-oriented holders remain, most of whom bought this as a spin-out from a dividend-paying parent. Rating-driven selling has already partly happened: Moody's rates the company B3 with a negative outlook, Wall Street Zen moved to its strongest sell rating on 21 July 2026, and Citizens JMP cut its target from $12 to $10 on 15 July 2026 while keeping a positive rating. The five-session decline into a 52-week low at $3.71 on 31 July 2026 has the texture of position liquidation ahead of the 5 August results rather than a clean capitulation -- there is no volume spike or single-day flush that would mark a washout low. The absence of a completed flush is precisely why waiting has value here: the shareholder base has not yet been cleared, and there is no natural bid, because the company is the seller in this transaction and its own shares carry no offer price.
FIP.moderator_conclusion: This is a real, binding, dated event attached to the wrong side of a capital structure, and it should not be sized as the asymmetric special situation it was screened as. Everything on the event leg checks out: a definitive agreement signed 30 April 2026 to sell the Long Ridge power business to MARA Holdings for about $1.52 billion, a committed buyer that has cleared its own bondholder consents and keeps acquiring adjacent power assets, proper advisers on both sides, a filed regulatory application, and a contractual termination date of 30 November 2026 with a regulatory extension to 30 June 2027. Management has executed the financing plan competently -- refinancing a bridge into a $1.35 billion term loan, closing the Wheeling and Lake Erie acquisition and delivering 31% rail earnings growth, refinancing the Jefferson bonds. What fails is the risk leg, and it fails on verified facts rather than judgement. The level this position was underwritten against as a floor, $3.90, broke in the last week of July 2026; the shares closed at $3.73 on 31 July at a new 52-week low of $3.71, having fallen five sessions running. There is nothing structural beneath that price: book equity is negative $303.1 million, unrestricted cash was $37.9 million at 31 March 2026, the going-concern assessment leans on this very sale, and roughly $3.8 billion of debt and compounding preferred sits ahead of a $441 million equity stub -- including about $1.4 billion of rail-holding-company preferred that pays dividends in kind and is not redeemable until 2032. Because senior claims are that large, the equity swings about $2.35 a share for every single turn of the multiple applied to the operating businesses, and the entire published bull case rests on capitalising an earnings target at seventeen to eighteen times whose largest component -- $80 million from Repauno phase two -- does not begin operating until the first quarter of 2027, after the event window shuts. Probability-weight the paths honestly and fair value lands at about $3.70, essentially on top of the price. That is the definition of a fairly priced option, not a mispriced spread. The right posture is to wait, and the things to wait for are specific rather than atmospheric: the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order in docket EC26-92-000 without value-destroying output conditions, the deal actually closing with more than $300 million of net proceeds visibly applied to the 9.75% parent term loan, and confirmation at the second-quarter results on 5 August 2026 that Repauno phase two still reaches mechanical completion this autumn. Get those three and the seventeen-times case becomes underwritable and $8 to $10 is reachable. Alternatively, a price below about $2.50 would pay properly for what this actually is -- a leveraged call on infrastructure multiples over a scarce but heavily encumbered rail franchise. Buying it here, at fair value, with the floor already broken and the shares falling into the catalyst, is taking the option risk without the option price.
FIP.interrogator_dossier:
# FTAI Infrastructure Inc. (FIP) -- Event Dossier

Prepared 3 August 2026. All prices and filings verified against public sources on that date.

The one-line version: the catalyst is real and contractually binding -- a signed agreement to sell the Long Ridge power business to MARA Holdings for about $1.52 billion -- but it is a survival event, not a value-unlock event, and the downside floor this candidate was scored against has already given way.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC -- what the company is trying to become

FTAI Infrastructure was spun out of Fortress Transportation in 2022 as a grab-bag of hard assets: two freight railroads (Transtar, and Wheeling & Lake Erie, bought for $1.05 billion and closed in 2025), a deepwater crude and ammonia terminal on the Texas coast (Jefferson), a natural-gas storage and export terminal on the Delaware River (Repauno), and a 485-megawatt gas-fired power plant in Ohio (Long Ridge).

Across the last four quarters the story has narrowed sharply and deliberately. Management now describes the company as a freight-rail platform that happens to be carrying two terminals and a power plant it intends to sell. Chief executive Ken Nicholson framed the Long Ridge agreement on 30 April 2026 as a key step in the strategic plan, unlocking value to shareholders and deleveraging the company. On the first-quarter call in May, management went further and named Jefferson and Repauno as the next assets out the door, within twelve to eighteen months, with roughly $700 million of the resulting cash earmarked for parent-company debt.

That is a coherent plan. It is also an admission: the company is selling assets because the balance sheet demands it, not because the market is paying a premium.

## 2. THE EVENT -- is it real, dated and binding?

Yes on real and binding; qualified on dated.

- What: a definitive equity purchase agreement, announced 30 April 2026, to sell Long Ridge Energy & Power LLC -- a 485-to-505 megawatt combined-cycle gas plant at Hannibal, Ohio, working interests in gas wells, and roughly 1,600 contiguous acres on the Ohio River -- to a subsidiary of MARA Holdings for about $1.52 billion before closing adjustments.
- Who is buying: MARA Holdings, the former bitcoin miner now rebuilding itself as an artificial-intelligence data-centre and power company. Its commitment looks genuine rather than opportunistic: it has secured consents from holders of its 8.75% senior notes to permit the acquisition (June 2026), sold about $1.5 billion of bitcoin to fund its infrastructure push, and has kept buying power assets since -- a 1,200-acre powered site in Matagorda County, Texas on 9 July 2026. A buyer that keeps writing cheques for adjacent assets is not a buyer looking for a way out.
- What still has to happen: clearance under the Hart-Scott-Rodino antitrust act, and approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for the change of control under section 203 of the Federal Power Act. The joint application was filed on 8 May 2026 under docket EC26-92-000, with a comment deadline of 29 May 2026. Related railroad agreements also require Surface Transportation Board coordination.
- The dates that actually bind: the purchase agreement can be terminated by either side if the deal has not closed by 30 November 2026, extending to 30 June 2027 if regulatory conditions remain outstanding. Management's guidance is a close in the third quarter of 2026, with approval in the middle of the third quarter.

This matters for how the candidate was scored. The 30 September 2026 date in our board entry is management's guidance, not a contractual deadline. The binding outside date is two months later, with a further seven-month regulatory extension available. A slip past September is permitted by the contract and would not break the deal -- but it would break the timing assumption the position was underwritten on.

The live regulatory friction: on 29 May 2026 the independent market monitor for the PJM grid filed comments at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission urging that the transaction not be approved without a commitment from the buyer not to remove the Long Ridge capacity and energy from PJM markets to serve data-centre load. The monitor has taken the same position against comparable power-plant-to-data-centre acquisitions before. The buyer's answer is that it intends to keep participating in PJM markets. As of 3 August 2026 no order granting the authorisation has been published. This is the single open item, and it is the kind of item that produces conditions and delay rather than outright denial -- but delay is exactly what this balance sheet cannot absorb cheaply.

## 3. THE CLAIM VERSUS THE ARITHMETIC -- where the deal money actually goes

Management's own pro-forma figures, from the first-quarter 2026 presentation: total debt falls from $3.814 billion to $2.377 billion; parent-company debt from $1.310 billion to $1.019 billion; subsidiary non-recourse debt from $2.504 billion to $1.358 billion; corporate leverage (debt measured against earnings) from 9.5 times to 7.4 times.

Net cash to the company is more than $300 million, essentially all of which repays parent debt, saving about $30 million a year of interest. The $1.16 billion of debt that disappears was borrowed against Long Ridge itself and was never a claim on the rest of the company.

Read those figures honestly. The sale takes leverage from distressed to merely very high. Management's own stated destination is 5.1 times, which the sale alone does not reach. The price paid -- $1.52 billion for an asset that generated about $144 million of annualised earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation in the second half of 2025, with 76% of output contracted -- works out near eleven times. That is a fair price, not a windfall. The transaction is close to value-neutral on enterprise value and enormously positive on liquidity. Anyone underwriting this as a hidden-value unlock has the wrong model of it.

Where the earnings actually have to come from. Management's near-term target is $278 million of adjusted earnings excluding Long Ridge. The build is explicit: the first quarter's run rate annualises to roughly $176 million, plus $13 million from integrating Wheeling & Lake Erie with Transtar, plus $9 million from new Jefferson contracts, plus $80 million from Repauno phase two. Repauno phase two reaches mechanical completion in autumn 2026 and begins commissioning and operations in the first quarter of 2027.

So the largest single component of the target -- nearly a third of it -- is a construction project that will not produce a dollar of earnings until after the catalyst window closes. Segment detail for the first quarter of 2026: rail $40.2 million (up 31% year on year), Jefferson $14.4 million, Long Ridge $26.4 million, Repauno negative $2.3 million, consolidated $70.6 million.

## 4. THE FLOOR -- what actually backstops the price if the event disappoints

There is no verified floor. This is the finding that should govern the decision.

- The stock closed at $3.73 on 31 July 2026, down 6.75% that day, on its 52-week low of $3.71. Our board entry carried a live price of $4.16 and a downside floor of $3.90. The price is already through the floor, roughly 4% below it, and it got there falling five sessions in a row and eight of ten, down about 13% over that stretch. Over twelve months the shares are down roughly 37%.
- The claims ahead of the common shareholder are overwhelming. Against a market value of about $441 million on 118.2 million shares sit, after the sale closes, roughly $2.38 billion of debt plus a preferred-stock claim at the rail holding company. That preferred -- about $1 billion sold to funds managed by Ares Management to finance the Wheeling & Lake Erie purchase -- carried $970.5 million on the books at 31 March 2026 and would be redeemable at $1,417.49 per share, roughly $1.4 billion in total, with dividends paid in kind (added to the balance rather than paid in cash, so the claim compounds). Its earliest redemption is 25 August 2032. Total senior claims are therefore near $3.8 billion against a $441 million equity stub.
- Book equity is already negative: total equity attributable to the company was negative $303.1 million at 31 March 2026.
- The liquidity language is the standard substantial-doubt-alleviated formulation. The first-quarter filing states that the planned sale will further improve the liquidity position and that planned actions are considered probable to be implemented and to provide sufficient liquidity for the company to meet its obligations. That sentence is what a company writes when the going-concern question was live and management resolved it by pointing at the asset sale. If the sale slips materially, the sentence has to be rewritten.
- Cash is thin: $37.9 million unrestricted at 31 March 2026, with $189.6 million restricted.

Run the value the other way and the picture is stark. Because the claims are so large, the equity behaves like a call option on the multiple applied to the operating businesses. Capitalising the $278 million target and deducting $2.38 billion of debt and a $1.42 billion preferred claim across 118.2 million shares: at fourteen times the shares are worth about $0.76; at fifteen times about $3.13; at sixteen times about $5.50; at seventeen times about $7.87; at eighteen times about $10.20. Every single turn of multiple is worth roughly $2.35 a share. On today's actual earnings power -- roughly $198 million once the rail synergies and Jefferson contracts land but before Repauno produces anything -- the common is worth close to nothing at any conventional infrastructure multiple.

That is not defined risk. That is a leveraged option with an unbounded loss.

## 5. MANAGEMENT AND SPONSOR CREDIBILITY ON DELIVERY

The financing execution has been genuinely good, and it deserves credit: a bridge facility refinanced into a $1.35 billion term loan maturing February 2028 (at a punishing 9.75% coupon); the Wheeling & Lake Erie acquisition closed and the promised integration delivering, with rail earnings up 31% year on year in the first quarter of 2026; Long Ridge signed with Jefferies and Lazard advising and Skadden as counsel, a properly resourced process; $217.9 million of Jefferson 2024B revenue bonds refinanced on 1 July 2026 with a $230 million secured bridge loan from Jefferies Finance; and the $45 million Tidewater Logistics acquisition closed 29 June 2026.

The delivery on earnings has been considerably weaker. The first quarter of 2026 produced a net loss of $127.2 million and a loss per share of $1.32 against a consensus expectation near $0.35 -- a miss of a different order of magnitude, not a rounding error. Moody's rates the company B3 with a negative outlook. The equity has halved.

Two items deserve to be flagged as behaviour, not accounting. First, the Tidewater purchase was funded by upsizing the term loan -- adding parent-level debt during a quarter whose entire narrative was deleveraging. Second, the Jefferson refinancing did not remove a maturity; it moved $218 million from 2024-vintage bonds into a bridge loan due 30 June 2027. Bridges are meant to be crossed. This one has to be termed out inside twelve months.

## 6. RED AND GREEN FLAGS

Red flags: the stated downside floor of $3.90 broke in the last week of July 2026, with a new 52-week low at $3.71 and the shares falling into the catalyst rather than tightening toward it; preferred stock at the rail holding company that pays dividends in kind and compounds ahead of the common, with a redemption claim near $1.4 billion, more than three times the entire equity market value; negative book equity, and liquidity language in the filings that reads as going-concern doubt resolved by pointing at the pending sale; a first-quarter loss per share nearly four times the consensus expectation; new debt raised for an acquisition inside a deleveraging quarter, and a $230 million bridge loan due June 2027 still to be refinanced; nearly a third of the earnings target dependent on a construction project that does not begin operating until the first quarter of 2027 and has never earned a positive dollar; an open regulatory protest with no approval order published as of 3 August 2026; and a downgrade to the strongest sell rating by Wall Street Zen on 21 July 2026, alongside a Citizens JMP target cut from $12 to $10 on 15 July 2026 with a positive rating retained.

Green flags: the agreement is definitive and binding, with a committed and well-capitalised counterparty visibly still building in the same direction; the buyer has already cleared its own bondholder-consent hurdle, removing one of the two ways this deal could have died on financing grounds; the rail business is performing, at $40.2 million of quarterly earnings, up 31% year on year, from assets that are genuinely scarce -- short-line and regional railroads are local franchises that cannot be rebuilt; the sale removes $1.16 billion of debt and about $30 million a year of interest; three analysts carry targets between $8.75 and $12, so the gap between price and published fair value is not our invention; and two dated information events sit immediately ahead -- second-quarter results after the close on 5 August 2026 and the buyer's results on 6 August 2026.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The language has shifted from building to selling. A year ago the story was a diversified infrastructure platform; today the same management describes a sequence of disposals with the proceeds pre-assigned to debt. The common dividend, held at three cents a quarter, is now a rounding error against a 9.75% term loan -- it survives as a signal to income holders rather than as a return of capital, and it is the cheapest thing on the balance sheet to cut if the timeline slips.

Note also what the deal does not do for the equity. FTAI Infrastructure is the seller here, not the target. There is no offer price for its shares, no arbitrage spread, and no bid underneath the stock. Selling shareholders in a seller-side transaction get the proceeds, not a takeout -- which is precisely why the shares can and did fall while the deal remained fully on track.

## 8. VERDICT FOR THE DIRECTOR

Trajectory: turning. The company is mid-transformation from a levered infrastructure conglomerate into a freight-rail platform, and the transformation is being executed competently on financing terms and unevenly on operating results.

The single thing to weigh before sizing: this candidate was selected as a defined-risk special situation -- a live dated event with a floor underneath it. The event is live and binding; the floor is not there. The price has already traded through the level that was supposed to bound the loss, senior claims of roughly $3.8 billion sit ahead of a $441 million equity stub, and the value of that stub swings about $2.35 a share for every single turn of the earnings multiple applied to the operating businesses. The upside to $8 or $9 is arithmetically reachable, but only by capitalising an earnings target at roughly seventeen times -- a target whose largest component does not begin producing until the first quarter of 2027, after the event window shuts.

On the economic franchise itself: the railroads are a narrow but real moat -- regulated local franchises with switching costs that a competitor cannot replicate -- and there is no structural force eroding demand for freight rail or coastal terminals. The threat here is financial, not secular. But a narrow moat inside a capital structure this heavy accrues its value to lenders and preferred holders first, and to the common shareholder only after roughly $3.8 billion of claims are satisfied.

The honest characterisation is that this is a leveraged call option on infrastructure multiples with a real, dated event attached -- not an asymmetric, defined-risk trade. It should be sized as an option, or not taken until the regulatory approval and the actual cash application are on the tape.
