FUN.bull_thesis: The bull case is that the activist campaign eventually forces a sale of the whole company, and that the leverage on the balance sheet turns a modest move in the takeover multiple into a very large move in the share price. Six Flags Entertainment, which trades under the ticker FUN because the surviving entity of the July 2024 merger is the old Cedar Fair vehicle, runs regional amusement parks across North America. JANA Partners, an activist investment firm, disclosed an economic interest of about 9% on 21 October 2025 alongside Travis Kelce, former Gap and Lululemon chief executive Glenn Murphy, and technology executive Dave Habiger, and on 17 March 2026 publicly demanded the board explore an outright sale and replace its chair. That campaign is still live and has not been withdrawn. The board has already conceded a great deal: a new chief executive (John Reilly, announced 24 November 2025), an executive chairman brought in on 25 March 2026 (Richard Haddrill), a cooperation agreement with a second activist, H Partners, on 19 May 2026 that seated Rehan Jaffer on the board after the 26 May 2026 annual meeting, a new chief financial officer on 17 June 2026 and a new chief operating officer on 15 July 2026. Boards that concede governance this quickly sometimes concede the company a year later. The arithmetic is what makes the bull case worth stating at all. At $17.59 a share the equity is worth about $1.80B while enterprise value is about $7.21B, because net debt was $5.42B at 29 March 2026. The equity is therefore a thin slice on top of a very large debt load, and it is extremely sensitive to the multiple applied to earnings. On roughly $820M of full-year 2026 adjusted profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, a buyer paying about ten and a half times - a normal price for irreplaceable regional park land - produces roughly $31 a share, or about 75% above the current price. That is where the board entry's $31 target comes from. There is an operating leg too. The first quarter of 2026 was genuinely better: revenue up 12% to $225.6M, attendance up 4% to 2.9 million visits, spending per visitor up 6% to $69.26, and the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M to a $123M adjusted loss before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Management has said openly that the 27% margin earned in 2025 is not good enough against regional peers in the low thirties. If the new team closes even half that gap, the same multiple on higher earnings gets to a similar place without any sale at all. The seven-park disposal to EPR Properties for $331.4M in cash, agreed 4 March 2026 and closed in April for the US parks, shows the board will monetise assets under pressure. Conditions this case depends on: a credible buyer must actually appear and finance a deal with an enterprise value above seven billion dollars; the board must be willing to transact near ten and a half times rather than hold out; attendance must stabilise so that the earnings base being multiplied is real; and the quarterly net first-lien leverage covenant must not be tripped in the meantime.
FUN.bear_thesis: The bear case is that there is no sale, no date, and no floor - and that the same leverage which powers the bull case destroys the equity on the way down. Start with the event. Nothing about it is dated or binding. The 2026 annual meeting was held on 26 May 2026 and no activist slate went to a vote, so the proxy window that could have forced the issue this year has closed; the next natural pressure point is the nomination window for the 2027 meeting, which has no announced date. JANA's own release of 24 November 2025 disclosed that Glenn Murphy had de-grouped from the investor group to discuss a senior leadership role with the board and that Dave Habiger remained de-grouped to pursue a separate opportunity involving the company - two of three named operating partners absorbed into the target within weeks. The board seat that did change hands went to a different activist, H Partners, under the 19 May 2026 cooperation agreement. Every demand for a sale has been answered with something cheaper and adjacent: a chair, a director seat for someone else, seven peripheral parks. No sale process, strategic review or data room has been announced in any filing through 28 July 2026. Now the floor, which is the part of the board entry that does not survive contact with the tape. The entry assumes a downside floor of $16.50 against a live price of $17.59 - about 6% of risk. The shares traded at $12.51 within the last twelve months, 29% below that level. A price the security has recently traded straight through is not a floor. There is no asset backstop underneath it either. At 29 March 2026 the company held $116.5M of cash against $5.53B of total debt, $5.42B net, with $235M of minority interest ahead of common holders and total shareholders' equity down to $279M after a $1.19B net loss in the third quarter of 2025 (a loss of $11.80 a share) that wrote off merger goodwill. Retained earnings stand at negative $2.03B. Free cash flow is close to nothing: capital spending absorbed about 93% of operating cash flow over the trailing twelve months, leaving about $29M of trailing free cash flow against interest expense running near $95M a quarter. The company cannot deleverage out of cash flow; it can only sell assets. Because the equity is a thin slice of a $7.21B enterprise, one turn of multiple compression is worth roughly $10 a share. Eight and a half times $800M of earnings is about $15 a share; seven and a half times $760M is about $7. And the relevant market-clearing comparable points the wrong way: EPR Properties paid roughly eight and a half times for the seven-park package, well below the ten and a half times the $31 target requires. The near-term news flow is already confirming the bear case. On 19 July 2026 Citi cut its price target from $24 to $19 with a neutral rating and Guggenheim also cut, both citing softer attendance, with hazardous air quality from Ontario wildfires affecting fourteen parks across the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes during the peak season. Jefferies carries a below-consensus full-year 2026 estimate of about $865M and warns street attendance assumptions are too high. What would confirm the bear case: a weak second-quarter print on 6 August 2026; a third quarter that captures the July weather damage; any commentary that pushes the quarterly net first-lien leverage test toward its limit; and the passing of the 2027 nomination window without a slate.
FUN.sop_bull: Event-win value: about $30 to $31 a share. Derivation: a whole-company sale at roughly ten and a half times full-year adjusted profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of about $850M gives an enterprise value near $8.9B; subtract about $5.15B of expected year-end 2026 net debt (net debt was $5.42B at the seasonal peak on 29 March 2026, less the $331.4M of EPR proceeds received in April) and $235M of minority interest, leaving roughly $3.1B of equity across about 101.5 million shares. Ten and a half times is defensible for irreplaceable regional park land - Cedar Point, Knott's Berry Farm, Magic Mountain - in a financial buyer's hands, and it is the multiple implied by the board entry's own $31 target. A self-help path reaches a similar place more slowly: if the margin gap management has acknowledged (27% in 2025 against regional peers above 30%) is half closed, roughly $900M of earnings at nine and a half times is about $32 a share.
FUN.sop_bear: Verified downside floor: about $10 to $12 a share, not the $16.50 the board entry assumes. Derivation, three independent ways. First, the tape: the 52-week low is $12.51, set within the past twelve months, which is a level the market has already been willing to pay - and there is nothing structural beneath it. Second, the multiple: at eight and a half times - the rough multiple EPR Properties paid for the seven-park package in the only recent arm's-length transaction in these assets - on about $800M of earnings, enterprise value is $6.8B, which after $5.15B of net debt and $235M of minority interest leaves about $1.4B of equity, or roughly $14 a share; at seven and a half times on $760M it is about $7. Third, the balance sheet offers no backstop at all: $116.5M of cash, $5.53B of total debt, $279M of book equity, negative $2.03B of retained earnings, tangible asset value of negative $2.24B, and trailing free cash flow of roughly $29M against interest expense near $380M a year. In an outright attendance recession that trips the quarterly net first-lien leverage covenant, the equity is worth materially less than $7. The honest statement is that this equity has no verified floor - $10 to $12 is a judgement about where forced sellers stopped last time, not a backstop.
FUN.sop_breakdown: Base case of about $18 a share, which is a probability-weighted blend rather than a single valuation, because a levered equity stub does not have a central case so much as a barbell. Weighting: roughly 20% chance of a whole-company sale at about ten and a half times earnings, worth about $30; roughly 40% chance the turnaround works without a sale and the market pays about nine and a quarter times a higher earnings base, worth about $22; roughly 40% chance attendance keeps sliding and the multiple compresses toward eight times or below, worth about $9. That blend is $18.60, which is within a dollar of the live price of $17.59. The parts, for orientation: enterprise value at the current price is about $7.21B, of which the operating park portfolio after the seven-park disposal is essentially all of it. Against that sit $5.42B of net debt at the 29 March 2026 seasonal peak (roughly $5.15B expected at year end after $331.4M of EPR proceeds received in April), $235M of minority interest, and $116.5M of cash. Common equity is the residual across about 101.5 million shares. Because debt is roughly three quarters of enterprise value, each single turn of multiple on about $820M of earnings is worth roughly $8 to $10 a share to the equity - which is why the honest fair value is a range spanning more than three times from bottom to top, and why the mean sits almost exactly on the market price. There is no measurable edge in this valuation.
FUN.risk_reward: Roughly 1.6 to 1 gross, and negative once probability is applied - not the 2.6 to 1 the board entry claims. Upside to the event-resolved target of about $30 is roughly +71% from $17.59. Downside to the verified floor of about $10 to $12 is roughly -32% to -43%. The board entry's 2.6 to 1 depended entirely on a $16.50 floor implying only 6% of risk, and that floor was broken by the market at $12.51 within the past twelve months. Adjusting for odds makes it worse: the sale outcome carries perhaps a one-in-five chance with no date and no identified buyer, while the downside scenarios are being actively confirmed by July attendance news and two broker target cuts. The expected value sits at or slightly below the current price.
FUN.catalyst_summary: An undated, non-binding activist push by JANA Partners (about 9% economic interest, sale demand letter 17 March 2026) that the board has so far answered with governance changes and asset sales rather than a sale process; the 2026 proxy window closed at the 26 May 2026 annual meeting without a contested vote, and the claimed $16.50 downside floor was already broken at $12.51 within the past year, so the asymmetry is roughly +71% against -35% rather than the 6%-risk trade it was written up as.
FUN.dated_milestone: No dated milestone attaches to the catalyst itself. The only firm dates on the calendar are operating, not event, dates: second-quarter 2026 results before the open on Thursday 6 August 2026 with a call at 8am Eastern, and the quarterly net first-lien leverage covenant test under the 2024 credit agreement at each quarter end. The activist forcing points that have already passed are the 26 May 2026 annual meeting (held with no contested vote) and the 19 May 2026 cooperation agreement with H Partners. The next potential forcing point is the director nomination window for the 2027 annual meeting, which has not been announced and sits roughly six to nine months ahead.
FUN.forcing_function: There is no genuine forcing function in place today, and that is the central finding. What would have forced a re-rating - a contested vote at the 26 May 2026 annual meeting - did not happen; JANA ran no slate, and the board seat that changed hands went to a different activist, H Partners' Rehan Jaffer, under a cooperation agreement signed 19 May 2026. Two of the three operating partners JANA named in its October 2025 group had already de-grouped by 24 November 2025 to pursue roles with the company. Three things could become forcing functions, in descending order of likelihood. First, and nearest, second-quarter results on 6 August 2026 - but that is an earnings print, and the evidence points to it being a risk rather than a catalyst, given Citi's 19 July 2026 cut from $24 to $19 and Guggenheim's cut, both on soft attendance including wildfire smoke advisories across fourteen parks. Second, further asset sales in the pattern of the $331.4M EPR Properties disposal, which deleverage but also shrink the earnings base being multiplied. Third, the 2027 director nomination window, which would let JANA actually run the slate it threatened - unannounced, and roughly six to nine months away. A whole-company sale remains possible but has no date, no announced process, and no identified buyer, and would require financing an enterprise value above seven billion dollars.
FUN.consensus_delta: The disagreement here is not with Wall Street's view of the business - it is with our own board entry's view of the risk. The street is, if anything, roughly right: Citi cut to $19 with a neutral rating on 19 July 2026, Guggenheim cut on softer attendance while keeping a $28 target, and Jefferies sits below consensus at about $865M of full-year 2026 earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, warning that street attendance and revenue assumptions are too optimistic. The shares at $17.59 sit between the bear and bull marks. That is a market doing its job. Where we disagree with the write-up that brought this name to the committee is on two specific claims. The first is that the downside is bounded at $16.50. It is not - the shares printed $12.51 within the last twelve months, and the balance sheet offers nothing beneath that: $116.5M of cash against $5.53B of total debt, book equity of $279M, tangible asset value of negative $2.24B, and trailing free cash flow near $29M. The second is that the activist process is a live catalyst. On the evidence it has been managed rather than obeyed: the sale demand of 17 March 2026 was answered with an executive chairman on 25 March, a cooperation agreement with a different activist on 19 May, and an annual meeting on 26 May with no contested vote. The one genuine expectations gap that could work in the bull's favour is that the market may be underrating the operating recovery: the first quarter of 2026 showed attendance up 4%, spending per visitor up 6% to $69.26 and the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M, and management has openly targeted the gap between its 27% margin and regional peers above 30%. But the first quarter is the smallest quarter of the year, and July's weather damage lands in the third-quarter print reported in November. That gap will not be settled in this window.
FUN.valley_of_death: The next three to nine months are where this position is most exposed, and the exposure is already visible rather than hypothetical. The immediate event is second-quarter results on 6 August 2026. The second and third quarters are the entire year for a regional park operator, and the July news flow has been bad: on 19 July 2026 Citi cut its target from $24 to $19 citing hazardous air quality from Ontario wildfires affecting fourteen parks across the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes, with health advisories telling people to stay indoors during peak season; Guggenheim cut on the same theme. That damage falls into the third-quarter print reported in November, so there are two consecutive negative-skew events between now and the end of the year. Underneath sits the leverage. Net debt was $5.42B at 29 March 2026 against roughly $820M of expected annual earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, or about six and a half times. The 2024 credit agreement carries a maximum net first-lien leverage covenant tested at the end of every quarter, so a bad season does not merely dent earnings - it compresses the headroom in a maintenance test. Interest expense runs near $95M a quarter. Free cash flow cannot help: capital spending absorbed about 93% of operating cash flow over the trailing twelve months, leaving roughly $29M of trailing free cash flow. The only real deleveraging lever is more asset sales, and each one sells earnings as well as debt. The mechanical risk to be explicit about: because the equity is only about a quarter of a $7.21B enterprise value, a disappointing season that takes the multiple from about nine times to about eight times is worth roughly $9 a share to the common - more than half the current price - without anything dramatic happening to the debt.
FUN.positioning_washout: The forced selling has mostly already happened, which is why the shares are near the bottom of a $12.51 to $31.99 range rather than in free fall. The old Cedar Fair was for decades an income vehicle with a substantial distribution, and its shareholder register was built accordingly. The dividend now stands at zero. That eviction of the yield-focused base is complete, not pending - it is the single biggest reason the shares de-rated from the low thirties. Similarly, the merger-arbitrage and merger-synergy holders who bought the 2024 Cedar Fair and Six Flags combination have had two years and a $1.19B goodwill write-off in the third quarter of 2025 to leave. What remains is a register split between event-driven money that bought the JANA story after October 2025 and value money underwriting the parks. The unfinished risk is on the event side: if the second-quarter print on 6 August 2026 is weak and the activist process visibly stalls into the 2027 nomination window, the event-driven holders have no reason to stay, and their exit is not disciplined by valuation. With a market value under $1.8B, that flow moves the price. There is also index risk - a company this size with negative book momentum can face mechanical selling on a downgrade out of mid-cap benchmarks. On the constructive side, a register that has already lost its income holders and taken its impairment is a cleaner starting point than one still shedding them. But 'the washout has happened' is a reason to look, not a reason to own - and it does not create a floor.
FUN.moderator_conclusion: Pass for now. This came to the committee described as a defined-risk special situation - risk about 6% to make about 76%, with the loss bounded by a floor at $16.50. Verification does not support either half of that. On the event: JANA Partners' demand that the board sell the company is real and still live, but it is undated, non-binding, and dependent on a buyer who has not appeared to finance an enterprise value above seven billion dollars. More importantly, the board has answered it without conceding it. Since the 17 March 2026 sale letter the company has installed an executive chairman (25 March 2026), signed a cooperation agreement with a different activist, H Partners, seating Rehan Jaffer (19 May 2026), held its annual meeting with no contested vote (26 May 2026), and filled out a turnaround management team with a new chief financial officer (17 June 2026) and chief operating officer (15 July 2026). Two of the three operating partners JANA originally named had already left the group by 24 November 2025 to pursue roles with the company. Boards that intend to sell hire bankers and announce reviews; this one hired operators. The proxy window that could have forced the question in 2026 has closed, and the next one is unannounced and roughly six to nine months away. On the floor, which matters more: there isn't one. The shares traded at $12.51 within the past twelve months, 29% below the level the write-up treats as protected. Behind that price sits $116.5M of cash against $5.53B of total debt, book equity of $279M, retained earnings of negative $2.03B after the $1.19B write-off in the third quarter of 2025, and trailing free cash flow of roughly $29M against interest expense near $380M a year. This is a levered equity stub in which the common is about a quarter of a $7.21B enterprise value, so one turn of multiple compression is worth roughly $9 to $10 a share. The only recent arm's-length transaction in these assets - EPR Properties paying $342M gross for seven parks - clears at roughly eight and a half times, below the ten and a half times the $31 target requires. Run the probabilities honestly and fair value lands at about $18 - a fifth of the outcomes around $30 on a sale, two fifths around $22 if the turnaround works, two fifths around $9 if attendance keeps sliding. That mean is within a dollar of the $17.59 market price. There is no edge in the valuation, and the near-term skew is negative: second-quarter results land 6 August 2026, July's wildfire-smoke attendance damage lands in the November print, Citi cut to $19 on 19 July and Guggenheim cut as well, and the quarterly net first-lien leverage covenant is tested through all of it. None of this says the business is worthless. The first quarter of 2026 was genuinely better - attendance up 4%, spending per visitor up 6% to $69.26, the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M - and the land under Cedar Point, Knott's Berry Farm and Magic Mountain cannot be replicated. If the new team closes the margin gap it has publicly acknowledged, this is a much better stock in two years. But that is a leveraged turnaround underwritten on execution, and it belongs in a different book with different sizing, not in an event sleeve where the whole justification is a bounded loss. What would change the answer: a formally announced strategic review or sale process; an identified bidder with committed financing; a JANA slate filed for the 2027 annual meeting; or the shares in the low teens after a capitulation print, where the reward-to-risk that was claimed at $17.59 would actually exist.
FUN.interrogator_dossier:
# FUN - Six Flags Entertainment Corporation

## Event-driven special situation: activist campaign for a sale of the company

**Interrogator dossier - forensic read of the EVENT, not the franchise.**
Prepared 28 July 2026. All prices and filings verified against live sources on that date.

---

## 0. WHAT THIS TRADE ACTUALLY IS

Six Flags Entertainment trades under the ticker FUN because the surviving legal entity of the
July 2024 merger is the old Cedar Fair vehicle. The company runs regional amusement parks
across North America - Cedar Point, Knott's Berry Farm, Magic Mountain, Great Adventure and
roughly forty others after recent disposals.

The reason this name reached our board is not the parks. It is JANA Partners, an activist
investment firm, which on 21 October 2025 disclosed an economic interest of about 9% alongside
the retired NFL player Travis Kelce, former Gap and Lululemon chief executive Glenn Murphy, and
technology executive Dave Habiger. On 17 March 2026 JANA sent the board a public letter
demanding it explore an outright sale of the company and remove the board chair. Our board
entry values a successful outcome at $31 a share against a supposed downside floor of $16.50,
implying reward-to-risk of about 2.6 to 1.

The core question for this dossier is narrow: is that event real, dated and binding, and is
that floor real? The answer to both is no.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC - HOW THE EVENT HAS ACTUALLY DEVELOPED

The campaign has moved through four visible stages, and the direction of travel is away from a
sale, not toward one.

**Stage one - the stake (21 October 2025).** JANA discloses roughly 9% economic interest with a
celebrity-plus-operator group. The framing is collaborative: work with the board and management
to improve the guest experience and enhance value.

**Stage two - the group dissolves into the company (24 November 2025).** In its own release
applauding the hire of John Reilly as president and chief executive, JANA discloses that Glenn
Murphy "has de-grouped from the JANA-led investor group to advance discussions with Six Flags on
a potential senior leadership role with the Board," and that Dave Habiger "remains de-grouped
from the JANA-led investor group to enable him to pursue a complementary, but separate,
opportunity involving the Company." This is the language of a settlement, not a proxy fight. Two
of the three named operating partners left the activist group to take company roles within five
weeks of the stake being announced.

**Stage three - the escalation (17 March 2026).** With the shares still falling, JANA publicly
demands an immediate sale process and the ouster of the board chair, naming Murphy and Habiger
as prospective directors. This is the high-water mark of the campaign and the moment our board
entry was almost certainly seeded.

**Stage four - the board absorbs the pressure without selling (March to July 2026).** The
company's answer has been governance and asset sales, not a sale process:

| Date | Action | What it substitutes for |
|---|---|---|
| Nov 2025 / Dec 2025 | John Reilly appointed president and chief executive | New management instead of new owners |
| 4 March 2026 | Agreements to sell seven parks to EPR Properties, $331.4M cash ($342M gross) | Piecemeal asset sales instead of a whole-company sale |
| 25 March 2026 | Richard "Dick" Haddrill named executive chairman, effective immediately | Chair replacement conceded, sale not conceded |
| April 2026 | US portion of the EPR sale closes | Cash in, but only about 6% of net debt |
| 19 May 2026 | Cooperation agreement with H Partners; Rehan Jaffer joins the board after the annual meeting, replacing Arik Ruchim | A different activist is settled with a board seat |
| 26 May 2026 | 2026 annual meeting of stockholders held | The 2026 proxy window closes |
| 17 June 2026 | Ash Walia appointed chief financial officer | |
| 15 July 2026 | Mark Pauls appointed chief operating officer | |

Read the table as a whole and the pattern is unmistakable. Every demand JANA made has been
answered with something other than the thing it asked for. The chair was replaced - with a
turnaround executive chairman, not with a banker running a process. Board refreshment happened -
through a cooperation agreement with a *different* activist, H Partners. Assets were sold - seven
peripheral parks, not the company. And no sale process, strategic review, or data room has been
announced in any filing or release through 28 July 2026.

---

## 2. IS THE CATALYST REAL, DATED AND BINDING?

**Real: yes, partially.** JANA is a serious, well-resourced activist with a genuine 9% economic
interest and a public demand on the record. The campaign has not been withdrawn. That is more
than nothing.

**Dated: no.** There is no date attached to anything. Our own board entry carries the catalyst as
undated, and the verification confirms it. Worse, the one date that mattered has passed: the 2026
annual meeting was held on 26 May 2026. Director nominations for that meeting closed months
earlier, and no JANA slate went to a vote. The next natural forcing point - the nomination window
for the 2027 annual meeting - sits roughly six to nine months out and has no announced date.

**Binding: no.** Nothing here is contractual. A sale requires a third party to appear, agree a
price, and finance a transaction with an enterprise value above seven billion dollars against an
equity market value of under two billion. No bidder has been publicly identified. Reports of
"private equity interest" trace to commentary about the turnaround-heavy composition of the new
board, not to a disclosed approach.

The honest classification is a soft, non-binding, serially open-ended catalyst: real pressure,
no date, no contract, and a counterparty that does not yet exist.

---

## 3. THE FLOOR - THIS IS WHERE THE THESIS BREAKS

The board entry claims a downside floor of $16.50 against a live price of $17.59. That would mean
risking about 6% to make about 76%. It is not credible, and the tape has already falsified it.

**Falsification one - the stock has already traded 29% below the claimed floor.** The 52-week
range is $12.51 to $31.99. The claimed floor of $16.50 was breached within the last twelve months.
A level the security has recently traded straight through is not a floor.

**Falsification two - there is no asset backstop, because the debt eats it.** From the balance
sheet at 29 March 2026:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Cash and equivalents | $116.5M |
| Total debt (incl. finance leases) | $5.53B |
| Net debt | $5.42B |
| Minority interest | $235M |
| Total shareholders' equity | $279M |
| Enterprise value at $17.59 | ~$7.21B |
| Market capitalisation | ~$1.80B |

The equity is a thin slice - roughly a quarter of enterprise value - sitting on top of $5.4B of
net debt. That is the definition of a levered stub. Small changes in the multiple the market
applies to earnings swing the equity violently. Working the arithmetic on a full-year 2026
adjusted profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (adjusted EBITDA) of about
$820M, and using year-end net claims of roughly $5.4B including the minority interest:

| Multiple applied | Implied enterprise value | Implied value per share |
|---|---|---|
| 7.5x | $6.15B | ~$7 |
| 8.5x | $6.97B | ~$15 |
| 9.25x | $7.59B | ~$21 |
| 10.5x | $8.61B | ~$31 |

Two things fall out. First, the $31 target is not a mystery - it is simply a takeover multiple of
about 10.5 times. Second, and far more important, a single turn of multiple compression from
today takes the shares to roughly $7. There is no cash, no net asset value, and no unencumbered
collateral underneath this equity to stop that. The relevant market data point cuts the wrong
way: EPR Properties paid $342M gross for seven parks, a price consistent with roughly eight and a
half times their earnings - below, not above, where the whole company trades today.

**Falsification three - the earnings themselves are unstable.** Free cash flow is close to zero
once capital spending is taken out: capital expenditure absorbed about 93% of operating cash flow
over the trailing twelve months, leaving trailing free cash flow of roughly $29M against a $1.8B
market value. Interest expense runs about $95M a quarter, or close to $380M a year. The company
wrote off a very large amount of merger goodwill in the third quarter of 2025, posting a $1.19B
net loss (a loss of $11.80 a share) in that quarter alone. Shareholders' equity is down to $279M
and retained earnings stand at negative $2.03B.

The verified floor is not $16.50. On the evidence it is somewhere between $10 and $12 - the recent
low of $12.51 with no support beneath it - and in a genuine attendance recession it is
meaningfully lower. The trade as written on the board risks roughly 35% to make roughly 75%, not
6% to make 76%.

---

## 4. CREDIBILITY OF THE SPONSOR AND THE COUNTERPARTY

**JANA: credible as an investor, compromised as a forcing agent.** The firm has a long record and
a real position. But it let two of its three named operating partners de-group into company roles
within weeks, and it did not run a slate at the 2026 annual meeting. A separate activist, H
Partners, took the board seat that was available. An activist whose personnel end up inside the
company, and whose board seat goes to someone else, has been managed rather than obeyed.

**The board: credibly resistant.** Executive chairman Haddrill, a new chief executive, a new chief
financial officer and a new chief operating officer, all appointed within nine months, form a
management team assembled to fix the business, not to sell it. Boards that intend to sell hire
bankers and announce reviews. This one hired operators.

**Management on the numbers: early and mixed, but not evasive.** The first quarter of 2026 was
genuinely better - revenue up 12% to $225.6M, attendance up 4% to 2.9 million visits, spending
per visitor up 6% to $69.26, and the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M to a $123M adjusted EBITDA
loss. The first quarter is the smallest quarter of the year and carries little information. Mr
Reilly has been candid that the 27% margin the company earned in 2025 is not acceptable against
regional peers in the low thirties, which is honest, but he has not put a number or a date on the
improvement.

**The tape since has gone the other way.** On 19 July 2026 Citi cut its price target from $24 to
$19 with a neutral rating, and Guggenheim also cut on softer attendance, citing hazardous air
quality from Ontario wildfires affecting fourteen parks across the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes
during the peak season. Jefferies carries a below-consensus full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA
estimate of about $865M and warns that street attendance and revenue assumptions are too high.

---

## 5. RED FLAGS

- **The claimed floor is not a floor.** The shares traded at $12.51 within the last year, 29%
  below the $16.50 the board entry treats as protected.
- **The proxy window for 2026 has closed.** The annual meeting was held 26 May 2026 without a
  contested vote. The nearest hard forcing point is the 2027 nomination window, unannounced.
- **The activist group has been partially absorbed.** Two of three named operating partners
  de-grouped in November 2025 to pursue roles with the company.
- **Leverage is the dominant variable.** Net debt of $5.42B against about $820M of expected
  annual earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation is roughly six and a half
  times. The credit agreement carries a maximum net first-lien leverage covenant tested every
  quarter, which limits how much room a bad season leaves.
- **No free cash flow to deleverage with.** Trailing free cash flow of roughly $29M cannot move a
  $5.4B debt load. Deleveraging depends entirely on further asset sales.
- **The dividend is gone.** The payout is zero, which for a business that spent decades as an
  income vehicle means the natural holder base has already been evicted.
- **Peak-season demand is deteriorating right now.** Two brokers cut targets in July on soft
  attendance, in the quarter that makes the year.
- **The asset-sale comparable prices the company below the target multiple.** EPR paid roughly
  eight and a half times for the seven-park package; the $31 target needs about ten and a half.

## 6. GREEN FLAGS

- The activist campaign is live and has not been withdrawn; the 9% economic interest remains
  disclosed.
- The board has visibly conceded on governance - a new executive chairman in March 2026 and a
  cooperation agreement seating H Partners' Rehan Jaffer in May 2026 - which is the pattern that
  sometimes precedes a sale by a year or more.
- The asset base has genuine local scarcity. Cedar Point, Knott's Berry Farm and Magic Mountain
  sit on land that cannot be replicated, which is why a financial buyer can underwrite a bid at
  all.
- Operating momentum in the first quarter of 2026 was real - attendance, pricing and spending per
  visitor all moved the right way, and the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M.
- The seven-park disposal closed and brought in $331.4M of cash, proving the board will sell
  assets under pressure.
- A management team built for a turnaround is now fully in place: chief executive from December
  2025, chief financial officer from 17 June 2026, chief operating officer from 15 July 2026.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling detail is the substitution pattern. Every time JANA asked for the company to be
sold, the company gave it something adjacent and cheaper: a chair, a director seat to a rival
activist, seven parks. That is a board that has read the leverage on its own balance sheet and
concluded that a forced sale at a depressed multiple hands the entire premium to the debt. With
net debt at roughly six and a half times earnings, a buyer at eight and a half times leaves
shareholders with a stub; a buyer at ten and a half times leaves them with $31. The board is
holding out for the second, and it can afford to wait far longer than a shareholder can.

The second signal is the H Partners agreement. When a company settles with the second activist
on the register while the first is publicly demanding a sale, it has found a way to look
responsive without doing the thing that was demanded. That is skilful defence, and it is bearish
for anyone underwriting a near-term sale.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Trajectory: deteriorating.** Not because the business is collapsing - the first quarter
genuinely improved - but because the *event* has weakened at every step since March 2026. The
demand was made, the proxy window passed without a vote, the board answered with governance and
asset sales, and the shares have fallen from the low twenties toward the bottom of their range
while two brokers cut targets on soft peak-season attendance.

**The single thing the director must weigh:** this position is not the defined-risk special
situation the board entry describes. The catalyst is undated, non-binding and dependent on a
buyer who has not appeared, and the downside floor of $16.50 has already been broken by the
market within the past twelve months. Sizing it as a 6%-risk trade would be a serious error. It
is a levered equity stub in which one turn of multiple compression is worth roughly $10 a share.

**On the franchise, for completeness:** the moat is narrow and real - irreplaceable regional
land and local scarcity - but the evidence says it is eroding, with a 27% margin against peers
above 30%, a return on invested capital of about 4.4%, and attendance that needs weather and
consumer health to cooperate. The structural threat from competing experience spending is
manageable rather than terminal; this is a leverage and execution problem, not a melting

GDOT.bull_thesis:
The bull case is that a signed, shareholder-approved break-up closes on schedule and pays out more than the market currently marks it at. Green Dot is being dismantled into two halves under an Agreement and Plan of Merger dated 23 November 2025: Smith Ventures buys the non-bank financial-technology business for $690 million in cash, and CommerceOne Financial Corporation, a small Birmingham, Alabama bank holding company, takes Green Dot Bank into a newly listed parent (to trade on the New York Stock Exchange as CONE). Each Green Dot share converts into $8.11 in cash plus 0.2215 shares of that new company.

Four things make completion the strong base case. First, the vote is banked: at special meetings on 23 June 2026, Green Dot holders approved by 40,869,891 for against 139,918 opposed - over 99% of votes cast, roughly 72% of shares outstanding - and CommerceOne holders approved unanimously. Second, there is no financing hole. The $8.11 is funded directly out of the $690 million purchase price, which is split $155 million into the combined bank as regulatory capital, $65 million to repay debt, and $470 million to Green Dot shareholders. No lender can withdraw a commitment because there is no commitment to withdraw. Third, two independent buyers each underwrote a different half, so the price was tested twice, and the terms have not moved in the eight months since signing. Fourth, a contractual outside date of 23 November 2026 - automatically extending 90 days to 23 February 2027 if regulatory approvals remain outstanding - bounds how long capital can sit trapped.

If the deal closes and the new bank is valued anywhere near the bankers' own work, the payout is well above today's price. Citi's dividend-discount analysis, disclosed in June 2026 supplemental filings, valued the combined bank's equity at $590 million to $755 million, which implies total consideration of $15.45 to $17.51 per Green Dot share. Management's own illustrative range, given on the 24 November 2025 call, was $14.23 to $19.18. The $155 million capital injection lands inside the bank you end up owning, and the seven-year exclusive sponsor-bank agreement with the privatised fintech gives the new company a contracted revenue stream from day one rather than a standing start.

The conditions that must hold are narrow and specific: the Federal Reserve, the Alabama State Banking Department and the Utah Department of Financial Institutions all approve; the new shares list without incident; and the newly public bank finds enough natural buyers in its first weeks of trading that the forced supply from Green Dot's existing holders does not overwhelm it.
GDOT.bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require the deal to break. It only requires the stock leg to be worth what the market already says it is worth - which is what makes this position unattractive at $13.16 rather than merely risky.

Only $8.11 of today's price, about 62%, is contractual cash. The other 38% is 0.2215 shares of a company that does not trade yet, cannot be hedged (there is no listed CommerceOne security to sell short), cannot be elected out of, and carries no collar, no cash election and no contingent value right. Back out the cash and the market is paying $5.05 for that stub, implying about $22.80 per new share and roughly $399 million for the entire new bank - some 32% below the low end of Citi's own valuation. That persistent discount is not inattention. Roughly 12.6 million shares, about 72% of the new company's register, are about to be handed to people who bought a Provo, Utah fintech: small-cap growth funds, payments funds, and index funds that will be mechanically deleted from Green Dot and have no mandate to hold a two-state community bank. The supply is forced and the natural buyer base has to be built from zero.

The approval risk is also real rather than procedural. Green Dot Bank operates under a Federal Reserve consent order dated 19 July 2024 carrying a $44 million civil money penalty, covering compliance risk management, unfair and deceptive practices in prepaid card marketing and servicing, and anti-money-laundering failures including inadequate disclosure of refund-processing fees between 2017 and 2022. The order required a third-party root-cause review, an outside transaction-monitoring firm and written board-oversight plans. The acquirer inheriting that problem is a bank founded in 2018 with under $1 billion of assets, buying a bank with roughly $6.65 billion of assets and $4.6 billion of deposit-type liabilities as of 31 March 2026. A much smaller acquirer absorbing a larger bank under live enforcement is exactly the profile that slows an application. The guided close has already drifted about one quarter, from an expected second quarter of 2026 at announcement to the third quarter now, and as of 28 July 2026 no Federal Reserve order has been published and no approval has been announced.

If it does break, there is no contractual backstop. Tangible book value is about $10.03 a share ($940.5 million equity less $369.0 million intangibles over roughly 57 million shares). The undisturbed price of $11.80 on 21 November 2025 is not a safe anchor either - the shares had already run from $10.56 on 18 November that same week, and that price embedded eight months of public strategic-review optionality. A failed process on a business with negative trailing return on equity of about -7.7% plausibly resolves to $10.50-$11.00, with the 52-week low of $9.31 as the overshoot. Against that, the shares at $13.16 sit about 20% above the floor and above both the 50-day ($13.06) and 200-day ($12.34) averages, having been flagged repeatedly by momentum screens through June and July 2026. You would be buying strength, not capitulation, in a name whose upside is contractually capped at the offer.

GDOT.sop_breakdown: Probability-weighted across the two outcomes, because the parts here are a payout, not a business. Cash leg: $8.11 a share, contractual and funded out of Smith Ventures' $690 million purchase price ($155 million into the bank as capital, $65 million to repay debt, $470 million to shareholders) - this part carries deal risk but no financing risk. Stock leg: 0.2215 shares of New CommerceOne, marked at $6.00 for the base case, which sits above the market's own $5.05 mark (an implied $22.80 per new share) and below the $6.12 embedded in management's $14.23 low end, reflecting that first-week trading of an orphaned bank with forced sellers will likely print below the bankers' $33.6-$43.0 range. Value at close: $8.11 + $6.00 = $14.10. Value on break: $11.00. Assign an 85% chance of closing given the completed votes, absent financing condition, unchanged terms and hard outside date, against a 15% chance the Federal Reserve application stalls on Green Dot Bank's live July 2024 consent order. That gives 0.85 x $14.10 + 0.15 x $11.00 = $13.64. Sensitivity that matters: mark the stub at the market's own $5.05 instead and the base case falls to $12.84, below today's price. The entire remaining edge is a judgement on the stub's first weeks of trading, not on whether the deal closes.

GDOT.forcing_function: Publication of the Federal Reserve Board's approval order under Section 3 of the Bank Holding Company Act, together with sign-offs from the Alabama State Banking Department and the Utah Department of Financial Institutions. That single event releases the $8.11 cash payment and triggers the New York Stock Exchange listing of New CommerceOne under the ticker CONE. Three separate Federal Reserve approvals are required: for the merger subsidiary to become a bank holding company by acquiring Green Dot Bank, for New CommerceOne to become a bank holding company by indirectly acquiring both banks, and for the merger of CommerceOne into New CommerceOne. Hart-Scott-Rodino antitrust clearance and the exchange listing approval also sit in the queue. The hard boundary is the 23 November 2026 termination date, extending to 23 February 2027 if approvals are still pending. The complication is that this forcing function resolves the deal but not the valuation: the moment approval lands, the price question shifts entirely to what an orphaned community bank stub prints at in its first week of trading.
GDOT.consensus_delta:
The interesting disagreement here is not between us and Wall Street - it is between the market and the company's own bankers, and the market is winning the argument.

The published sell-side and management framing says Green Dot holders are receiving $14.23 to $19.18 a share (chief financial officer, 24 November 2025), with Citi's dividend-discount work implying $15.45 to $17.51. The shares have never traded at any of those levels. They closed at $11.81 on announcement day, one cent above the prior close - the deal was worth essentially nothing to the market on the day it was struck - and eight months later, with both votes banked, they sit at $13.16, still below the floor of management's range. That is not a slow-moving market. It is a considered, persistent discount on the one part of the package nobody can observe.

Where the street assumption is factually weak is the treatment of the stock leg as though it were currency. Only $8.11 is money. The rest is 0.2215 shares of an unlisted bank, and the valuations quoted in support of the higher numbers are forward constructs: Performance Trust applied 110%-130% of projected 31 December 2029 tangible book value, and Citi used a 2.5% perpetuity growth rate against a 12.63% discount rate. Those are answers to 'what might this bank be worth in three-plus years if it executes', not 'what will 12.6 million orphaned shares fetch in week one'. Quoting $19.18 as deal proceeds is a category error, and quoting $14.23 as a target embeds an assumption that the new bank trades at $27.63 when the market currently says $22.80.

Our disagreement with the board's own catalyst entry is sharper than our disagreement with the street. That entry carried a $14.23 target against an $11.80 floor for a risk-reward of 1.56, which back-solves to an entry near $12.75. At $13.16 the identical arithmetic gives 0.79, and against a properly derived $11.00 floor it gives 0.49. The thesis has not changed; the price has, and the compensation has gone with it. A second, quieter delta: the recent buyers are momentum and value screeners (top-tier Zacks rank, 'near 52-week high' and 'attractive price-to-sales' lists through June and July 2026), not merger arbitrageurs. They are buying a fintech chart and will be handed a community bank.
GDOT.valley_of_death:
There is no cash-burn hump or maturity wall here - the $65 million debt repayment out of the purchase price handles the balance sheet, and the business is improving into the close, with June-quarter earnings of $0.40 a share against a $0.30 estimate. The next three to nine months carry a different kind of risk: regulatory silence, followed by a listing.

The first hazard is the Federal Reserve application itself. Green Dot Bank has been operating under a consent order since 19 July 2024, carrying a $44 million civil money penalty for compliance risk management failures, unfair and deceptive practices in prepaid card marketing and servicing, and anti-money-laundering deficiencies including inadequate disclosure of refund-processing fees between 2017 and 2022. The remediation obligations - third-party root-cause review, outside transaction monitoring, written board-oversight plans - are still live. The Federal Reserve must now satisfy itself that CommerceOne, a bank founded in 2018 with under $1 billion of assets, has the management capacity and capital to run a $6.65 billion bank with roughly $4.6 billion of deposit-type liabilities sourced through prepaid and banking-as-a-service programmes. That is a genuine supervisory question. The guided window has already drifted one quarter, and every additional month of silence between now and the 23 November 2026 outside date will be read by the market as rising break risk, pressuring the shares toward the $11.00 floor well before any decision arrives.

The second and more probable hazard is the listing itself. Assume approval lands and the deal closes in the third or fourth quarter. Holders receive $8.11 in cash and a fractional share of a new company. There is no lock-up on a merger-consideration share, no supportive sponsor bid, no research coverage on day one, and no index membership. The stub could easily print below the $22.80 per new share the market currently implies before it finds the regional-bank buyers who would naturally own it. In that scenario the deal succeeds and the position still loses money - which is the specific way this trade goes wrong, and it does not require anything to break.
GDOT.positioning_washout:
This is the most under-priced dynamic in the situation, and it runs the wrong way for a buyer at today's price.

Green Dot is currently owned as a small-cap financial-technology and payments name: index and small-cap growth funds, payments-sector specialists, and - visible in the June and July 2026 tape - momentum screeners drawn in by a top-tier Zacks rank, a price above the 200-day average of $12.34, and appearances on 'near 52-week high' and 'undervalued price-to-sales' lists. At closing, roughly 12.6 million New CommerceOne shares, about 72% of that company's register, land in those accounts. Essentially none of them can or will hold it. Index funds are mechanically deleted from Green Dot and have no mandate for a newly listed two-state bank holding company. Payments and fintech funds have no mandate either. The natural owner - a regional-bank investor - has never heard of it and has no research to read.

So the forced selling in this situation happens after the catalyst, not before it, and it falls on the asset you are left holding rather than the one you are buying. That is the inverse of the setup this funnel is built to exploit. In a classic washout you buy from distressed sellers ahead of an event; here the event hands you a security into a wave of distressed sellers.

Note also what is absent: Green Dot itself is not washed out. At $13.16 it trades above both its 50-day ($13.06) and 200-day ($12.34) averages, roughly 20% above its broken-deal floor and only 15% off its 52-week high of $15.41. There is no capitulation to buy. The only genuine capitulation on the horizon belongs to the stub, and it is worth waiting for rather than paying ahead of.

The event is real, binding and very likely to complete. That is not the question. The question is whether $13.16 pays you for taking it, and it does not.

What is verified: an Agreement and Plan of Merger signed 23 November 2025; shareholder approvals completed 23 June 2026 with over 99% of Green Dot votes cast in favour and CommerceOne unanimous; consideration fixed at $8.11 in cash plus 0.2215 shares of a new listed bank holding company; the cash funded from Smith Ventures' $690 million purchase price rather than from any financing commitment; no renegotiation in eight months; a contractual outside date of 23 November 2026 extending to 23 February 2027; and, as of 28 July 2026, no Federal Reserve order published and no bank approvals announced against a guided third-quarter close that has already drifted a quarter.

The reason this is a wait rather than a buy is arithmetic, not scepticism. Only 62% of the price is contractual cash. The remaining 38% is an unlisted, unhedgeable stub, and the market marks it at $5.05 - about 32% below the low end of the company's own banker's valuation. That discount is rational: at closing, roughly 12.6 million shares of a small orphaned bank get handed to fintech and index holders who cannot own it. Probability-weight the outcomes honestly - 85% chance of closing at about $14.10, 15% chance of breaking to $11.00 - and fair value is about $13.64, some 3.6% above the price. Mark the stub at the market's own number instead and fair value is $12.84, below the price. Either way the upside is capped at the offer while the downside to an $11.00 floor, which is an estimate rather than a contract, is 16%. That is roughly 0.5 to 1, and it is a material deterioration from the 1.56 recorded when this position was struck near $12.75. The spread has been collected.

The residual risk is not the one the file was opened for. It is not 'will the Federal Reserve say yes' - though Green Dot Bank's live July 2024 consent order and a sub-$1 billion acquirer taking on a $6.65 billion bank make that a real, non-procedural question. The residual risk is that the deal closes exactly as promised and the position still loses money, because an orphaned community bank stub prints below $22.80 in its first week of trading. A trade whose main failure mode is the successful outcome does not deserve fresh capital at this price.

Wait for the price, not the news. Below roughly $12.60 the reward against the $11.80 undisturbed-price reference returns to two-to-one; below roughly $12.15 it does so against the harder $11.00 floor. Either level would likely appear on the first headline of regulatory delay, which on the current drift is more likely than not. Hold what is held; do not add here.
GDOT.interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Event Dossier — Green Dot Corporation (GDOT)
### Event-driven special situation: the CommerceOne / Smith Ventures break-up
Prepared 28 July 2026. Last traded price **$13.16** (close of 27 July 2026, NYSE).
Built from SEC filings (8-K, DEFM14A, Form 425), company releases, Federal Reserve
enforcement records and market data. No earnings-call transcript bundle was available for
this run, so the usual transcript sections are answered against the deal record instead, and
no management quotation appears here unless sourced to a specific dated document.

---

## 1. WHAT THE EVENT ACTUALLY IS

Green Dot is not being bought whole. On 23 November 2025 the company signed an agreement to
split itself in two and sell each half to a different buyer:

- **CommerceOne Financial Corporation**, a privately held bank holding company in Birmingham,
  Alabama (its subsidiary CommerceOne Bank was founded in 2018 and held roughly **$892 million**
  in total assets across two locations with 59 employees as of March 2026), takes Green Dot
  Bank. The two banks are then placed under a brand new, publicly traded parent — "New
  CommerceOne" — which intends to list on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker CONE.
- **Smith Ventures, LLC** buys Green Dot's non-bank financial-technology operations and takes
  them private, to be run as an independent company. The privatised fintech signs a
  **seven-year exclusive sponsor-bank agreement** with the new bank, which is what lets both
  halves function apart.

For every Green Dot share you hold at closing you receive a fixed package: **$8.11 in cash
plus 0.2215 shares of New CommerceOne**. Former Green Dot holders end up owning roughly 72%
of the new bank company.

**Where the cash comes from matters, and it is good news.** Smith Ventures pays **$690 million
in cash** for the fintech. That sum is carved up as follows: **$155 million** injected into the
combined bank to bolster liquidity and regulatory capital, **$65 million** to repay existing
debt, and the remaining **$470 million** distributed to Green Dot shareholders — which, over
roughly 57 million shares, is the $8.11. The cash leg is therefore funded out of a purchase
price, not out of a financing commitment that a lender could pull.

That second half of the package is the whole argument, and it is worth stating plainly at the
top: **this is not a cash deal.** Only about 62% of the value at today's price is contractual
cash. The rest is stock in a company that does not yet trade, whose price nobody can observe,
and whose first day of trading is the moment the value is actually set.

---

## 2. IS THE CATALYST REAL, DATED, AND BINDING?

**Real and binding: yes, on strong evidence.**

| Test | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Signed agreement | Agreement and Plan of Merger, 23 Nov 2025, unanimously approved by the Green Dot board | Binding |
| Shareholder approval | Special meetings held **23 June 2026**. Green Dot: 40,869,891 for / 139,918 against / 52,234 abstaining — over 99% of votes cast, about 72% of shares outstanding. CommerceOne: 100% in favour, about 69% of outstanding | Cleared, and not close |
| Financing condition | None disclosed in the merger proxy; the cash comes from the $690M purchase price | No financing hole |
| Two independent buyers | A bank buyer and a separate fintech buyer, each wanting a different half | Two parties had to underwrite the price; harder to walk |
| Break fees | Green Dot pays CommerceOne $27.0M on specified terminations; CommerceOne pays Green Dot $3.5M in reverse; the fintech buyer pays Green Dot $40.0M if the separation agreement terminates in certain cases | The asymmetry (Green Dot's is nearly eight times the reverse fee) says Green Dot is the more motivated seller |

**Dated: partly.** There is no single hard calendar date on which the deal is guaranteed to
complete. What exists is:

- A **company-guided window** — "expected to be completed in the third quarter of 2026,"
  repeated in the 23 June 2026 announcement. A quarter, not a date.
- A **contractual outside date** — the merger agreement terminates on **23 November 2026**,
  automatically extendable by 90 days to **23 February 2027** where required regulatory
  approvals are still outstanding. That is the hard boundary: nine weeks away at the guided
  pace, seven months at the outside.

So the correct description is a binding contract with a soft target inside a hard contractual
boundary. That is stronger than a management aspiration and weaker than a regulator's
scheduled decision date.

**One qualifier the board's catalyst entry does not capture: the window has already drifted.**
At announcement the companies pointed to four-to-six months for approvals, and contemporaneous
trade coverage carried an expected close "during the second quarter of 2026." The guidance now
reads third quarter. That is roughly one quarter of slippage — unremarkable for a bank
application, but it is drift, not adherence, and it should be priced as such.

---

## 3. WHAT IS ACTUALLY LEFT TO CLEAR

Everything discretionary that remains sits with bank regulators:

1. **Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System** — approval under Section 3 of the Bank
   Holding Company Act, in three separate pieces: for the merger subsidiary to become a bank
   holding company by acquiring Green Dot Bank; for New CommerceOne to become a bank holding
   company by indirectly acquiring both banks; and for the merger of CommerceOne into New
   CommerceOne.
2. **Alabama State Banking Department** (CommerceOne Bank's home regulator).
3. **Utah Department of Financial Institutions** (Green Dot Bank's home regulator).
4. Hart-Scott-Rodino antitrust clearance and NYSE listing approval for the new shares.

**Verification as of 28 July 2026: no Federal Reserve order approving this transaction has been
published, and neither company has announced receipt of any of the three bank approvals.** The
most recent transaction news of any kind remains the 23 June 2026 shareholder-vote
announcement; company news since then has been operating items (an Everest Group earned-wage-
access ranking on 27 July, a Treasury Prime cash-network partnership on 25 June). The catalyst
has **not fired**, and it has **not been abandoned** — it is sitting in the regulators'
in-trays with roughly nine weeks left in the guided quarter.

---

## 4. HOW CREDIBLE IS THE SPONSOR ON HITTING IT?

Four observations, none of them fatal, all of them worth pricing.

- **Green Dot's own credibility is the weak leg.** The company put itself up for strategic
  review in early 2025 after a severe de-rating; the reference "unaffected" price the bankers
  used was about **$7.45 (7 March 2025)**. It is selling because the standalone business
  stopped working, not from strength. Trailing-twelve-month results show a net loss — return on
  equity of about **−7.7%** and a negative earnings yield — against a positive but modest
  operating return on assets of about 0.4%. Management is a motivated seller, which helps
  completion and hurts negotiating leverage. The board has also granted the chief executive a
  bonus explicitly tied to completing the merger: alignment with closing, but also a reminder
  that the people quoting you a $14.23 value are paid to get it done.
- **CommerceOne is small and private, buying something much larger than itself.** A bank
  founded in 2018 in Birmingham, with under $1 billion of assets, is taking on Green Dot Bank,
  whose balance sheet carried about **$6.65 billion of assets at 31 March 2026** — roughly
  $4.6 billion of that in customer deposit-type liabilities. Regulators will look hard at
  management capacity, capital, and the compliance record of a bank whose deposits arrive
  through prepaid and banking-as-a-service programmes.
- **Green Dot Bank is not a clean applicant, and the prior read of this file missed it.** On
  **19 July 2024** the Federal Reserve Board issued a consent order against Green Dot
  Corporation and Green Dot Bank carrying a **$44 million civil money penalty**. The findings
  covered compliance risk management, unfair and deceptive practices in the marketing, selling
  and servicing of prepaid debit cards, and anti-money-laundering failures — including
  inadequate disclosure of refund-processing fees in tax-refund services between 2017 and 2022.
  The order compelled a third-party root-cause review, an outside transaction-monitoring firm,
  and written board-oversight and improvement plans. **A bank under a live enforcement action
  is exactly the profile that slows a Federal Reserve application**, because the regulator must
  satisfy itself that a much smaller acquirer can manage the problem it is inheriting. This is
  the single most likely cause of further delay, and the tail where the deal actually fails.
- **No one has wobbled.** Both boards recommended it, both shareholder bases voted for it
  overwhelmingly, no party has sought to renegotiate, and the terms are unchanged from November
  2025 through the June 2026 vote. Operationally the business is improving into the close —
  **June-quarter earnings of $0.40 a share beat the $0.30 estimate**, and 2025 revenue grew
  about 21% (though net income fell about 270% into a loss over the same year).

---

## 5. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR — WHAT ACTUALLY BACKSTOPS THE PRICE

If the deal fails, what is a Green Dot share worth? Three verified anchors:

| Anchor | Value per share | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Tangible book value (equity less intangibles) | **about $10.03** | Q1 2026 balance sheet: $940.5M total equity less $369.0M of intangibles = $571.5M, over roughly 57.0M shares |
| Undisturbed market price before the deal | **$11.80** | Closing price on 21 November 2025, the last trading day before announcement |
| Fifty-two-week low | **$9.31** | Trailing twelve months |

The honest floor sits between the first two, not at the top of them. The $11.80 undisturbed
price already contained eight months of public strategic-review optionality — that price was
itself partly a bet that a deal would happen, and the shares had run from **$10.56 on
18 November to $11.80 on 21 November**, the trading week before the news. Strip the deal
expectation out after a failed process, add a trailing-twelve-month net loss, and a broken deal
plausibly resolves toward **$10.50 to $11.00**, with $9.31 as the overshoot if sentiment runs.
Small offsets exist: a $3.5 million reverse fee (about $0.06 a share) or, in the
separation-agreement scenarios, $40 million from the fintech buyer (about $0.70 a share).
Neither changes the picture.

**Working floor: $11.00.** It is real in the sense that tangible book and a regulated deposit
franchise sit underneath it. It is **not** a hard floor in the sense a cash-tender arbitrage
enjoys — nothing contractual holds the price there, there is no cash election, no collar, and
no contingent value right.

The uncomfortable arithmetic: the shares trade at **$13.16, about 20% above that floor**. There
is no margin of safety in the price today. You are paid for the deal closing, and only for that.

---

## 6. THE PART EVERYONE UNDER-PRICES: THE STOCK LEG

This is where the real work is, and where the received "$14.23 target" falls apart under
inspection.

The often-quoted $14.23 is the **bottom** of management's own illustrative range of **$14.23 to
$19.18** per share, given by the chief financial officer on the 24 November 2025 call. The top
of that range is not a closing value at all: the supporting work applied **110% to 130% of
projected 31 December 2029 tangible book value** (Performance Trust) and a dividend-discount
model at a 2.5% perpetuity growth rate and a 12.63% discount rate producing a $1,160 million
undiscounted terminal value (Citi). Treating $19.18 as deal proceeds is a category error — it
is what the stub might be worth after three or more years of successful bank operation.

Separately, in supplemental disclosures issued in June 2026 (prompted by three disclosure
lawsuits — Phillips, 27 May 2026; Richardson, 28 May 2026; Zaccagnino, 8 June 2026, all in New
York state courts, all disclosure-only claims the companies call meritless), Citi's
dividend-discount analysis put the combined company's equity value at **$590 million to $755
million**, implying total consideration of **$15.45 to $17.51** per Green Dot share.

Work the arithmetic back. About 57.0 million Green Dot shares times the 0.2215 exchange ratio
produces roughly 12.6 million New CommerceOne shares, and if that is 72% of the new company,
the whole company has about 17.5 million shares. Citi's $590–755 million therefore implies
**$33.6 to $43.0** per New CommerceOne share.

Now read the tape. At **$13.16**, after subtracting the $8.11 of contractual cash, the market is
paying **$5.05 for 0.2215 shares — an implied $22.80 per New CommerceOne share, or roughly
$399 million for the whole new bank.** That is about **32% below the low end of the banker's own
valuation**, and 17% below the stub value embedded in management's own $14.23 floor.

Some of that gap is ordinary deal risk and the time value of waiting. Most of it is not. Most of
it is the market saying, correctly in my view, that **the day this thing lists is the day it gets
sold.** Roughly 72% of the register of a brand-new, thinly covered, $400–750 million
Alabama-and-Utah bank holding company is about to be handed to people who bought a Provo, Utah
financial-technology company: small-cap growth funds, payments-sector funds, and index funds
that will be mechanically deleted from Green Dot and have no mandate to hold CONE. None of them
chose a community bank. The supply is forced and the natural buyer base — regional bank
investors — has to be built from zero.

So the load-bearing uncertainty in this trade is not "will the Federal Reserve say yes." It is
**"what does an orphaned bank stub print at when 12.6 million shares come looking for a bid in
week one."**

---

## 7. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**Concerning**
- **The reward is now smaller than the risk, and it has decayed since we entered.** Working
  backwards from the board's recorded risk-reward of 1.56 against a $14.23 target and an $11.80
  floor implies an entry near **$12.75**. At today's $13.16 the same arithmetic gives **0.79**.
  Against the more honest $11.00 floor it is roughly **0.49**. The spread has been collected
  while the position sat still.
- Only 62% of today's price is contractual cash; 38% is an unobservable stock leg whose value
  will be set by forced sellers, cannot be hedged (there is no listed CommerceOne security to
  sell short), and cannot be elected out of.
- Green Dot Bank operates under a live July 2024 Federal Reserve consent order; the pending
  approval is not a formality.
- The guided close has already drifted roughly one quarter, from the second quarter of 2026 to
  the third.
- The shares are not washed out. At $13.16 they sit above both the 50-day ($13.06) and 200-day
  ($12.34) averages, and the stock has been repeatedly flagged by momentum and value screens
  through June and July 2026. You are buying strength, not capitulation — an unusual and
  unwelcome starting point for a special situation.
- The standalone franchise is loss-making on a trailing basis, so the fallback is asset value,
  not earnings power.
- Green Dot's $27.0 million break fee is nearly eight times CommerceOne's reverse fee, which
  tells you which side wanted this more.

**Reassuring**
- The vote is done and it was not close: over 99% of votes cast.
- No financing condition — the $8.11 is funded from the $690 million purchase price, and a
  further $155 million of that price goes in as bank capital, which strengthens the stub you
  receive.
- Terms unchanged for eight months; no renegotiation, no wobble.
- Two separate buyers each wanted a different half, so both pieces were independently
  underwritten.
- A contractual outside date of 23 November 2026, extendable to 23 February 2027, bounds how
  long capital can be trapped.
- The litigation is the standard disclosure-only variety, already answered with supplemental
  filings, with no injunction sought or granted.
- The operating business is beating expectations into the close.

---

## 8. VERDICT FOR THE DIRECTOR

The event is genuine, documented, shareholder-approved and unconditional on financing.
Credibility of the **event** is high. What is low is the **compensation for taking it**, and the
reason is that the market has already done the work: the shares have drifted up toward the
cash-plus-discounted-stub value, so the remaining spread of roughly 8% to management's own
conservative $14.23 is being offered against a 16–20% fall to a floor that is an estimate rather
than a contract.

Run the expectation honestly. Give the deal an 85% chance of closing. Mark the stub at $6.00 —
above the market's $5.05, below management's $6.12 — for a closing value near $14.10. Value a
broken deal at $11.00. The probability-weighted result is about **$13.64**, roughly 3.6% above
today's price. Mark the stub at the market's own $5.05 instead and the expectation falls to
**$12.84**, below today's price. The entire remaining edge in this position is a judgement about
the first-week trading of an orphaned community bank.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing: you are not buying a defined-risk cash arbitrage —
you are buying $8.11 of cash and a pre-listing position in a small orphaned bank, at a price
that already assumes the deal closes.** Size it as a stub-equity bet with deal risk attached,
never as a cash spread. If the position is to be added to, the level that restores a two-to-one
reward against the $11.80 reference floor is **below roughly $12.60**; against the harder $11.00
floor, below roughly $12.15.

The moat question is close to moot, and the honest answer is unflattering: the franchise is
being dismantled precisely because prepaid and banking-as-a-service economics have been ground
down by payment-app, neobank and stablecoin competition — a structural force, not a cycle. The
bank charter retains scarcity value, which is exactly why it found a buyer, but a licence you
can sell is not the same thing as an earnings moat, and negative returns on equity alongside 21%
revenue growth is the signature of a franchise that was losing, not compounding.
