KDP.bull_thesis:
The event works if the coffee spin-off actually happens on something close to the stated timetable and the market then values the two halves the way it values their peers. Keurig Dr Pepper has already done the hard, irreversible part: the $18 billion cash purchase of JDE Peet's, the Dutch coffee group behind Jacobs, Douwe Egberts and Peet's, settled on 1 April 2026 with 96.22% of shares tendered, rose to 97.75% in the follow-on window, delisted from Euronext Amsterdam on 30 April 2026, and the company implemented a post-closing demerger whose stated purpose is to enable the separation. That is completed legal machinery, not an intention.

What is left is a tax-free spin-off of the coffee business, leaving a North American refreshment-beverage company behind. The bull case is a sum-of-the-parts case (valuing each business separately and adding them up). Beverage Co. would be a pure-play North American drinks company built on Dr Pepper, the number-two carbonated soft drink in the United States and still gaining share, plus Canada Dry, Snapple and a growing energy portfolio, distributed through a direct-store-delivery network that is expensive for anyone to replicate. On roughly $13.3 billion of 2027 revenue at a high-twenties margin, that is about $3.85 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. Peers of that quality trade at 15 to 19 times that measure; today the whole company trades at roughly 9.8 times consensus 2027 earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, and about 12.3 times 2027 earnings per share of $2.53, against packaged-food and drinks peers at 17 to 20 times earnings.

Global Coffee Co. would be one of the largest coffee businesses in the world by volume, combining the Keurig single-serve system in North America with JDE Peet's international roast-and-ground and instant portfolio, at roughly $16.4 billion of revenue. It is a slower, more commodity-exposed business, but the market pays 9 to 11 times cash profit for that kind of asset, and JDE Peet's itself was taken out around the upper end of that band.

The conditions the bull case depends on are specific and checkable. First, the company has to name a chief executive for the coffee business and file the registration statement that turns 'early 2027' into an actual distribution date. Second, leverage has to come down: management has said plainly that separation timing depends on 'achievement of key milestones, including appropriate leverage levels at each company,' and combined borrowings sit near 4.5 times cash profit. Third, green-coffee costs, which have been compressing US coffee results all year, need to stabilise so the coffee company can be floated on a clean multiple rather than a trough one. If all three land, the parts are worth roughly $42 a share on favourable assumptions, and the operating business is meanwhile holding up: first-quarter 2026 net sales rose 9.4% to $3.98 billion with adjusted earnings of $0.39 a share, guidance for $25.9 to $26.4 billion of 2026 net sales and low-double-digit constant-currency earnings growth has been reaffirmed twice, and the company has met or beaten estimates in each of the last four quarters.
KDP.bear_thesis:
The event fails, in the way these usually fail, by simply not arriving on time. There is no date. The separation was described as operationally ready 'by end of 2026' in October 2025, still carried a year-end 2026 target in February 2026, and became 'targeted for early 2027' on 23 June 2026 — one slip already, with the target explicitly conditioned on leverage levels and market conditions the company does not control. Nothing binds the company to a distribution date, no registration statement for the coffee company has been filed, and there is no contractual payout of any kind. This is a goal, not a schedule.

The leadership prerequisite has just been vacated for the second time in nine months. Sudhanshu Priyadarshi, originally slated to run the coffee company, was moved out of the chief financial officer role in November 2025 and off that plan. Rafael Oliveira was named chief executive of the future coffee company on the day the acquisition closed in April 2026, and told the company in June 2026 he was leaving at the end of July for an outside role. The search has restarted. Bank of America called it a setback precisely because the timetable now depends on hiring. A company cannot run a spin-off roadshow for a business with no chief executive, so the practical earliest date is later than the stated one.

The deeper problem is what the common shareholder actually owns. The acquisition was not funded with debt and ordinary shares. Three claims now sit ahead of or alongside the common: about $9 billion of new long-term debt plus roughly $5 billion of assumed JDE Peet's bonds; $4.5 billion of Series A convertible perpetual preferred stock co-led by Apollo and KKR, upsized from $3 billion on 23 February 2026, paying 4.75% a year, ranking senior for dividends and on liquidation with a $1,000-per-share liquidation preference, never maturing, and carrying registration rights that give the holders a path to sell; and a pod-manufacturing joint venture into which Apollo, KKR and Goldman Sachs Asset Management put about $4 billion for 49%, showing up as $3.9 billion of minority interest at 31 March 2026. Note what was sold there: half the economics of K-Cup pod manufacturing, the highest-margin part of the coffee business. Roughly $36 billion of debt, preferred and minority claims now stands between enterprise value and the share. A parts valuation that subtracts only bonds overstates the answer by about $6 a share.

That leverage — near 4.5 times cash profit — is what turns a dull staples stock into a levered call option. A 10% shortfall in profit combined with one turn of multiple compression takes roughly a third off the equity. And the profit shortfall has a live source: elevated green-coffee costs have been pressuring the US coffee business all year, and the company has just multiplied its coffee exposure. Free cash flow yield is about 3.7% and interest costs have risen sharply.

Finally, the index-flow leg of the thesis points the wrong way. When a spin-off happens, funds that track the parent's index are typically forced to sell the newly distributed company. That creates a discount in the coffee spin-off after the fact — it is not a tailwind for shares held beforehand. If anything, holders face a dividend that must be split between two companies (the current $0.23 quarterly payout, $0.92 a year, yields about 3.0%) and an income-oriented shareholder base with no natural reason to stay. What confirms the bear case: the separation target moving past mid-2027, a coffee chief executive still unnamed by the year-end 2026 results, or a 2026 guidance cut on coffee input costs at the 6 August 2026 second-quarter report.
KDP.sop_bull: Favourable parts valuation, roughly $42 a share. Beverage Co.: about $13.3 billion of 2027 revenue at a 30% margin gives roughly $4.0 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation; at 16 times, the multiple a high-quality North American drinks pure-play with mid-single-digit growth can command, that is about $64 billion of enterprise value. Global Coffee Co.: about $16.4 billion of revenue at a 22% margin gives roughly $3.6 billion of the same measure; at 11 times, in line with where JDE Peet's itself was acquired, that is about $39.6 billion. Deduct roughly $2 billion for separation costs and stranded overhead, giving about $101.6 billion of combined enterprise value. Subtract net debt of about $26 billion (assuming two more years of cash generation reduces it), the $4.5 billion convertible perpetual preferred, and the $3.9 billion pod joint-venture minority interest, and about $67 billion of common equity remains across roughly 1.36 billion shares — near $49. Haircut that back to about $42 to allow for the convertible preferred converting into shares and for the debt allocation between the two companies landing less favourably than assumed.
KDP.sop_bear: Adverse parts valuation, roughly $26 a share — and this, not the $28.50 the board file carried, is the honest downside floor. Beverage Co.: about $12.8 billion of revenue at a 29% margin gives roughly $3.7 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation; at 13 times, reflecting a company still carrying separation overhang, that is about $48.1 billion. Global Coffee Co.: coffee profit misses on elevated green-coffee costs at roughly $3.1 billion; at 8.5 times, the multiple a leveraged, slower-growth coffee company earns without a chief executive or a track record, that is about $26.4 billion. Deduct $2.5 billion of separation and stranded costs for about $72 billion of enterprise value. Subtract net debt of about $28.5 billion (leverage stays near 4.5 times because the spin slips), the $4.5 billion preferred and the $3.9 billion pod minority, leaving about $35 billion of common equity, or roughly $26 a share. Three independent checks land in the same place: the 52-week low is $24.88, $26 is about 10.3 times 2027 consensus earnings of $2.53, and the $0.92 annual dividend yields 3.5% there — the level at which income buyers historically step in. Crucially, this is a valuation floor, not a hard one: there is no deal-break price, no cash backstop and no contractual payout beneath this stock.
KDP.sop_breakdown: Base case of about $36 a share, the probability-weighted midpoint of the two cases (roughly 55% weight on the favourable path, 45% on the adverse one). Beverage Co. contributes about $3.85 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation at 15 times, or roughly $57.8 billion of enterprise value — a little over $20 a share after its share of the claims. Global Coffee Co. contributes about $3.35 billion at 10 times, or roughly $33.5 billion. Less about $2.5 billion of separation and stranded costs, combined enterprise value is close to $88.8 billion. From that, subtract roughly $27.5 billion of net debt, the $4.5 billion convertible perpetual preferred and the $3.9 billion pod joint-venture minority interest — about $35.9 billion of claims ahead of the common — leaving roughly $52.9 billion of equity across 1.36 billion shares. That is about $38 on those multiples; rounding down to $36 reflects the real possibility that the timetable slips again and that the debt split between the two companies is less shareholder-friendly than assumed. For reference, the street's median target is $37 and the consensus is $34.40, so this base case sits inside, not outside, what is already published.
KDP.risk_reward: About 1.3 to 1, not the 2.8 to 1 carried in the board file. From $31.12, the upside to the $36 base case is roughly 16%, and to the $37 street median target roughly 19%. The downside to the honest floor of $26 is roughly 16%. The board file's 2.8-to-1 came from pairing a top-of-range $37.70 target with a $28.50 floor, and that floor is simply the 200-day moving average ($28.62) rather than anything that backstops value. Correct the floor for the $4.5 billion of perpetual preferred and $3.9 billion of pod joint-venture minority interest that sit ahead of the common, and the asymmetry is roughly symmetric. This is a fairly priced situation with an unscheduled catalyst, not a defined-risk special situation.
KDP.catalyst_summary: The tax-free spin-off of the coffee business is real and structurally in motion but carries no date: 'targeted for early 2027' as of 23 June 2026, already pushed back from an end-of-2026 goal, conditioned on leverage and market conditions, with the coffee chief executive seat vacant since the end of July 2026 and no registration statement filed. Upside to about $36 against a soft floor near $26 — roughly 1.3 to 1.
KDP.dated_milestone: The only firm date on the calendar is second-quarter 2026 results, released before the market opens on Thursday 6 August 2026, with a call at 8:00 a.m. Eastern hosted by chief executive Tim Cofer and chief financial officer Anthony DiSilvestro. That is the first full quarter including JDE Peet's and the next point at which the separation timetable, the debt split and the dividend policy can be updated. The separation itself has no date: management's language on 23 June 2026 was 'targeted for early 2027,' subject to milestones including appropriate leverage at each company and supportive market conditions. Completed and verified dates behind us: tender offer settlement 1 April 2026 at 96.22% tendered; post-closing acceptance to 97.75% settled 15 April 2026; Euronext Amsterdam delisting 30 April 2026; bridge loan repaid 30 March 2026.
KDP.forcing_function:
Two prerequisites, neither of which yet exists, are what would convert this from a story into a dated event. First, the naming of a chief executive for Global Coffee Co. The board reopened that search on 23 June 2026 under chairman Pamela Patsley after Rafael Oliveira — named to the role only in April 2026 — resigned effective the end of July. No spin-off gets a distribution date before its chief executive is hired. Second, the filing of the registration statement for the coffee company with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the document that sets the record and distribution dates and publishes standalone financials, the debt allocation and the dividend policy for both halves. That filing is the moment the market can finally price the two businesses separately, and it is the true forcing event.

A third, weaker trigger is deleveraging itself: management has tied timing to 'appropriate leverage levels at each company,' so each quarter of debt paydown mechanically brings the date closer. The nearest checkpoint on all three is the 6 August 2026 second-quarter report.
KDP.consensus_delta:
Here is the uncomfortable part: on the parts valuation, we largely agree with Wall Street, which is exactly what an expectations-arbitrage framework is supposed to flag as a warning. Consensus sits at a $34.40 average and a $37 median target, with a $39 high and a $28 low. JPMorgan raised its target to $38 on 23 July 2026, Bank of America added the stock to its high-conviction list on 21 July 2026, and Barclays' own parts work points above the current price on improving leverage and what it calls waning transaction uncertainty. The board file's $37.70 target is effectively the street median. There is no variant view in buying a sum-of-the-parts story that every major broker has already published.

Where we do disagree with the street is on two mechanics it appears to be waving through. First, the capital structure. Most published parts work deducts bond debt and stops there. It does not fully deduct the $4.5 billion Series A convertible perpetual preferred — senior, never-maturing, 4.75%, participating in common dividends on an as-converted basis, with a $1,000-per-share liquidation preference — or the $3.9 billion minority interest created when Apollo, KKR and Goldman Sachs Asset Management bought 49% of the pod-manufacturing joint venture for about $4 billion. Those are permanent claims on the very cash flows the parts valuation is capitalising, worth roughly $6 a share. The street's enthusiasm was priced against an enterprise value that is understated.

Second, timing. The street is underwriting 'early 2027' as though it were scheduled. It is not. The target has already moved once, it is conditioned on leverage the company is still working down, and the three price-target raises all came after the designated coffee chief executive resigned — meaning the market raised numbers on the parts while ignoring the process. Our view is that mid-to-late 2027 is at least as likely as early 2027, and every quarter of delay is a quarter of carrying leverage near 4.5 times through a period of elevated coffee costs. The discount is real; the reason it exists is also real, and the street is treating it as friction rather than as risk.
KDP.valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months carry more downside surprise than upside. The immediate one is second-quarter results on 6 August 2026, three days from this review. It is the first full quarter with JDE Peet's consolidated, and green-coffee costs have been elevated all year — the stock has already underperformed the consumer-staples sector over the past quarter on exactly that concern, falling from roughly $33.30 in early July to $31.12, with a 52-week range of $24.88 to $35.94. Consensus expects $0.55 of diluted earnings per share against $0.49 a year ago. A guidance trim on coffee input costs would hit a stock that has just absorbed three bullish broker notes, which is the setup that produces the sharpest single-day falls.

The structural pressure is the balance sheet. Total debt stood at $25.7 billion against $0.9 billion of cash at 31 March 2026, before the April closing consumed the roughly $18 billion of acquisition funding held in current assets, and combined leverage is targeted near 4.5 times cash profit including about $5 billion of assumed JDE Peet's bonds. On top of that sits $214 million a year of preferred dividends at 4.75% on $4.5 billion, plus the 49% of pod-manufacturing profit that now belongs to outside investors. Free cash flow yield is about 3.7% and the ordinary dividend costs roughly $1.25 billion a year. That is a thin cushion for deleveraging on the timetable the spin requires.

The third risk is integration itself, conducted with a hole at the top of the coffee business. Rafael Oliveira left at the end of July 2026; Tim Cofer is running coffee in the interim while preparing to lead the other company. Cross-border integrations of this size lose people, and this one is losing them at the moment the acquired business is meant to be readied for its own listing. Any of these — a coffee-cost guidance cut, a leverage-driven delay, or an integration stumble — pushes the separation date out without breaking the thesis, which is the worst outcome for a position sized to an event: the story survives, the clock does not.
KDP.positioning_washout:
The shareholder base is the wrong one for what this company is becoming, and the separation is what forces the change. Keurig Dr Pepper has been owned as a defensive staples holding paying a $0.23 quarterly dividend, $0.92 a year, for a yield near 3.0%, with modest leverage. It is now a 4.5-times-levered company mid-way through splitting in two, with $8.5 billion of senior and minority capital from private-credit sponsors in its structure.

Three mechanical selling pressures are queued. First, the dividend must be divided between two companies at separation and neither policy has been announced. Income mandates that require a stated yield cannot hold a position through an unannounced payout reset, and a slower-growth coffee company carrying its share of the debt is unlikely to fund the income half of that split generously.

Second — and this is the point the board file has backwards — index flow works against the parent, not for it. Funds tracking the S&P 500 hold Keurig Dr Pepper because it is in the index. When the coffee company is distributed, those funds receive shares in a company that is not in their benchmark, and unless the index committee adds it they must sell mechanically, often within days. That forced supply creates a discount in the newly listed coffee company; it does no favours for the shares held beforehand. The genuine forced-seller opportunity in this situation is a trade in the spin-off, six or more months from now, and it is not available today.

Third, the convertible perpetual preferred carries registration rights, giving Apollo, KKR and the co-investors a defined path to convert and sell. That is a supply overhang with no fixed date, sitting above a share count of roughly 1.36 billion. The washout that would make this interesting — income holders capitulating into a dividend reset, taking the stock toward the $26 to $28 area — has not happened. Buying before it does is paying for a re-rating while the sellers are still in the building.
KDP.moderator_conclusion:
The verdict is to wait, not to pass. This is a genuine transformation, executed so far with real competence, priced at a genuine discount — and it has no date.

Start with what is verified. The enabling acquisition is finished: $18 billion for JDE Peet's, settled 1 April 2026 with 96.22% of shares tendered, taken to 97.75%, delisted from Amsterdam on 30 April 2026, with a post-closing demerger implemented specifically to make the separation possible. That is not a promise, it is completed corporate machinery, and it distinguishes this from the average 'strategic review' story. Operations are holding too — first-quarter 2026 net sales up 9.4% to $3.98 billion, guidance reaffirmed twice including on the day the coffee chief executive's resignation was disclosed, four straight quarters at or above estimates.

Now the part that decides the sizing. The event we are actually being asked to underwrite — the coffee spin-off — is not scheduled. It was 'operationally ready by end of 2026' in October 2025 and became 'targeted for early 2027' on 23 June 2026, explicitly subject to leverage levels and market conditions. No registration statement has been filed. The chief executive designated to run the coffee company resigned at the end of July 2026, the second time that seat has emptied in nine months, and the search has restarted. Companies do not set distribution dates for businesses without chief executives. That is a soft, non-binding catalyst with no contractual payout, and in a book built on dated events it does not earn a front-foot allocation.

The floor is the second problem. The board file carried $28.50; that is the 200-day moving average, a chart level. Beneath this stock there is no deal-break price, no cash backstop and no contractual payment — only a staples multiple applied to a balance sheet at 4.5 times cash profit, with $4.5 billion of perpetual preferred and $3.9 billion of pod joint-venture minority interest standing ahead of the common. Deduct those properly and the defensible floor is about $26, corroborated by the $24.88 52-week low, by 10.3 times 2027 consensus earnings, and by a 3.5% dividend yield. Against a $36 base case that is roughly 1.3 to 1 from $31.12 — respectable, not asymmetric, and well short of the 2.8 to 1 the file carried.

Third, we would be joining a crowd. Consensus is $34.40 average and $37 median; JPMorgan went to $38 on 23 July and Bank of America put the name on its high-conviction list on 21 July. Our $36 sits inside the published range. A special-situation position pays for seeing what the market has not; here the market sees the parts perfectly well and is discounting the process — the leverage, the timing and the missing chief executive — which is precisely what we also cannot resolve.

Finally, the index-flow premise in the original file points the wrong way. Forced index selling hits the distributed company after the split, creating a discount in the coffee spin-off. It is not a tailwind for the parent beforehand. The real forced-seller trade in this situation is a future trade in the spin-off, and it is at least two or three quarters away.

So: wait for the wash-out, and be specific about it. Two developments convert this into an entry at any price: a named chief executive for the coffee company, or the registration statement filing that sets a record date. Either one turns an undated goal into a scheduled event and re-rates the reward-to-risk immediately. Absent those, one price does the same job — $28 or below, which is roughly 11 times 2027 earnings and puts the honest floor within about 8%, restoring genuine asymmetry. The 6 August 2026 second-quarter report, three days out, is the nearest thing to a trigger in either direction: a coffee-cost guidance cut could deliver that price, and a separation-timetable update could deliver the date. Watch it; do not front-run it.
KDP.interrogator_dossier:
# Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP) — Event Dossier

**Date of review:** 3 August 2026 · **Live price:** $31.12 (Nasdaq close, 31 July 2026 tape; market cap ~$42.3B)
**The event under examination:** a tax-free spin-off of the coffee business ("Global Coffee Co.") out of Keurig Dr Pepper, leaving a North American refreshment-beverage company ("Beverage Co.") behind.

This is not a judgement on whether Dr Pepper is a good business. It is a judgement on one question: is there a real, dated, binding corporate event that forces the market to re-price this company, and if the event does not arrive, what actually stops the stock from falling?

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC — how the story has evolved

The story began in August 2025, when Keurig Dr Pepper announced two things at once: it would buy JDE Peet's, the Dutch-listed global coffee group behind Jacobs, Douwe Egberts and Peet's, for roughly $18 billion in cash; and it would then split itself into two separately listed companies. Management's argument was that the combined company had become two businesses with almost nothing in common — a fast-growing North American drinks business (Dr Pepper, Canada Dry, Snapple, plus newer energy brands) bolted onto a slow-growing, commodity-exposed global coffee business — and that separating them would let each be valued on its own merits.

The buy side of that plan has been executed, and executed well. The tender offer for JDE Peet's was declared unconditional with 96.22% of shares tendered, settled on 1 April 2026, and rose to 97.75% after the post-closing acceptance window. Crossing 95% let the company start statutory buy-out proceedings under Dutch law, terminate the Euronext Amsterdam listing (last trading day 29 April 2026, delisted 30 April 2026), and implement a post-closing demerger — a restructuring step whose explicit purpose is to make the later separation possible. That is real, verifiable, completed corporate machinery, not a press release.

The sell side — the actual spin — has drifted. In late October 2025 management said the company would be "operationally ready to separate by end of 2026." Coverage of the February 2026 financing update still carried a year-end-2026 target, hedged by the phrase that timing depends on "achievement of key milestones, including appropriate leverage levels at each company, and supportive market conditions." By the 23 June 2026 announcement, the target had become "early 2027." That is one slip of roughly one to two quarters, and the language has moved from a date to a condition.

The second drift is in leadership, and it matters more than the calendar. The coffee chief executive seat has now emptied twice. Sudhanshu Priyadarshi, originally slated to run the coffee company, was replaced as chief financial officer in November 2025 and removed from that plan. Rafael Oliveira was named chief executive of the future Global Coffee Co. on the day the JDE Peet's deal closed in April 2026 — and told the company in June 2026 that he was leaving at the end of July for an outside chief executive role. The board has reopened the search, led by chairman Pamela Patsley, who will chair the coffee company's board after separation. Bank of America called the departure a setback specifically because the search has to restart ahead of a targeted 2027 spin.

**Read-through:** the acquisition is finished; the separation is not scheduled. A company cannot file a registration statement, run a roadshow, and set a distribution date for a business that has no chief executive.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS — testing the event, not the franchise

| Management claim | Verified evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| The JDE Peet's acquisition will close in the first half of 2026 | Settled 1 April 2026; 97.75% tendered; Amsterdam delisting 30 April 2026 | Delivered, on time |
| The company will separate into two listed companies | Board-approved; post-closing demerger implemented as the enabling step | Structurally in motion |
| Separation "by end of 2026" (Oct 2025 / Feb 2026) | Restated as "early 2027" on 23 June 2026 | Slipped |
| 2026 net sales of $25.9–$26.4 billion and constant-currency adjusted earnings-per-share growth in a low-double-digit range | Reaffirmed at first-quarter results on 23 April 2026 and again on 23 June 2026 | Holding, so far |
| First-quarter 2026 momentum | Net sales $3.98 billion, up 9.4% reported and 8.1% in constant currency; adjusted diluted earnings per share $0.39 | Delivered |
| Combined leverage of about 4.5 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation | Balance sheet at 31 March 2026 already shows $25.7 billion of total debt against $0.9 billion of cash, with roughly $18.0 billion of acquisition funding parked in current assets awaiting the April close | Consistent, and heavy |

The financial trajectory is respectable but the balance sheet has been transformed. Full-year 2025 revenue was $16.60 billion with reported earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of $4.19 billion. Consensus for 2027 — the first clean full year with coffee included — is roughly $29.9 billion of revenue, $7.64 billion of that same earnings measure, and $2.53 of earnings per share. At $31.12 the stock trades on about 12.3 times that 2027 figure, against large-cap packaged-food and drinks peers at roughly 17 to 20 times. So the optical discount is real.

**The forensic catch that a naive parts-valuation will miss.** The $18 billion was not funded with debt and common equity alone. Three separate claims now sit ahead of, or alongside, the ordinary shareholder:

1. **$4.5 billion of Series A convertible perpetual preferred stock**, co-led by Apollo and KKR with an anchor commitment from accounts advised by T. Rowe Price, upsized from $3 billion on 23 February 2026. It pays 4.75% a year, ranks senior to common stock for dividends and on liquidation with a $1,000-per-share liquidation preference, participates in common dividends on an as-converted basis, and is perpetual — it never matures. The investors have registration rights, meaning a defined path to sell into the market.
2. **A pod-manufacturing joint venture** into which an investor partnership backed by Apollo, KKR and Goldman Sachs Asset Management put roughly $4 billion for a 49% stake. This shows up as $3.9 billion of minority interest on the 31 March 2026 balance sheet. Note what was sold: 49% of the economics of K-Cup pod manufacturing — the single highest-margin node in the coffee business, the "blade" in the razor-and-blade model.
3. **Roughly $9 billion of new long-term debt plus about $5 billion of assumed JDE Peet's bonds.**

Add it up and something close to $36 billion of debt, preferred and minority claims sits between enterprise value and the common share. Any sum-of-the-parts that values the whole coffee business and subtracts only bond debt overstates per-share value by roughly $8.4 billion, or about $6 per share. This is the most important single number in the file.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Stable on operations, softening on the separation. Management has reaffirmed the 2026 outlook twice in three months, including on the same day it disclosed the loss of the coffee chief executive — a deliberate choice to separate operational confidence from separation confidence. The wording on the split has moved in one direction only: from "operationally ready by end of 2026," to a conditional year-end-2026 target, to "targeted for early 2027." Nobody has said the split is at risk; nobody has committed to a date either.

Tim Cofer, the chief executive, has said he will run the coffee business himself in the interim and become chief executive of Beverage Co. after the split. That is a candid admission that the coffee company is currently being run by someone whose future is at the other company.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY — high on operations, medium on timing

On the numbers, credibility is good. The company has met or exceeded consensus earnings estimates in each of the past four quarters, and the first quarter of 2026 came in ahead. On the transaction, credibility is excellent: an $18 billion cross-border tender that clears 96% and delists on schedule is hard, and they did it.

On separation timing, credibility is medium at best. One slip has already happened, the target is explicitly conditioned on leverage levels and market conditions the company does not control, and the leadership prerequisite has just been vacated for the second time. Reliability score on the event date: **Medium**.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions recur and none has a public answer:

- **How is the debt split?** Which company carries how much of the roughly $28 billion of net debt is the single largest determinant of what each share is worth, and it has not been disclosed. A coffee company loaded with the leverage is a very different security from a beverage company loaded with it.
- **What happens to the dividend?** The current $0.23 quarterly payout, $0.92 a year, yields about 3.0%. After the split it must be divided between two companies, and neither policy has been stated.
- **Where does the preferred and the pod joint venture land?** The convertible preferred was issued at the level intended to become Beverage Co.; the 49% pod-manufacturing stake is coffee-side economics. How these are allocated determines the real per-share value on both sides.

The pressure point management is not addressing is green-coffee cost. Elevated arabica prices have been compressing US coffee results all year, and the company now has vastly more coffee exposure than it did twelve months ago — at exactly the moment it wants to sell that business to the public market on a clean multiple.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**Red flags**

- The separation is undated. "Targeted for early 2027," conditioned on leverage and market conditions, is a goal, not a commitment (23 June 2026).
- The coffee chief executive seat is empty for the second time in nine months; the search restarted in June 2026. No registration statement for the coffee company has been filed.
- About $8.5 billion of non-common capital — $4.5 billion of perpetual preferred at 4.75% and $3.9 billion of pod-joint-venture minority interest — permanently reduces what the common shareholder owns. Selling 49% of pod manufacturing is selling the best margin pool in the coffee business.
- Leverage of roughly 4.5 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation makes the equity a levered call option: a 10% shortfall in profit combined with a one-turn multiple de-rating removes roughly a third of the share price.
- The dividend is a candidate for a reset at separation, and a 3%-yield shareholder base is not the natural owner of a levered, mid-split company.
- The index-flow leg of the thesis points the wrong way. When a spin happens, index funds that track the parent must mechanically sell the new company. That creates a discount in the coffee spin-off, not a gain in the shares you hold beforehand.

**Green flags**

- The hard part is done. The tender cleared 96.22%, settled 1 April 2026, reached 97.75%, delisted 30 April 2026, and the post-closing demerger — the legal step that makes the separation possible — has been implemented.
- The bridge loan was repaid early on 30 March 2026 out of preferred and joint-venture proceeds, removing short-term refinancing risk.
- Operating results are holding: first-quarter 2026 net sales up 9.4%, guidance reaffirmed twice, four consecutive quarters at or above consensus.
- Board-level commitment is visible in governance, not just words: a chairman designated for the coffee company's board, independent boards planned for both.
- The street has warmed rather than cooled — JPMorgan raised its target to $38 on 23 July 2026, Bank of America added the stock to its high-conviction list on 21 July 2026, and Barclays' own parts analysis points above the current price.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The financing tells you what management was worried about. Upsizing the preferred from $3 billion to $4.5 billion and selling half the pod business to private-credit sponsors, rather than issuing common stock, says the board judged the share price too low to sell — a bullish signal about their view of value, and a bearish one about the cost, because perpetual 4.75% preferred with registration rights and a liquidation preference is expensive, permanent capital.

The second signal is the phrase "appropriate leverage levels at each company." Read plainly, that is the company telling you the spin will not happen until each side can stand on its own balance sheet. With combined leverage near 4.5 times and free cash flow yield at roughly 3.7%, deleveraging to a level where two investment-grade companies can be carved out takes time. The date is a function of the balance sheet, and the balance sheet says "not soon."

The third signal is that the last three price-target raises came *after* the coffee chief executive resigned. The market is pricing the parts, not the process. That means the parts story is already consensus.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Trajectory: turning.** This is a company deliberately reconstructing itself into two different companies, and it is roughly halfway through.

**What the director must weigh before sizing:** the event is real but it is not scheduled, and the downside is not backstopped by anything hard. There is no deal-break price, no cash floor, no contractual payout — if the spin slips to late 2027 or is shelved, nothing catches the stock except a staples multiple on a levered balance sheet. The board file carried a floor of $28.50; that number is the 200-day moving average ($28.62), a chart level rather than a value backstop. The defensible floor, built from an adverse parts valuation with the preferred and minority claims properly deducted, is closer to $26 — near the 52-week low of $24.88, about 10.3 times 2027 consensus earnings, and a 3.5% dividend yield. Using the honest floor, the reward-to-risk from $31.12 is roughly 1.3 to 1, not the 2.8 to 1 the board file carried.

**Moat.** Narrow but genuine on the beverage side: Dr Pepper is the number-two carbonated soft drink brand in the United States and gaining share, supported by a direct-store-delivery distribution network that is expensive to replicate — an intangible-brand and scale-distribution moat. On the coffee side it is eroding: the Keurig razor-and-blade model faces unlicensed pod competition and declining single-serve volumes, and the acquired JDE Peet's business earns structurally lower margins than legacy Keurig, so the blended returns profile of the combined coffee company is below what Keurig alone once earned. Selling 49% of pod manufacturing narrows it further.

**Secular threat.** Manageable. Coffee and carbonated drinks are not being structurally displaced; the pressure is commodity cost and channel mix, which are cyclical and negotiable, not terminal. The cheapness here is a leverage-and-complexity discount, not a melting-ice-cube discount.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 3 | TRAJECTORY: PIVOTING | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: ERODING | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable

LBTYK.bull_thesis:
The bull case is that Liberty Global finishes taking itself apart and the market is forced to price the pieces instead of the conglomerate. At $9.59 (close, 27 July 2026) the whole company is worth about $3.27 billion on roughly 341 million shares. Against that, management's own raised year-end 2026 target for holding-company cash is about $2.0 billion, or roughly $5.86 a share, and the Liberty Growth portfolio of private investments carries an independently appraised value of $2.9 billion, or about $8.50 a share. Those two items alone come to roughly $14.36 a share. Buying the stock today therefore means paying about a third less than the cash and the investment portfolio are said to be worth, and receiving every operating telecom business for nothing. Chief executive Mike Fries made exactly that point on the 24 July 2026 call, noting the price then implied “essentially zero equity value attributed to our Liberty Telecom operations.”

The event meant to close that gap is the separation and Amsterdam listing of Ziggo Group, which combines VodafoneZiggo in the Netherlands with Telenet in Belgium into a single Benelux operator of roughly 13 million customers and about 6.6 billion euros (roughly $7.7 billion) of annual revenue. Liberty intends to distribute about 90% of it to its own shareholders, with Vodafone keeping 10%.

What makes this credible rather than promotional is that the sponsor has done it once already and the sub-milestones keep clearing. Liberty spun off Sunrise, its Swiss operator, in November 2024; management values that distributed stake at about $12 per Liberty Global share today, and it trades in Zurich at roughly 8 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. Since then: the Belgian regulator approved the Wyre-Proximus fiber-sharing agreement (cleared the day before the July call); every approval needed to buy Vodafone's half of the Dutch joint venture has been obtained, with closing due by the end of July 2026; new leadership for Ziggo Group was named and starts 1 September 2026; and management has raised about $1.2 billion this year, roughly $900 million from portfolio disposals plus a $340 million loan against the Wyre stake, which let it lift the year-end corporate cash target from about $1.5 billion to about $2.0 billion. On the strength of that progress Fries pulled the timing forward rather than pushing it back, saying the company is “a bit more ambitious on the timing of the spin off. And we are currently saying mid-2027 versus H2 2027.”

The private marks are also getting validated in cash rather than in slides. The company fully exited EdgeConneX in the second quarter for $604 million of proceeds, described as about four times the original investment over roughly ten years and better than a 30% annual return.

Underneath the event, the asset actually being separated is improving. VodafoneZiggo added 7,200 broadband customers in the quarter, its best result in more than six years, plus 31,700 postpaid mobile customers, with fixed revenue per user up 0.6%. Telenet added 6,100 broadband and 2,200 postpaid customers. If management delivers the stated equity story for Ziggo Group - leverage down to 4.5 times and free cash flow of 500 million euros by 2028 - and the market applies the free-cash-flow yield it already applies to Sunrise, Fries argues the listed Benelux group is worth up to $14 per Liberty Global share on its own.

Conditions that must hold: the Dutch stake purchase closes on schedule; the Belgian and Dutch asset sales of 1.2 to 1.4 billion euros execute and bring subsidiary debt down; the Benelux customer recovery continues rather than reverses; the private portfolio marks hold up as further positions are sold; and the board actually files and completes the listing rather than exercising its right to abandon it.
LBTYK.bear_thesis:
The bear case is that the discount is real, deserved, and self-perpetuating - and that nothing forces it to close for at least a year while the business underneath it shrinks.

Start with what actually broke. The board entry for this name carried a downside floor of $9.50. On 24 July 2026, the day second-quarter results landed, the stock traded as low as $9.30 intraday and closed at $9.60 on about 4.1 million shares, roughly five times its recent daily volume. The floor was breached within hours of the print and has not been recovered: the 27 July close was $9.59. It was never a floor; it was a recent price level, and the stated risk-to-reward of 4.7 to 1 was computed when the stock was near $11, which is where it traded when the results deck was written. The setup has moved materially against that entry.

The second-quarter numbers themselves were poor. Revenue of $1,172.0 million fell 7.7% as reported and 6.0% on a like-for-like basis. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of $324.9 million fell 3.1%. Adjusted free cash flow was negative $150.4 million, and the company posted a net loss of $357.8 million. Retained earnings have fallen from about $8.02 billion at September 2025 to about $5.08 billion at June 2026 - close to $3 billion of accumulated losses in three quarters. Consolidated net debt stands at about $6.66 billion.

The clearest problem is the asset that is not being separated. Virgin Media O2, the UK business Liberty owns half of alongside Telefonica, is deteriorating: revenue down 7.9% on a like-for-like basis, 28,200 broadband customers lost and 63,000 postpaid customers lost in the quarter, with full-year guidance for both revenue and earnings to decline 3% to 5% against capital spending of 2.0 to 2.2 billion pounds and adjusted free cash flow of only about 200 million pounds. Chief financial officer Charles Bracken conceded that “leverage is above our 4 to 5x target, and that credit spreads are currently elevated,” and on refinancing added “we acknowledge recent trading levels” - an admission the bonds have widened. A leveraged, shrinking half-stake can be worth zero, and in a bad enough outcome it can consume holding-company resources rather than contribute them.

Now attack the floor itself. The roughly $2.0 billion of corporate cash is not shareholder cash. It is the purchase price for Vodafone's half of the Dutch business. Fries said plainly the company will “end the year exactly where we started the year from a cash point of view” - the asset sales funded the acquisition. That cash converts into an illiquid, leveraged telecom equity, and there is no dividend and no share repurchase creating a bid underneath the stock. The $2.9 billion investment portfolio is an appraisal, not a bid, with the top five positions accounting for more than half of it; concentrated private marks are exactly what gets cut when funding markets tighten. Haircut the portfolio by half and assign the operating telecoms nothing, and the honest floor is about $8.00 a share, roughly 17% below the current price rather than the 2% the board entry implied.

Finally, the event is soft and distant. There is no record date, no listing prospectus, no scheduled shareholder vote. The company's own words are “as early as mid-2027” - about eleven months away - the transaction still requires shareholder and exchange approvals, and the board explicitly retains discretion to abandon it. The headline value target also leans on 2028 assumptions: the $14-per-share figure for Ziggo Group requires free cash flow of 500 million euros, against combined guidance today of roughly 100 million euros at VodafoneZiggo and 20 million euros at Telenet. That is close to a fourfold increase in two years, and it is the weakest load-bearing number in the entire case.

What would confirm the bear: the mid-2027 language slipping back toward late 2027 or later; the Wyre stake sale missing its year-end 2026 to first-quarter 2027 window or clearing below the carrying mark; a writedown in the investment portfolio; further widening in Virgin Media O2 credit; or the Benelux customer recovery stalling before the listing.
LBTYK.sop_bull: Roughly $30 a share if the separation completes on the guided path and the market pays Sunrise-like multiples for the pieces. Built up on roughly 341 million shares: holding-company cash of about $2.0 billion, or $5.86 a share, taken at face value; the Liberty Growth private portfolio at its full independently appraised $2.9 billion, or $8.50 a share, which the EdgeConneX exit at about four times cost supports; Ziggo Group at management's stated ceiling of $14 a share, which requires the Benelux group to reach 500 million euros of free cash flow and 4.5 times leverage by 2028 and to be valued on the 10.5% to 13.5% free-cash-flow yield the market already applies to Sunrise; the 50% Virgin Media O2 stake recovering to about $1.50 a share as leverage comes down; and Virgin Media Ireland plus residual items at about $0.50. Note that the $12 a share of already-distributed Sunrise stock is deliberately excluded - shareholders hold it directly and it is not value inside these shares. Management's own “from an $18 stock we have a clear opportunity to create $37 to $40 of value” framing double-counts it; this figure does not.
LBTYK.sop_bear: About $8.00 a share, and this is the verified floor, not the board's $9.50. Built up on roughly 341 million shares: holding-company cash of about $2.0 billion, or $5.86 a share, using management's own raised year-end 2026 target and crediting it in full even though it is committed to the Vodafone purchase; the Liberty Growth portfolio haircut by half to about $1.45 billion, or $4.25 a share, on the grounds that appraisals are not bids and the top five positions are more than half the total; and the operating telecoms - the 50% Virgin Media O2 stake, Ziggo Group and Virgin Media Ireland - carried at zero, which is close to what the market pays for them today. That sums to about $10.11, from which roughly $2 a share is deducted for holding-company running costs, the risk that resources are drawn down to support a leveraged Virgin Media O2, and the discount the market persistently applies to a holding company that has not completed its break-up. For cross-reference, tangible book value - equity less goodwill and other intangibles - is about $13.32 a share and reported book value about $27.05, so the bear case is well inside accounting values. The severe case, in which the listing is abandoned and the portfolio is written down further, is closer to $6.50.
LBTYK.sop_breakdown:
Two numbers matter and they answer different questions. The sum of the parts, if the break-up completes and the value is recognised, is about $17.50 to $18.00 a share: holding-company cash $5.86, the Liberty Growth portfolio at a 25% haircut to its appraised mark $6.38, Ziggo Group at about half of management's $14 ceiling to reflect that the 500-million-euro free-cash-flow target is a 2028 number against roughly 120 million euros guided today $7.00, the 50% Virgin Media O2 stake $1.00, and Virgin Media Ireland plus residuals $0.50 - about $20.74 before applying a 15% discount for holding-company frictions and the eleven months of execution still required, giving roughly $17.60.

The base case actually used is lower, because the event is not certain. Weighting the event-resolved target of $18.00 at 60% and the verified downside floor of $8.00 at 40% gives about $14.00 a share. Against the 27 July close of $9.59 that is roughly 46% of expected upside. The 60% weighting reflects a sponsor that has completed this exact transaction before and has cleared every sub-milestone so far, offset by the absence of any binding date, filing or vote, and the board's retained right to walk away.
LBTYK.risk_reward: About 5.3 to 1 on corrected inputs, better than the 4.7 to 1 the board claimed but for a different reason than the board gave. From the 27 July 2026 close of $9.59, upside to the event-resolved target of $18.00 is about +88%; downside to the verified floor of $8.00 is about -17%. That is $8.41 of upside against $1.59 of downside. The board's stated ratio used a $9.50 floor and a price near $11 - and that floor was breached intraday at $9.30 on 24 July 2026 and has not been regained. So the ratio has improved only because the price fell through the advertised floor, not because the floor held. Measured against the probability-weighted base case of $14.00 rather than the target, the ratio is a more sober 2.8 to 1.
LBTYK.catalyst_summary: Ziggo Group, the combined Dutch and Belgian business, is set to be spun off and listed in Amsterdam “as early as mid-2027” - no record date, no filing, about eleven months out - offering roughly +88% to an $18 event-resolved value against about -17% to a verified $8.00 asset floor, with the stock at a 52-week low of $9.59 after the 24 July 2026 results.
LBTYK.dated_milestone:
Verified on 28 July 2026 against the second-quarter results released 24 July 2026, the investor call of the same date, and the 1 June 2026 leadership announcement; no new disclosure has landed since the 24 July current report and quarterly report, so the status below is current.

No binding date exists for the event itself. The firm dates that do exist are preparatory: closing of the purchase of Vodafone's 50% interest in VodafoneZiggo by 31 July 2026, with all approvals already obtained; the new Ziggo Group chief executive and chief financial officer taking office on 1 September 2026, with the balance of the leadership team to be announced in September 2026; the sale of a stake in Wyre targeted for year-end 2026 or the first quarter of 2027; and 1.2 to 1.4 billion euros of Belgian and Dutch asset sales under way to reduce subsidiary debt. The listing itself is guided only as “as early as mid-2027”, accelerated from a prior “second half of 2027”, and remains subject to shareholder and exchange approval with the board retaining the right to abandon it.
LBTYK.forcing_function:
There is no single hard date that forces a re-rating, and that is the central weakness of this setup. The genuine trigger is the filing of a listing prospectus for Ziggo Group together with a scheduled shareholder vote, because that is the moment the separation stops being a plan and becomes a transaction with a calendar. That filing has not happened and has not been scheduled.

Before it, four checkpoints will move the odds. First, closing the purchase of Vodafone's half of the Dutch business by 31 July 2026 - imminent, fully approved, and foundational, because Ziggo Group cannot be formed without it. Second, the September 2026 completion of the Ziggo Group management team, which converts an intention into an operating company with its own leadership and reporting line. Third, the sale of the Wyre stake, targeted for year-end 2026 or the first quarter of 2027, which both tests the private marks in cash and funds the Belgian deleveraging the equity story depends on. Fourth, third-quarter results in late October 2026, the next occasion on which the mid-2027 language will either be reaffirmed or quietly stretched.

There is also a mechanical flow event further out. Because the shares to be distributed will list on Euronext Amsterdam rather than in the United States, index funds and mandates that cannot hold a foreign listing will be forced to sell the distributed stock. That is the classic post-separation supply that tends to create a better entry in the spun business than in the parent - a reason to expect the value to be recognised after the listing rather than on the day it happens.
LBTYK.consensus_delta:
The market is treating Liberty Global as a leveraged European cable operator and valuing it off consolidated, declining earnings - revenue down 7.7% in the second quarter, adjusted free cash flow of negative $150.4 million, a net loss of $357.8 million. On that lens the stock looks like a melting ice cube and $9.59 looks generous.

What that lens misses is that the consolidated figures include businesses being actively dismantled while excluding where the value sits. Holding-company cash at the raised year-end 2026 target of about $2.0 billion is $5.86 a share. The independently appraised Liberty Growth portfolio at $2.9 billion is $8.50 a share. Together that is roughly $14.36 against a $9.59 stock - a 33% discount to cash and investments alone, with every operating telecom business thrown in free. That is not a soft claim: management raised the cash target from $1.5 billion after beating its own disposal plan by a wide margin, banking about $1.2 billion year to date, and it realised EdgeConneX in the quarter for $604 million at roughly four times cost and better than a 30% annual return. The street is marking a portfolio to scepticism that has just been marked to cash at a premium.

The second thing the street has wrong is direction of travel on the event. The consensus reflex on any European telecom break-up is that it slips. This one was pulled forward: mid-2027 from the second half of 2027, on the back of a Belgian regulatory approval, full approval to buy out Vodafone's Dutch stake, and named leadership.

But there is a bull-side consensus error too, and honesty requires naming it. Published bullish work has run base cases as high as $27 a share by treating the holding-company cash as shareholder value and the appraised portfolio at face. It is neither free nor liquid: the cash is the purchase price for the Vodafone stake and converts into an illiquid leveraged equity, and the portfolio is five big private positions carried at appraisal. The market's discount is not irrational - it is a reasonable haircut for concentration, illiquidity, and a half-stake in a UK operator whose bonds have widened and whose leverage management admits sits above target. The genuine disagreement is narrower than the bulls claim: roughly $18 of parts value, not $27.
LBTYK.valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are the hard part, because every source of support is switched off while the trigger is still a year away.

Cash generation is negative right now. Adjusted free cash flow was negative $150.4 million in the second quarter and the company posted a $357.8 million net loss, on top of roughly $3 billion of accumulated losses since September 2025. Consolidated net debt is about $6.66 billion.

The holding-company cash cannot help the share price. It is earmarked for the Vodafone purchase closing by 31 July 2026 - Fries said the company will “end the year exactly where we started the year from a cash point of view” - and there is no dividend and no share repurchase. Nothing bids for the stock on weakness, which is precisely why it cut through the $9.50 level on the print without pausing and has stayed below it since.

The sharpest near-term risk is Virgin Media O2. Revenue fell 7.9% on a like-for-like basis; the business lost 28,200 broadband and 63,000 postpaid customers in the quarter; guidance is for revenue and earnings both to decline 3% to 5% while capital spending runs at 2.0 to 2.2 billion pounds, leaving adjusted free cash flow of about 200 million pounds. Management acknowledged leverage above the 4 to 5 times target, elevated credit spreads, and unfavourable trading levels on its bonds. If UK credit widens further, the market will start pricing the possibility that the parent has to support it - which attacks the cash floor directly.

There is also execution risk in the Belgian restructuring itself. Wyre is drawing a large underwritten facility to repay a roughly $2.3 billion intercompany loan to Telenet and pay a $400 million dividend, with Telenet then retiring 2028 maturities. That plumbing has to work, in a market where the company itself says spreads are elevated.

Finally, the calendar. Third-quarter results in late October 2026 are the next opportunity for the mid-2027 language to be stretched. Any softening there, or a Wyre stake sale that misses its window or clears below the carrying mark, would take the stock toward the $8.00 floor well before any listing document exists.
LBTYK.positioning_washout:
The forced selling has partly already happened, and the more interesting wave is still ahead.

This shareholder base is not yield-driven - there is no dividend to cut - so the classic income-fund exodus does not apply. It is a value and event-driven register, and that register capitulated on the results. The stock traded to $9.30 intraday on 24 July 2026 on about 4.1 million shares, roughly five times its recent daily volume, closing at $9.60 and setting a 52-week low against a $13.12 high in February. It closed 27 July at $9.59 on continued heavy turnover of about 4.5 million shares across the share classes, so the break has been held rather than reversed. That is what exhaustion looks like: a heavy break of a widely watched level, then a market that will not bid it back. One secondary source reported an unusual spike in put buying on the A shares around the print - roughly 33,000 contracts against a typical 714 a day - which, if accurate, points to hedging or bearish positioning immediately after the results rather than accumulation. That is a single low-quality source and should be treated as colour, not evidence.

The absence of a company bid matters more than usual. With repurchases off while cash funds the Vodafone purchase, there is no price-insensitive buyer to absorb tax-loss selling into year-end 2026, and this stock is sitting on losses for anyone who bought above $11.

The larger mechanical event comes at the separation itself. Liberty holders will receive shares in a company listed on Euronext Amsterdam, not in the United States. Index funds tracking US benchmarks, and mandates barred from holding foreign-listed securities, will have to sell the distributed stock regardless of value. That indiscriminate supply is the well-worn reason spun-off companies are often cheapest in the weeks after listing. For this thesis it cuts two ways: it argues the value gets recognised after the listing rather than at it, and it argues the better entry may eventually be in Ziggo Group itself rather than in the parent today.
LBTYK.moderator_conclusion:
This is a good ratio attached to a slow, soft trigger, and it arrives after the advertised safety net has already given way. Both halves of that sentence need to be held at once.

What is genuinely strong: the sponsor. Liberty Global has completed this exact manoeuvre before - Sunrise, spun in November 2024, is worth roughly $12 per Liberty share to holders who received it - and every checkable sub-milestone for the second one has cleared. Belgian regulatory approval is in hand, all approvals to buy Vodafone's half of the Dutch business are obtained with closing due by 31 July 2026, leadership is named for 1 September 2026, about $1.2 billion has been raised against plan, and the year-end cash target was raised rather than cut. Management pulled the timing forward, to mid-2027 from the second half of 2027. Meanwhile the asset being separated is improving: VodafoneZiggo posted its best broadband quarter in more than six years. The valuation gap is real and arithmetic, not rhetorical - about $14.36 a share of cash and appraised investments against a $9.59 stock, with the operating telecoms free.

What disqualifies it from size today: the event is not dated. “As early as mid-2027” is roughly eleven months away, with no record date, no listing prospectus, no scheduled vote, and an explicit board right to abandon. That is a plan, not a scheduled event, and nothing forces the market's hand in the meantime. Worse for the entry premise, the $9.50 downside floor this name was admitted on did not survive its first test - the stock traded through it to $9.30 on 24 July 2026 and has closed below it every session since, at a 52-week low. Rebuilding the floor honestly from the balance sheet puts it near $8.00: holding-company cash of $5.86 a share, which is committed to an acquisition rather than distributable, plus the private portfolio at a 50% haircut, with the telecoms at zero. A real floor exists. It just sits about 17% lower than the one that was underwritten.

And the interim is genuinely unpleasant. Free cash flow is negative, there is no buyback and no dividend to support the shares, and the half-owned UK operator is losing broadband and mobile customers with leverage above target and credit spreads management concedes are elevated.

So: wait, with named conditions rather than a vague hope of a flush. Three things would change this from a watch to a purchase. First, a Ziggo Group listing prospectus filed or a shareholder vote scheduled - the moment the event acquires a calendar. Second, the Wyre stake sale completing at or above its carrying value in the year-end 2026 to first-quarter 2027 window, which would test the private marks in cash for a second time after EdgeConneX. Third, price: the balance-sheet floor is near $8.00, and a wash toward $8.50 would offer a genuine margin of safety rather than the notional one this name was entered on. Conversely, if the October 2026 results stretch the mid-2027 language, the thesis weakens rather than merely waits.

The value case underneath is sound - a verifiable discount to cash and investments, run by a team that has delivered a separation before - and the odds have improved slightly as the price fell while the parts did not. It simply does not need to be owned this month, and the discipline of this funnel is that an undated event eleven months out, entered below a floor that has already broken, does not earn real capital.
LBTYK.interrogator_dossier:
# Liberty Global (LBTYK) — Event Dossier

**Event under examination:** the planned separation and Euronext Amsterdam listing of "Ziggo Group", the newly formed Benelux telecom company combining VodafoneZiggo in the Netherlands with Telenet in Belgium.
**Prepared:** 28 July 2026. **Live price:** $9.59 (close, 27 July 2026; the A shares closed at $9.83). **Market value:** about $3.27 billion on roughly 341 million shares.
**Re-verification:** checked again on 28 July 2026. Nothing new has been disclosed since the second-quarter results — the company's most recent filings remain the current report and quarterly report both dated 24 July 2026. The event status below is unchanged, and the share price has slipped a further eleven cents to a fresh low.

---

## 0. THE HEADLINE FINDING

Two things are true at once here, and the board entry for this name captures neither cleanly.

First, the sponsor is credible and the plan is moving forward, not backward. On the 24 July 2026 second-quarter call, chief executive Mike Fries said the company is "a bit more ambitious on the timing of the spin off. And we are currently saying mid-2027 versus H2 2027." That is an acceleration. Most soft catalysts in this funnel slip; this one was pulled forward, and it was pulled forward because real, checkable building blocks were completed.

Second, the event is still not a dated, binding one. There is no record date, no listing prospectus, no shareholder vote scheduled. The company's own language is "as early as mid-2027" — roughly eleven months away — and the board retains the discretion to abandon the transaction. An eleven-month soft target is a plan, not a hard, scheduled event.

The more damaging finding concerns the downside floor. The board entry carries a floor of $9.50. On 24 July 2026, the day of the second-quarter results, the stock traded as low as $9.30 intraday and closed at $9.60. The floor has already been breached, and the stock has not recovered it — the 27 July close of $9.59 is below it again. It was not a floor; it was a recent price. The board's stated risk-to-reward of 4.7 to 1 was struck when the stock was near $11, which is where it was trading when the results deck was written. The setup has moved against the entry since.

That said, when I rebuild the floor from the balance sheet rather than from the chart, a real one does exist — it just sits lower, around $8.00. On corrected inputs the asymmetry is intact and slightly better than a week ago, because the price fell while the parts did not. The problem with this name today is not the ratio. It is that the event is undated and far away, the near-term cash generation is negative, and the advertised safety margin was overstated.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC — what management is actually doing

Liberty Global is deliberately taking itself apart. This is not a compounding story and management does not pretend otherwise.

The template was set in November 2024, when the company spun off Sunrise, its Swiss operator, to shareholders. Fries now values that distributed stake at about $12 per Liberty Global share, noting Sunrise trades in Zurich at roughly 8 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, or a 10.5% to 13.5% free-cash-flow yield (free cash flow divided by market value). Importantly, that $12 sits in shareholders' hands already — it is not value still inside the shares being analysed here, and any thesis that counts it twice is wrong.

Ziggo Group is the second act. It combines the Dutch and Belgian operations into a single Benelux group of roughly 13 million customers and €6.6 billion (about $7.7 billion) of annual revenue. The structure is a hybrid: Liberty Global intends to distribute about 90% of the shares to its own shareholders, with Vodafone retaining 10% following Liberty's purchase of Vodafone's half of the Dutch joint venture.

Alongside that, the company has been converting its private investment portfolio — "Liberty Growth" — into cash. Fries described the strategy plainly: "despite the size and scale and growth prospects of our businesses, we believe our stock today reflects no value for these assets."

**Read:** the narrative has been consistent and it is being executed against, not merely narrated. That is unusual and it counts.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs EVIDENCE (forensic)

| Management claim | Hard evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| The separation is "on track" and now targeted for mid-2027 | Belgian regulator approved the Wyre–Proximus fiber-sharing agreement (announced on the 24 July call as having cleared "yesterday"); all approvals obtained to buy Vodafone's 50% of the Dutch business, closing by end-July 2026; chief executive and chief financial officer for Ziggo Group named, effective 1 September 2026 | **Supported.** Each block is verifiable and each has actually cleared |
| Cash generation from asset sales is ahead of plan | About $1.2 billion raised year to date: roughly $900 million of Liberty Growth disposals plus a ~$340 million loan secured against the Wyre stake. Year-end corporate cash target raised from about $1.5 billion to about $2.0 billion | **Supported, and over-delivered** |
| The private portfolio marks are real | Full exit of EdgeConneX completed in the quarter for $604 million of proceeds, described as about four times the original investment over roughly ten years and above a 30% annualised return | **Supported by one large realisation.** One data point is not the whole portfolio, but it is the right kind of evidence |
| The stock prices the telecom operations at nothing | At about $11, management called it a 20% discount to the appraised value of cash plus the growth portfolio alone. At the 27 July close of $9.59 that discount is roughly 33% | **Arithmetically correct.** Whether the appraisals are worth their marks is the open question |
| Ziggo Group can be worth "up to $14 per Liberty share" | This requires leverage down to 4.5 times and free cash flow of €500 million by 2028. Today the two halves guide to roughly €100 million (VodafoneZiggo) and €20 million (Telenet) | **Aspirational.** It needs free cash flow to rise roughly fourfold in two years. This is the single weakest load-bearing number in the bull case |

Where the story is poorer than the numbers: the second quarter itself was soft. Revenue of $1,172.0 million fell 7.7% as reported (6.0% on a like-for-like basis); adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of $324.9 million fell 3.1%; adjusted free cash flow was **negative $150.4 million**, and the company posted a net loss of $357.8 million. Retained earnings have fallen from about $8.02 billion at September 2025 to about $5.08 billion at June 2026 — close to $3 billion of accumulated losses in three quarters.

---

## 3. THE OPERATING BUSINESSES — where the risk actually sits

The Benelux assets going into the spin are stabilising. VodafoneZiggo added 7,200 broadband customers, its best quarter in more than six years, plus 31,700 postpaid mobile customers, with fixed revenue per user up 0.6%. Telenet added 6,100 broadband and 2,200 postpaid customers. That matters: the asset being separated is improving into the event.

The problem is the asset **not** being separated. Virgin Media O2, the UK business Liberty owns half of alongside Telefónica, is deteriorating. Revenue fell 7.9% on a like-for-like basis; it lost 28,200 broadband and 63,000 postpaid customers in the quarter; full-year guidance is for revenue and earnings both to decline 3% to 5%, with adjusted free cash flow of only about £200 million against capital spending of £2.0–2.2 billion. Chief financial officer Charles Bracken acknowledged directly that "leverage is above our 4 to 5x target, and that credit spreads are currently elevated," adding that on refinancing "we acknowledge recent trading levels" — an admission the bonds have widened.

This is the honest reason the shares are at a 52-week low. The market is not disputing the Benelux plan; it is marking the UK stake toward zero and questioning whether it stays there.

---

## 4. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR — rebuilt from the balance sheet

The board entry's $9.50 floor does not survive contact with the tape. Here is what does, per share on roughly 341 million shares:

- **Corporate cash after the Vodafone purchase**, using management's own raised year-end 2026 target of about $2.0 billion: **$5.86**. Note carefully what this cash is for. Fries said the company will "end the year exactly where we started the year from a cash point of view" — the asset sales funded the acquisition of Vodafone's stake. This is a war chest that converts into an illiquid, leveraged telecom holding. It is not distributable to shareholders and there is no buyback supporting the stock.
- **Liberty Growth portfolio** at the appraised $2.9 billion: **$8.50**, with the top five holdings more than half the total. At a 50% haircut for the fact that appraisals are not bids: **$4.25**.
- **Operating telecoms at zero** in the adverse case.

That gives a defensible floor near **$8.00**, roughly 17% below the 27 July close — not the 2% the board entry implied when it was written. For cross-reference, tangible book value (equity less goodwill and other intangibles) is about $13.32 per share, and reported book value about $27.05, against a $9.59 stock.

**Red flags on the floor:** the cash is committed, not free; the portfolio marks are appraisals concentrated in five positions; consolidated net debt is $6.66 billion; free cash flow is currently negative; and there is no dividend or repurchase creating a bid. **Green flags:** the EdgeConneX realisation validated the marks at one large position, more than $4 billion has been refinanced across the credit silos this year, and a further €1.2–1.4 billion of Belgian and Dutch asset sales is under way to cut subsidiary debt, with a Wyre stake sale targeted for year-end 2026 or the first quarter of 2027.

---

## 5. SPONSOR CREDIBILITY

High, with one caveat. This management team has completed a separation of exactly this type before, and the result was good — Sunrise is worth roughly $12 per Liberty Global share to holders who received it. They have beaten their own cash-raising plan this year rather than missed it. They obtained every approval needed for the Dutch stake purchase. They named the incoming leadership. They pulled the timing forward rather than pushing it back. And they told shareholders that internal estimates of the synergies now exceed the $1 billion of net present value previously announced, while declining to publish the higher number — restraint rather than promotion.

The caveat: the equity story they are selling for Ziggo Group rests on 2028 targets, and the value they quote for it is prefaced with "up to". Fries framed the whole endeavour as "from an $18 stock when we announce the Sunrise spin off, we have a clear opportunity to create $37 to $40 of value" — a promotional figure that includes the already-distributed Sunrise shares. Read the parts, not the headline.

---

## 6. WHAT THE DIRECTOR MUST WEIGH

The asymmetry is genuinely attractive and the sponsor is genuinely credible. But the event is roughly eleven months away, carries no record date and no filing, and can be abandoned at the board's discretion — while the company burns cash, the UK stake deteriorates, and no repurchase supports the shares. Nothing forces the market's hand before a listing prospectus exists.

The single most important thing to weigh: **this is a good ratio attached to a slow, soft trigger, entered after the advertised floor already gave way.** The correct response to that is patience with named conditions, not size.

---

## 7. VERIFIED EVENT STATUS

A real, well-progressed, company-guided separation with credible sub-milestones already cleared — but no fixed date, no filing, no binding obligation, and a target window that begins about eleven months out. It is strengthening, not slipping. It is still soft. Re-checked 28 July 2026: no change, no new disclosure since 24 July 2026.
